## Suggested Reading Paths {#sec-vol2-about-reading-paths}

The chapters are ordered so that each can draw on everything before it, but not every chapter consumes the one immediately before it. A dependency map derived from the chapters' own cross-references records which chapters build directly on which (@fig-vol2-chapter-dependencies). An arrow in the map means the later chapter uses a model, mechanism, or constraint that the earlier one establishes. Two features of the map guide the choice of path. First, every chapter lies on a route to @sec-conclusion, whose six principles cite every chapter of Parts I through IV, so no chapter is a dead end. Second, several dependencies cross part boundaries: distributed training builds on both the storage pipeline of @sec-data-storage and the collectives of @sec-collective-communication, and fleet efficiency (@sec-performance-engineering) builds on @sec-fleet-orchestration. Consecutive chapters without an arrow mark a change of thread rather than a gap. @Sec-collective-communication, for example, builds on the fabric model of @sec-network-fabrics rather than on the storage chapter that precedes it.

Epoch AI's database of notable models records, for each training run it can document, the compute the run consumed together with how many accelerators it used and for how long [@epochai2026notable]. Plotted run by run, training compute climbs steadily on a logarithmic scale, and it separates early single-node vision models from multi-node transformer training (@fig-training-compute-trend, panel a). Because training compute is the product of the accelerator count, the training duration, and the rate each accelerator delivers, the same records also show where the growth came from. Across the `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.run_count_str` runs from 2012 through 2024 that report all three, compute grew about `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.compute_mult_str` per year. The accelerator count grew `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.count_mult_str` per year, the duration `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.duration_mult_str`, and the delivered rate per accelerator, which folds in both faster hardware and better utilization, `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.rate_mult_str` (@fig-training-compute-trend, panel b). A higher delivered rate per accelerator supplied roughly half of the exponential. More accelerators running for longer supplied the other `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.fleet_share_pct_str`, and that half is the fleet's to deliver.

title: The Scale Discontinuity
caption: **The Scale Discontinuity**: On a single machine (left), the usual binding constraint is the memory wall between the accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and there are no peers to wait for. In a fleet (right), nodes exchange state over a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places the job and recovers it, so the three C$^3$ roles appear as separate components. The fabric can become the binding network wall, and failed and slow nodes become routine events that hold back the whole job.
alt: Two panels. Left, labeled single machine: one node frame holding four dark accelerator squares above four stacks of HBM layers, each accelerator joined to its stack by a link that crosses a red dashed band labeled memory wall; text below reads no peers to wait for. Right, labeled fleet: a scheduler and recovery box above a dashed enclosure holding eight small node frames in two rows, each a miniature of the left node with four accelerators; all connect to a central network fabric bar that sits inside a red dashed band labeled network wall. One node is marked failed, one is marked slow with a dashed red border, and the other six are labeled waiting. A legend maps dark blue to compute C1, amber to communication C2, and violet to coordination C3.
section: Span bracket: AlexNet to Llama 3, the climb the prose names.
context:
:::

Moving from one machine to many changes the governing physics of the system, not merely its device count. A single node is bound locally by the memory wall between its accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and it has no peers to wait for. A fleet executes across a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places and recovers the job, which exposes the workload to the network wall, to stragglers, and to routine node failures (@fig-scale-moment-discontinuity).

Each band is labeled with its part number and a short functional name for that part, and each row lists what it holds beside the icon that marks it in the chapter margin stacks; the Reliability & Control row, for example, is where orchestration, scheduling, and recovery live. Capabilities decided in a lower band constrain the choices available in the bands above it. The same stack, shaded to show each chapter's focus, appears beside the Purpose of every chapter.

Rows from bottom: Facility and Accelerators, Fabric and Storage, Distributed Execution, Reliability and Control, Runtime and Serving, Operations, Assurance, and Governance and Sustainability; each row shows its name, a short list of what it holds, and a small line icon at its right end. Short upward arrows join each band to the one above it, and a long upward arrow on the left is labeled lower bands constrain upper ones.
context:
```

Inside one H100 server, NVLink moves tensors between accelerators at `{python} InfiniBandStackRecap.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str` in each direction per accelerator. Once a training job spans racks, the same tensors leave through an InfiniBand NDR port at `{python} InfiniBandStackRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` (`{python} InfiniBandStackRecap.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str`) in each direction, a bandwidth step down of roughly `{python} InfiniBandStackRecap.step_down_mult_str` for an accelerator served by one such port. That step illustrates a general pattern. The layered structure of an ML system persists across scale, while the physics at each layer changes. The **fleet stack**\index{Fleet Stack!definition} names the fleet's layers by grouping them into four bands, Infrastructure at the bottom, then Distribution, Serving, and Governance at the top, with two rows in each (@fig-fleet-stack). At the bottom, the hardware substrate of one node becomes the Infrastructure band, an RDMA fabric spanning racks. There the binding constraint can shift from the memory wall\index{Memory wall!intra-node bound} to the network wall as network congestion and message-passing latency consume a growing share of step time. One layer up, system software (a single CUDA runtime managing PCIe direct memory access (DMA)) becomes the Distribution band. This band holds the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and RDMA libraries that coordinate thousands of processes across the fabric, together with the schedulers that place distributed jobs and the recovery machinery that restarts them. Efficient data movement inside each node remains a prerequisite, because a fleet of underutilized nodes only multiplies the waste.

title: Retryable Tasks vs. Shared Training Steps
caption: **Retryable Tasks vs. Shared Training Steps**: Map tasks (left) deliver their outputs independently, so a failed task is re-run on its own while the others finish; its missing output delays only the reducers that need it. In synchronous data-parallel training (right), the AllReduce needs every worker's gradient before the shared update can proceed, so a slow worker on the critical path holds the whole step and the healthy workers wait. How much the step stretches depends on overlap and the other costs of the step.
alt: Two timelines with time running left to right. Left, MapReduce: map tasks 1 and 2 run, emit a green output square, and are labeled done; map task 3 runs briefly, is marked failed with a red cross, and then a re-run alone bar on the same lane emits its output, which feeds a reduce bar on the lane below. Right, synchronous training: workers 0 and 1 finish their compute bars early and then show gray wait segments, while worker 2 runs a long red dashed bar labeled slow; all three bars end at an amber AllReduce band, after which an update bar runs on the lane below.
section: Independent tasks vs. synchronous training steps {#sec-introduction-traditional-vs-ml-fleet-dynamics-c43e}
context:
:::

The two execution pathways differ at the point of failure (@fig-traditional-vs-ml-fleet). In MapReduce, a failed map task is retried on its own while its peers complete. In synchronous data-parallel training, every worker holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of each batch. Before the shared parameter update can occur, every worker must contribute its gradient to an AllReduce, a collective operation that combines the gradients of all workers and returns the result to each of them. A slow map task can delay downstream reduction and job completion, but other map tasks finish without waiting; in synchronous training, by contrast, healthy workers sit idle whenever a straggler delays the collective.

title: The Compute-Communication Timeline
caption: **The Compute-Communication Timeline**: Illustrative fractions show how exposed communication and synchronization can take a growing share of a training step as a fixed workload spreads across more devices. The fractions are assumed scenarios, not measurements or predictions for a particular model or cluster; they motivate measuring the critical path at each scale.
alt: Stacked horizontal bars for 8, 64, 512, and 4,096 GPUs, each split into blue compute, amber communication, and gray sync or idle segments labeled with percentages: 75, 25, 0; 45, 50, 5; 32, 58, 10; and 20, 65, 15. Thin connector lines and a pale amber band link the communication segments from bar to bar, showing compute shrinking and communication widening.
context:
:::

That share grows as a fixed workload spreads across more devices, because each worker's local computation shrinks while its gradient exchange does not. Across illustrative tiers from 8 to 4,096 GPUs, compute can fall from 75 percent of the step to 20 percent as communication widens (@fig-compute-comm-timeline). The fractions are assumed regimes rather than measurements. Gradient size, local batch size, partition topology, and overlap determine where the critical path actually lies, so it must be measured at each scale.

title: Model Training Compute Trends
caption: **Model Training Compute Trends**: Training compute of notable models published from 1950 through 2025, on a logarithmic axis, with one least-squares trend fitted to each era. Before 2010 the fitted rate is about `{python} ComputeTrendEras.early_mult_str` per year, close to Moore's law (a doubling about every 2 years); in the deep learning era it is about `{python} ComputeTrendEras.deep_mult_str` per year, far steeper. The fastest stretch was steeper still. Within the 2012--2019 frontier subset measured by an earlier study [@amodei2018ai], compute doubled approximately every 3.4 months. This trajectory explains why efficiency has become a strategic imperative rather than an optional optimization. Data from @epochai2026notable, licensed under CC BY 4.0; many values are Epoch AI estimates, and the era break at 2010 follows @sevilla2022.

A dashed fitted line rises slowly through the sparse early points and is labeled 1.5 times per year. ```

The growth trajectory establishes demand for larger fleets; empirical scaling laws guide how that demand should be allocated. At the budgets traced at the scale moment, estimating the return on additional resources is an engineering necessity rather than a research curiosity. Over the longer history of AI, the growth rate of training compute itself changed around 2010 [@sevilla2022]. A fit to Epoch AI's records of notable models gives growth of about `{python} ComputeTrendEras.early_mult_str` per year before 2010, close to Moore's law, and of about `{python} ComputeTrendEras.deep_mult_str` per year in the deep learning era (@fig-compute-trends). The scale moment already decomposed that rate into accelerator count, run duration, and delivered rate per accelerator (@fig-training-compute-trend, panel b). A demand curve that steep makes misallocation expensive, which is why the model-loss measurements that follow matter.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute Optimality
caption: **Scaling Laws and Compute Optimality**: Test loss predicted by the fitted law of Kaplan et al. for models from $10^3$ to $10^9$ parameters. (a) Larger models reach any given loss with fewer training tokens and settle at a lower plateau. (b) The same curves against training compute; the dashed line is their lower envelope, the lowest loss any model size reaches at each budget. Each model leaves the envelope long before it converges, so compute-efficient training stops far short of convergence. The curves are drawn from the published fit of loss against parameter count and training steps at the paper's default batch size, not from training logs, and begin where the fit's early-training term falls to 5 nats. After @kaplan2020scaling.
alt: Two stacked panels. Top: test loss against tokens processed on a log axis from about 10 to the 8 to 10 to the 11, with seven curves for models from 10 to the 3 to 10 to the 9 parameters, shaded light to dark blue by size; each curve falls and flattens, and larger models sit lower. Bottom: the same curves against compute in PF-days, shifted right with model size, with an orange dashed lower envelope labeled compute-efficient frontier and a note that each model leaves the frontier long before it converges.
context:
```

Two further results appear in Kaplan's fitted curves across parameter scales from $10^3$ to $10^9$ (@fig-kaplan-scaling). Larger models are more sample-efficient, reaching a target loss with substantially fewer training tokens. Compute-efficient training therefore stops far short of full convergence, because an early-stopped larger model attains the target loss with less total compute than a smaller model trained to its plateau.

title: Optimal Compute Allocation
caption: **Optimal Compute Allocation**: For a fixed computational budget, language-model loss depends on how the budget is divided between model size and training data. (a) IsoFLOP curves for nine budgets from `{python} ChinchillaFits.budget_lo_math` to `{python} ChinchillaFits.budget_hi_math` FLOPs, drawn from the paper's parametric loss fit; each valley marks the best model size for its budget, and the valleys move toward larger models as the budget grows. (b) Compute-optimal parameter and token counts from the paper's IsoFLOP analysis, projected to the Gopher budget, where they reach `{python} ChinchillaFits.gopher_params_str` parameters and `{python} ChinchillaFits.gopher_tokens_str` tokens. The two panels use different fitting methods from the same paper, so their optima do not coincide exactly. After @hoffmann2022chinchilla.
alt: Two stacked panels. Top: training loss against parameter count on a log axis, with nine U-shaped curves shaded light to dark blue for budgets from 6 times 10 to the 18 to 3 times 10 to the 21 FLOPs; a dot marks each valley, and a dotted orange line through the dots moves down and to the right, labeled optimum moves to larger models as budget grows. Bottom: log-log lines of optimal tokens (green, upper) and optimal parameters (blue, lower) against training compute from 10 to the 18 to 10 to the 25 FLOPs, with a dashed vertical line at the Gopher budget where dots mark 1.4T tokens and 63B parameters.
context:
Holding the budget fixed and varying model size traces a U-shaped IsoFLOP curve\index{IsoFLOP curve!optimal model size} of training loss against parameter count, whose valley marks the best model size for that FLOP budget (@fig-compute-optimal, panel a). As the budget grows, the valley moves toward larger models, and the optimal parameter count and the optimal number of training tokens rise along coordinated power laws (panel b), so compute-optimal training\index{Compute-optimal training!resource allocation} advances model size and token volume in tandem. Projected to a larger budget, the fits call for `{python} ChinchillaFits.gopher_params_str` parameters trained on `{python} ChinchillaFits.gopher_tokens_str` tokens, about `{python} ChinchillaFits.projection_flops_math` FLOPs in total,[^fn-flops-work-rate] which is how compute-optimal frontiers guide resource allocation before cluster execution begins.

[^fn-flops-work-rate]: **FLOPs vs. FLOP/s**\index{FLOP/s vs. FLOPs}: FLOPs denotes total computational work (operations performed), while FLOP/s denotes hardware throughput (operations per second)\index{FLOP/s!work vs. throughput}; confusing the two leads to incorrect cost estimates. GPT-3 required `{python} Gpt3StatsScenario.gpt3_training_ops_str` of work; an A100 delivers `{python} Gpt3StatsScenario.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` of throughput. Dividing work by peak throughput gives ideal wall-clock time, the roughly `{python} Gpt3SingleAccelerator.ideal_years_str` years on one A100 computed at the scale moment. Actual time is approximately $\text{work}/(\EfficiencyHw \PeakRate)$, where the hardware utilization $\EfficiencyHw$ is the achieved fraction of peak throughput, so utilization below one multiplies ideal time by $1/\EfficiencyHw$.

title: Loss vs. Dataset Size across Model Scales
caption: **Loss vs. Dataset Size across Model Scales**: Test loss curves show how models of different sizes (393.2K to 708M parameters) benefit from increased training data. Larger models achieve lower loss, but all curves exhibit diminishing returns at high token counts. Points and curves are digitized from Figure 4 (left) of @kaplan2020scaling, so values carry the precision of a reading from the published plot.
alt: Log-scale scatter plot of loss vs. tokens in dataset. Six curves for model sizes from 393.2K to 708M parameters, shaded from light to dark blue by model size and labeled at their right ends; the three largest also use square, diamond, and triangle markers. Italic labels mark small models: capacity plateau between the two flattest curves, shared power-law descent along the line the larger curves follow together, and large models: lower floor, set under the lowest curve where it levels off below all the others.
context:
Those plateaus show why buying more accelerators for a project whose dataset is already exhausted wastes hardware on overfitting, whereas collecting more tokens for a project whose cluster cannot train a larger model strands data in storage. Applying scaling laws in practice is therefore a scarcity diagnosis that asks which resource prevents balanced growth first. Compute budget, data availability, and model size create three regimes with different optimal responses.

In a compute-limited regime\index{Compute-limited regime!resource allocation}, compute scarcity restricts scaling potential despite abundant training data; measured learning curves guide the allocation between model size and training tokens within that budget. In a data-limited regime\index{Data!limited regime}, computational resources exceed what the available dataset can support, meaning that increasing model size is useful only if validation measurements show that the available data can support additional capacity. Between these extremes lies the optimal regime\index{Optimal regime!Chinchilla frontier}, where compute and data grow in balance following compute-optimal scaling laws, as DeepMind demonstrated with Chinchilla by outperforming much larger models through proportional scaling of model size and training data [@hoffmann2022chinchilla]. Recognizing which regime governs a given project prevents common inefficiencies: over-parameterized models with insufficient training data, or under-parameterized models that waste available compute. For the fleet, the diagnosis decides where the next investment goes. A compute-limited project needs accelerator-hours, while a data-limited one gains more from the storage and data pipelines of @sec-data-storage than from additional accelerators.

For a single component, `{python} ReliabilityGap.four_nines_pct_str` availability corresponds to `{python} ReliabilityGap.four_nines_downtime_str` of unavailability per 365-day year. This is a time fraction, not a count of failures. If each node has an illustrative `{python} ReliabilityGap.node_availability_str` availability and an unreplicated job requires every node, the probability that all `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_small_str` required nodes are available simultaneously is only `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_1k_str`. Scale that job to `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_large_str` required nodes, and this probability drops to `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_10k_str`. Adding a nine to every node only postpones the collapse, because the exponent $\RequiredComponentCount$ eventually overwhelms any per-node availability below one (@fig-reliability-gap-collapse).

title: The C$^3$ Intersection Landscape
caption: **The C$^3$ Intersection Landscape**: Each circle is one operational dimension (Compute, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1$, the node substrate; Communication, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2$, the network backbone; Coordination, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$, the orchestration layer), labeled with the Fleet Law term it contributes to step time. Each pairwise lens names the interaction between two dimensions: hiding network latency behind computation, preserving training progress against failure, and synchronizing collectives. At the center, where all three meet, is fleet ML systems engineering. The techniques and chapters for each region are collected in @tbl-c3-intersections.
alt: Three overlapping circles labeled Compute C1 (node substrate, T compute over N), Communication C2 (network backbone, T comm of N), and Coordination C3 (orchestration layer, T sync of N). The pairwise overlaps are labeled hiding network latency (C1 and C2), preserving progress against failure (C1 and C3), and collective synchronization (C2 and C3). A box at the center, where all three overlap, reads fleet ML systems engineering.
context:
The dimensions interact at their pairwise intersections\index{C³ taxonomy!pairwise intersections}, where an intervention along one axis alters costs across another. At the intersection of compute and communication ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2$), overlapping transfers with arithmetic can hide network latency, but only while independent computation remains available. Between compute and coordination ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$), checkpointing preserves training progress against failure, yet it consumes execution resources; its frequency and placement trade present overhead against future recovery loss. Across communication and coordination ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$), collective synchronization depends jointly on transfer completion and participant readiness, so faster physical links alone cannot eliminate straggler waiting.

At the center ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$), all three constraints converge simultaneously. Partitioning a model determines both which device computes each operation and what information must cross the network; recovering a failed partition requires restoring the corresponding shared state. These dependencies explain why parallelism, state sharding, and serving policies must be designed together. Each dimension contributes one term to the distributed step time, and each pairwise overlap names an interface where the dimensions trade costs by hiding latency, preserving progress against failure, and synchronizing collectives (@fig-c3-taxonomy).

title: Anatomy of a Fleet Law Step
caption: **Anatomy of a Fleet Law Step**: Each row is one training step for the same workload, with local computation on the upper lane and communication and synchronization on the lower lane. Read the step length from the bracket, not from any single bar: overlap (gray band) removes only the transfer time that runs beneath compute, so doubling the devices halves $\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount$ yet leaves $\DistributedStepTime(2\DeviceCount)$ well past the ideal half-length step (dashed line), by the hatched span. Bar lengths are illustrative, not measured.
alt: Two timelines. Top, N devices: a long blue compute bar, and on a second lane an amber communication bar that starts under the end of the compute bar, followed by a violet synchronization bar; a gray band marks where the two bars overlap, and a bracket spans the whole step, with a tick at its midpoint. Bottom, 2N devices: a compute bar half as long, a slightly longer communication bar, a longer synchronization bar, and a shorter bracket. A dashed line drops from the midpoint tick, marking half the original step, and the part of the 2N step to the right of it is hatched and labeled beyond ideal.
context:
*   $\OverlappedTime$ is the Co-Design ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2$, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$) term, representing communication or coordination hidden behind useful compute via techniques such as interleaving forward and backward work across pipeline stages, running transfers on separate execution streams, and writing checkpoints asynchronously.

Doubling the device count shows why the subtraction matters. The local compute term falls to $\IronLawComputeTime/(2\DeviceCount)$, but communication and barrier synchronization persist, and the shorter compute window leaves less room to hide transfers, so $\OverlappedTime$ shrinks as well. The step on $2\DeviceCount$ devices therefore takes well over half as long as the step on $\DeviceCount$ (@fig-fleet-law-step).

## The Structure of This Textbook {#sec-vol2-introduction-structure}

Meeting those three fleet challenges requires climbing the fleet stack\index{Fleet Stack!textbook structure} in dependency order, because choices fixed in the physical substrate constrain every algorithm, runtime, and governance control built above it. The chapter sequence is therefore a dependency map rather than a topic inventory. Silicon, cooling, and network limits constrain training partitioning; partitioned algorithms create fault-tolerance and orchestration obligations; and those mechanisms support production operation. Requirements also flow in the other direction: security, governance, and service targets constrain which lower-layer designs are acceptable. Part I builds the physical cluster substrate, Part II coordinates distributed execution and fault recovery, Part III runs the fleet in production, from efficiency and serving through edge deployment and operations, and Part IV enforces governance, security, and sustainability invariants (@fig-vol2-roadmap).

title: The Four Infrastructure Walls
caption: **The Four Infrastructure Walls**: Read left to right, the examples illustrate four constraints at increasing physical scales; the workload and configuration determine which one binds. The node compares 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 with about 2,000 TFLOP/s of FP8 arithmetic; the four-node DGX H100 rack draws 33.5 kW; the pod compares per-direction NVLink bandwidth with one InfiniBand port, a ninefold budget gap; and the fleet assumes independent GPU failures, reducing a 50,000-hour per-GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) to about 2 hours between failures at 25K GPUs.
alt: An arrow runs from smaller to larger physical scale above four columns. Each column first draws its scale level as parts: a node chassis with 8 GPUs, a rack holding four nodes (32 GPUs), a pod of 32 racks (1,024 GPUs), and a fleet of many pods drawn as plain tiles (10K to 25K GPUs). Below each, a wall panel draws its constraint. Memory wall: a narrow HBM pipe feeds a large FP8 arithmetic block, labeled 3.35 TB/s of HBM feeding about 2,000 TFLOP/s. Power wall: two bars to scale, a traditional rack reaching a gray dashed line labeled 12 kW and a taller DGX H100 bar, labeled 33.5 kW per rack, nearly 3 times a 12 kW rack. Communication wall: a thick NVLink bar above a link one ninth as thick for InfiniBand, labeled 450 to 50 GB/s, a 9 times cliff. Reliability wall: on a log time axis from 1 hour to 10,000 hours, a long gray bar for one GPU and a short red bar for 25K GPUs, labeled MTBF about 2 hours at 25K, from 50,000 hours per GPU.

title: The Accelerator Spectrum
caption: **The Accelerator Spectrum**: Each die is drawn as a grid of 100 cells divided between arithmetic units (dark) and control, cache, and other logic (light), with the medium cells marking the spread of each approximate, illustrative share. Read left to right, the arithmetic share grows from 5 to 10 percent on a CPU to over 90 percent on a custom ASIC, because hardwired dataflow replaces instruction fetch, decode, and scheduling; each step buys throughput per watt by narrowing the range of model architectures the silicon runs well.
alt: Four square dies side by side, CPU, GPU, TPU, and custom ASIC, above an arrow running from general purpose to more specialized. Each die is a 10 by 10 grid of cells: dark cells for arithmetic units, medium cells for the range of estimates, and light cells for control, cache, and other logic. The dark share grows from left to right, labeled 5 to 10 percent for the CPU, 50 to 60 percent for the GPU, 70 to 80 percent for the TPU, and over 90 percent for the custom ASIC. A legend directly under the dies names the three cell types, and the arrow closes the figure below it.
context:
Specialized accelerators reduce this tax by replacing general-purpose control with a dataflow matched to the workload. In the approximate shares of @fig-accelerator-spectrum, the arithmetic fraction of the die rises from roughly 5--10 percent on a CPU to 50--60 percent on a GPU, 70--80 percent on a Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), and over 90 percent on a custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). The shares mark a direction rather than measured proportions for any product. The selection question is how much of the complete workload can use the specialized hardware.

:::

title: Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE) Architecture
caption: **Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE) Architecture**: A DGX H100 node (left) joins eight separately packaged GPUs through an NVSwitch fabric and must leave the chassis over InfiniBand to reach other nodes, so every exchange crosses a package, board, or network boundary. A WSE (right) instead uses most of a 300 mm wafer as one routed mesh of cores, each with local SRAM; defect-aware routing steers traffic around unusable cores, and the on-wafer mesh replaces off-package transfers for mapped operations. The WSE-3 figures are the vendor's reported totals and are not directly comparable to GPU HBM bandwidth.
alt: Two panels. Left: a DGX H100 node with eight GPU boxes labeled 80 GB, four above and four below a horizontal NVSwitch bar labeled 450 GB/s per GPU each way; an arrow labeled InfiniBand NDR, 50 GB/s per port, leads from the node to a dashed box labeled other nodes. Right: a circular wafer filled with a grid of small core squares joined by mesh links; one core is marked defective with a red X and a highlighted route bends around it. A legend identifies the core, the defective core, and the route, and a note reads WSE-3: 900,000 cores and 44 GB of SRAM, 21 PB/s aggregate SRAM bandwidth.
section: │       configuration, not the CS-3 registry TDP, so it stays a cited literal.
context:
For its 2024 WSE-3 configuration, Cerebras reported `{python} WaferScaleSpecs.core_count_str` AI-optimized cores, `{python} WaferScaleSpecs.sram_gb_str` of distributed on-chip SRAM, and `{python} WaferScaleSpecs.mem_bw_pb_per_s_str` of aggregate memory bandwidth in its registration filing [@cerebras2024s1]. These specifications are not directly comparable to GPU-cluster peak FLOP/s or high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth because the architectures expose different dataflows, memory organizations, precisions, and workload mappings. The durable comparison is topological: on-wafer links avoid package-, board-, and rack-level transfers for work that maps onto the fabric.

A multi-GPU chassis and a wafer-scale engine draw their package and board boundaries in different places (@fig-wafer-scale-engine). The eight GPUs of a chassis exchange state through NVSwitch, and transfers to other nodes cross the external network. A wafer-scale engine instead routes between `{python} WaferScaleSpecs.core_count_str` on-wafer cores on the 300 mm wafer\index{Wafer-scale integration!physical constraints}. Defect-aware routing\index{Wafer-scale integration!defect tolerance} lets the fabric use working regions despite local manufacturing flaws. In the documented CS-2 configuration, twelve power supplies in a 9+3 redundant arrangement could deliver up to 23 kW to the WSE-2 [@Cerebras2021]. That configuration-specific design illustrates why wafer-scale power delivery and cooling require system-level liquid-cooling hardware rather than a conventional accelerator heatsink.

title: Compute, Bandwidth, and Power Scale at Three Different Rates
caption: **Compute, Bandwidth, and Power Scale at Three Different Rates**: Dense FP16 Tensor throughput, memory bandwidth, and thermal design power for NVIDIA data center accelerators, normalized to the V100 on a log scale, where the shaded gap between the compute and bandwidth lines is the growth in arithmetic intensity a kernel needs to stay compute-bound. Compute rises 18$\times$, bandwidth 8.9$\times$, and TDP 3.3$\times$, so the endpoint gains in arithmetic exceed the gains in memory bandwidth and power allowance. These are peak specifications, not measured application throughput. Specifications come from the MLSysIM hardware registry.
alt: Line chart on a logarithmic growth axis with points placed at their release years, V100 (2017), A100 (2020), H100 (2022), and B200 (2024), so each slope is a growth rate per year. Series are labeled directly at their right ends: dense FP16 Tensor throughput reaching 18 times, memory bandwidth 8.9 times, and dashed thermal design power 3.3 times. The region between the throughput and bandwidth lines is shaded and widens after the A100; a leader into it reads about 2 times FLOP per byte.
context:
Each generation thus targeted the bottleneck its predecessor exposed. Volta added dedicated matrix hardware, Ampere widened mixed-precision support, Hopper added FP8 for Transformer workloads, and Blackwell worked around the die-size limit with two dies in one package. Because architects choose those targets by profiling the workloads of their era, accelerator design follows model architecture, which is why Transformer workloads have shaped accelerator design since 2017.

Because accelerator generations turn over faster than the facility that houses them, a data center must anticipate refresh cycles before the first rack arrives. Those generations also changed interconnect capacity and power (@tbl-gpu-evolution). From V100 to B200, dense FP16 throughput rose 18$\times$, memory bandwidth 8.9$\times$, and thermal design power (TDP) 3.3$\times$ (@fig-gpu-scaling-trends). These are growth multiples over the whole span, not annual rates, and their ratios carry the planning lesson. Each byte delivered from memory must now feed about twice as many operations, and each watt of the power allowance supplies more than five times as many peak operations. The first ratio changes which workloads can approach peak throughput; the second, multiplied by device count, sets the proposed rack load. A facility refreshed only for compute density therefore outruns both its memory delivery and its cooling envelope.

title: Accelerator Memory Tiers
caption: **Accelerator Memory Tiers**: Peak memory bandwidth and capacity separate local-SRAM designs (solid stars), HBM accelerators (half-tone filled circles), and edge and shared-LPDDR devices (hollow squares); all three are memory, so they share one hue and differ by marker. The dotted arrow marks the design trade-off: moving data closer to compute raises bandwidth but reduces capacity.
alt: Log-log scatter plot of memory capacity vs. peak memory bandwidth. All markers use one blue memory hue, and a shaded region encloses each cluster in three clearly stepped tints, darkest for the tier nearest compute: solid stars for local-SRAM designs at low capacity and very high bandwidth, with the outlying WSE-3 wafer in its own small region near 44 GB, half-tone filled circles for HBM accelerators at tens to hundreds of gigabytes and lower bandwidth, and hollow squares for edge and shared-LPDDR devices at the lowest bandwidth. A dotted arrow points from the HBM cluster toward the SRAM cluster, labeled closer to compute: more bandwidth, less capacity.
context:
The implications are concrete in our running example. Our `{python} InfraSetup.frontier_params_b_str` model's weights occupy `{python} MemoryBandwidthIntroRecap.weights_fp16_gb_str` in FP16. In dense autoregressive decode at batch size 1, each generated token uses all of those weights, whose footprint far exceeds on-chip storage, so every token must stream them in from memory. Suppose, hypothetically, that one H100 could hold them. Streaming the whole `{python} MemoryBandwidthIntroRecap.weights_fp16_gb_str` through that device's HBM at about `{python} MemoryBandwidthIntroRecap.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` takes over 100 ms per token, long enough to be a perceptible pause between generated words. No real H100 holds the model, so the figure is a floor on bandwidth demand rather than a prediction of deployed latency, but it shows that the memory wall is a delay a user can notice, not an abstract architectural ratio.

Three levers lower that floor. Sharding spreads the weights across more memory paths, so each path streams fewer bytes. Quantization shrinks the bytes themselves. Reuse lets each fetched byte feed more arithmetic, which HBM's bandwidth and on-chip tiling make possible. The Roofline Model, recapped for one machine in @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-roofline, tests whether the resulting data supply can feed the arithmetic units. Its ridge point, peak arithmetic divided by memory bandwidth, is the number of operations a kernel must perform per byte fetched before arithmetic rather than memory becomes the limit. The ridge point recurs throughout the analysis below, and @sec-compute-roofline evaluates it for the H100. Where each architecture places its bytes sets how much bandwidth those levers can draw on (@fig-accelerator-memory-tier-map), because moving the active working set closer to arithmetic increases available bandwidth while reducing the capacity that can reside there.

title: HBM 3D-Stacked Architecture
caption: **HBM 3D-Stacked Architecture**: Left: high-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies on a base logic die, links them vertically with through-silicon vias (TSVs), and places the stack on a silicon interposer beside the GPU die, so each stack reaches the GPU over a 1,024-bit interface only millimeters long. Right: DDR5 instead sits on a DIMM across the motherboard, reached over a 64-bit channel through centimeters of board trace. The wider, shorter path raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit, but HBM bandwidth and capacity remain finite, so the memory wall moves rather than disappears.
alt: Two cross-section panels. Left, HBM stacked beside the die: a GPU die and a stack of eight DRAM dies on a base logic die sit side by side on a silicon interposer above the package substrate, with dashed vertical TSVs through the stack and a thick short link through the interposer labeled 1,024 bits wide, millimeters long. Right, DDR5 across the board: a CPU with its memory controller and a DIMM holding several DRAM chips stand on a motherboard, joined by a thin trace through the board labeled 64 bits wide, centimeters long.
context:
The physical distance from the DIMM slot to the processor die is measured in centimeters, and every centimeter of copper trace introduces capacitance, signal attenuation, and energy loss. At DDR5 data rates (4,800--6,400 MT/s per pin), the signal conditioning circuits must compensate for significant channel impairment, consuming substantial power per bit transferred. Increasing the data rate on these long traces requires progressively more power for signal conditioning, creating a diminishing-returns curve that DDR5 is already approaching.

HBM sidesteps that board-level degradation through 2.5D integration (@fig-hbm-architecture). Instead of driving signals horizontally across centimeters of motherboard trace over a narrow 64-bit bus, it stacks DRAM dies vertically and places the stack beside the processor on a silicon interposer.

title: The H100 Roofline Landscape
caption: **The H100 Roofline Landscape**: Attainable FP16 throughput is the lower of two ceilings, the memory-bandwidth slope (blue) and the compute roof (orange), which meet at the dashed ridge point. Each dot places a representative workload by its arithmetic intensity; workloads left of the ridge stay capped by bandwidth however much compute the chip offers, and only those to its right can approach peak throughput.
alt: Log-log roofline plot for H100 FP16 showing memory-bound and compute-bound regions with five ML workloads from LLM decode at the low-intensity left edge to LLM training on the compute roof.
context:
A measured workload point below its roofline ceiling needs further diagnosis. Dependencies, insufficient parallel work, irregular accesses, synchronization, and power limits can all prevent a kernel from approaching that ceiling. The gap identifies a question for profiling; it does not establish that software optimization can recover the entire difference.

Whole phases spread even wider than individual operators. The idealized intensities of decode and training differ by `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.train_gap_mult_str`, which is why the same hardware shows widely different utilization across them. Batch-1 decode sits near `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.decode_intensity_str`, far left of the ridge and deeply bound by memory bandwidth, while large-batch training near `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.train_intensity_str` crosses the ridge and reaches the compute roof (@fig-roofline-landscape). The training point assumes that `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.training_batch_size_str` tokens on one accelerator share each weight read, the local reuse that a large global batch alone does not guarantee, so it counts tokens rather than sequences and local rather than global batch. It is a contrast case, not a universal intensity for training. Actual placement requires counting bytes at the memory level being modeled and accounting for tensor shapes, fusion, and reuse.

title: Two Fabrics inside One Eight-GPU Node
caption: **Two Fabrics inside One Eight-GPU Node**: NVSwitch joins all eight GPUs for GPU-to-GPU traffic, but every path to host memory, storage, or the network runs through a PCIe tree rooted at one of two CPU sockets. A GPU, its InfiniBand host channel adapter (HCA), and the host DRAM it reaches most cheaply therefore sit in one non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domain, and a transfer to the other socket's DRAM also crosses the socket link. The two PCIe switches per socket are schematic; switch count and lane routing vary by server design.
alt: Two dashed frames side by side, labeled NUMA domain 0 and NUMA domain 1. Each frame holds a Host DRAM box joined to a CPU box labeled PCIe root complex; a short link joins CPU 0 to CPU 1 across the gap, labeled socket link, remote host-DRAM access crosses here. Under each CPU, thin lines branch to two PCIe switch boxes, and each switch connects to two blue GPU boxes and two amber HCA boxes, numbered G0 to G7 and N0 to N7. A wide amber bar labeled NVSwitch fabric, NVLink among all eight GPUs, regardless of socket, spans both frames below the GPUs, and each GPU connects down to it with a thick line. A legend distinguishes thick NVLink lines from thin PCIe x16 lines.
context:
A standard DGX H100 node features two host CPUs, each managing a PCIe root complex\index{PCIe!root complex contention}, and PCIe switches fan those lanes out. Each of the `{python} BandwidthHierarchyPcieRecap.gpus_per_node_str` GPUs and each of the `{python} BandwidthHierarchyPcieRecap.nics_per_node_str` InfiniBand host channel adapters (HCAs, the network interface cards of an InfiniBand fabric) has its own x16 link (@fig-node-pcie-numa). This configuration provides an aggregate theoretical bandwidth of about `{python} BandwidthHierarchyPcieRecap.node_pcie_aggregate_tb_per_s_str` within the chassis. However, this bandwidth is shared among competing traffic streams. During a single training step, the PCIe bus simultaneously carries host-to-GPU data batches, GPU-to-HCA gradient shards for inter-node AllReduce (via GPUDirect remote direct memory access (RDMA)), and periodic CPU-to-NVMe checkpoint writes. Contention between these streams can cause unexpected pipeline stalls, particularly when gradient synchronization saturates the links typically used for data loading.

The dual-CPU architecture introduces significant non-uniform memory access (NUMA)\index{NUMA!GPU data loading} effects. The 8 GPUs are physically partitioned, with 4 connected to CPU 0's root complex and 4 to CPU 1's. A GPU connected to CPU 0 can reach CPU 0's DRAM through its local PCIe root complex, whereas access to CPU 1's DRAM also traverses the inter-socket link. The latency and bandwidth penalty depends on the processor, socket interconnect, PCIe topology, transfer size, and concurrent traffic, so no fixed percentage applies across nodes. Data-loading pipelines should measure this topology and place worker processes, pinned buffers, NICs, and target GPUs within the same NUMA domain when the local path improves sustained ingestion. Placement is therefore part of the parallelism strategy, because a scheduler that ignores PCIe roots, NIC locality, and NUMA domains can turn an otherwise valid tensor- or pipeline-parallel plan into a host-bound bottleneck.

title: Intra-node GPU Topology Comparison
caption: **Intra-node GPU Topology Comparison**: Three ways to wire eight GPUs inside one node. Left: a ring gives each GPU only two links, so traffic between distant GPUs passes through up to four hops. Center: a full mesh reaches every peer in one hop but needs $\AcceleratorsPerNode-1$ links per GPU and $\AcceleratorsPerNode(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1)/2$ links in total, which becomes impractical to route beyond about eight GPUs. Right: an NVSwitch fabric gives each GPU one set of links to the switch and puts every pair one switch hop apart, with up to 450 GB/s per direction per H100 SXM GPU (900 GB/s bidirectional); that per-GPU injection bandwidth is not the aggregate bisection bandwidth of the switch fabric.
alt: Three panels of eight GPUs labeled G0 to G7, each highlighting the path from G0 to G4 in a thick line. Left, Ring: the GPUs sit on a circle linked only to neighbors; the highlighted arc passes G1, G2, and G3, with its links numbered 1 to 4; the footer reads G0 to G4: 4 hops, 2 links per GPU. Center, Full mesh: a faint link joins every pair and the direct G0 to G4 link is highlighted; the footer reads G0 to G4: 1 hop, 7 links per GPU, 28 links in all. Right, NVSwitch: four GPUs above and four below a horizontal NVSwitch fabric bar, each joined to it by one link, with the G0 and G4 links highlighted; the footer reads G0 to G4: 1 switch hop, 1 set of links per GPU.
context:
Given the bandwidth hierarchy, the node must connect 8 accelerators with enough bandwidth for tensor-parallel operations across their private memories. A switched fabric can provide full bisection bandwidth, enough capacity across any equal division of the endpoints to carry their full injection rate. Comparing a ring, a mesh, and a switched design shows what connectivity costs and which communication patterns it supports.

Eight GPUs in one chassis can be wired as a ring, a full mesh, or a switched fabric (@fig-node-topology-comparison). A ring\index{Network topology!ring} is inexpensive, needing only $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ links for $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ GPUs, and suits ring-AllReduce, in which each GPU sends to one neighbor while receiving from the other so that every link stays busy. Tensor parallelism, however, issues frequent collectives after sharded matrix operations. These include ReduceScatter, which leaves each participant with one shard of a combined result, and AllGather, which assembles shards at every participant. A ring's fixed multi-hop paths (up to four hops between distant GPUs) constrain those patterns. A full mesh\index{Network topology!full mesh} reaches every peer in one hop but needs $\AcceleratorsPerNode(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1) / 2 = 28$ links for 8 GPUs, a count that grows quadratically and soon becomes impractical to route. The NVSwitch\index{NVSwitch!non-blocking fabric} crossbar\index{Crossbar switch}\index{NVSwitch!crossbar topology} puts every pair one switch hop apart and provides full-bisection switched connectivity with a manageable number of switch chips.

title: The Power Delivery Path
caption: **The Power Delivery Path**: Energy passes through five conversion stages between the medium-voltage grid and the sub-volt supply at the GPU die, and each stage loses a few percent as heat; the band's height is drawn proportional to the power it carries. The per-stage losses shown are illustrative round values, not measurements of a particular facility; compounded, they lose about a fifth of the power, so delivering 1 MW to the dies draws about 1.3 MW before cooling. PUE uses an IT-equipment boundary and includes facility conversion losses as well as cooling; these losses must not be counted twice. The critical engineering challenge is the rack power distribution unit (PDU) to voltage regulator module (VRM) transition, where 10--40 kW of power must be delivered within a single cabinet.

The band starts about 1.3 MW tall and ends at 1 MW, and at each stage a thin orange strip peels off downward as heat, labeled about 5, 3, 3, 5, and 8 percent. A dark bracket and a pale tinted region mark the span from the rack PDU through the VRM, labeled inside each cabinet, 10 to 40 kW per rack.

The propagation is visible at both ends of the stack in published data. Vendors publish a power rating for each accelerator package, and @fig-chip-vs-cluster-power (a) collects those ratings across `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.chip_count_str` NVIDIA, Google, AMD, and Intel parts. The ratings follow each vendor's own convention (TDP, maximum board power, or maximum TGP), so they bound design envelopes rather than measure consumption, but they climb steadily from one generation to the next. Panel (b) plots the facility power of supercomputers that Epoch AI tracks for AI work, together with the largest one operating at each date [@epochai2026supercomputers; @pilz2025supercomputers]. From 2013 through 2021 that record stayed between `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.plateau_low_power_str` and `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.plateau_power_str`, a level set by national high-performance computing systems. The Frontier supercomputer raised it to `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.frontier_power_str` in `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.break_year_str`, and AI training clusters then lifted it to about `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.sys_last_power_str` by `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.end_year_str`, a `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.sys_growth_mult_str` increase in three years. Over the same three years the rating of one package rose from the H100's `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.h100_tdp_str` TDP to the `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.chip_last_label_str`'s `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.chip_last_power_str` maximum TGP, roughly a `{python} ChipVersusSystemPower.chip_growth_mult_str` increase across the two rating conventions. Hotter packages explain only a small part of the jump. The rest comes from the number of accelerators a single system joins together and the facility built to feed them, which is why the power wall at fleet scale is a provisioning problem for the building as much as a thermal problem for the chip.

title: Air and Liquid Heat Paths
caption: **Air and Liquid Heat Paths**: Air transfers chip heat through a heat sink and moving air; direct-to-chip liquid cooling transfers it through a cold plate and coolant. Both require heat rejection. Capacity, parasitic energy, and water use depend on the engineered system rather than the cooling medium alone.
alt: Two side-by-side cross sections above a shared heat rejection box, separated from it by a dashed line between server and rack and facility. Air: a thin supply line rises from heat rejection and feeds cool air arrows through a finned heat sink on a chip; the warm air leaving it collects into one line that runs down to heat rejection. Direct-to-chip liquid: a cool supply tube rises from heat rejection to a cold plate on the chip, and a warm return tube carries heat back down to heat rejection.
context:
: **Cooling Architecture Trade-Offs**: Feasible rack density follows from the particular equipment and facility design. The example design points differ by `{python} CoolingDesignPoints.density_ratio_mult_str` in rack power, yet there is no universal rack-power threshold or PUE that separates air and liquid cooling. Compare qualified operating envelopes and total facility energy. {#tbl-cooling-limits}

Direct-to-chip liquid cooling supports higher heat flux than forced air because cold plates route chip heat directly into circulating fluid with high volumetric heat capacity before reaching facility heat rejection, whereas air systems rely on convective dissipation across finned heat sinks (@fig-cooling-comparison). Ambient wet-bulb temperature (the lowest temperature that evaporation can bring outdoor air to, which bounds evaporative heat rejection) and rack power density determine whether an air, liquid, or hybrid loop satisfies the chip junction temperature envelope.

title: Historical Network Bandwidth Scaling
caption: **Historical Network Bandwidth Scaling**: Intra-node NVLink, inter-node InfiniBand and Ethernet, and the PCIe host bus, plotted per direction on a common log scale by the year each generation first shipped, 2010 to 2025. The aggregate NVLink budget exceeds the external-port budgets in these configurations; collective completion time also depends on payloads, provisioning, routing, and overlap. Rates and first-product years from IEEE 802.3, InfiniBand Trade Association, PCI-SIG, and NVIDIA specifications and product announcements.

caption: **The Bandwidth Cliff in a Training Step**: Illustrative timelines on a common millisecond axis for the same compute phases: an 8-GPU intra-node job (top) with an assumed 1 ms AllReduce, and a 64-GPU inter-node job (bottom) with an assumed 30 ms AllReduce. These durations illustrate an exposed communication cost rather than predict a particular fabric. The AllReduce phase (red) grows from a thin sliver to a larger share of the step. Without overlap, model computation waits during AllReduce. The compute phases occupy 99.5 percent and 87 percent of these illustrative schedules, a gap of 12.5 percentage points; these shares are not arithmetic utilization measurements.
alt: Two illustrative horizontal Gantt rows drawn to scale on a shared time axis marked 0, 100, 200, and 230, labeled Time (ms). The top row, labeled Intra-node, 8 GPUs, NVLink, and 99.5% compute, shows Forward (100 ms) and Backward (100 ms) blocks followed by a thin red AllReduce (1 ms) sliver. The bottom row, labeled Inter-node, 64 GPUs, IB, and 87% compute, shows the same Forward and Backward blocks followed by a wider red AllReduce (30 ms) block, with a red brace beneath it labeled 30 ms idle per step.
context:
Which traffic must cross that gap depends on how the job is partitioned. The same hierarchy keeps tensor parallelism, with its per-layer exchanges, inside the NVLink domain and lets pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas span nodes, the combination called 3D parallelism whose schedules are developed in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-hybrid-parallelism-3d-loop. The fabric adds one lever to that placement. Each data-parallel replica can sum gradients over several microbatches before an exchange (gradient accumulation\index{Gradient accumulation!communication frequency}), reducing how often it must cross the node boundary at the cost of changing the batch and update schedule.

Exposed communication leaves gaps between dependent compute phases. Two assumed training schedules on a common 230 ms axis, each containing 100 ms forward and backward compute phases, make that cost visible (@fig-bandwidth-cliff-gantt). The 8-GPU intra-node case assumes a 1 ms AllReduce and spends 99.5 percent of the step in those compute phases; the 64-GPU inter-node case assumes a 30 ms AllReduce and spends 87 percent in computation. The two AllReduce durations are illustrative inputs chosen to show the effect, not values derived from the link rates above, and the percentages are shares of the schedule rather than measured arithmetic utilization.

L2, transport: RDMA, RoCEv2, GPUDirect, alpha-beta cost model. L3, switch and topology: fat-tree, rail-optimized, dragonfly, torus. L4, fabric behavior: PFC, ECN and DCQCN, incast, adaptive routing. L5, cluster design: pod integration, job placement, failure domains. Beside each band a small schematic shows the level's concrete form: L1, a four-level stepped waveform between two transceivers labeled SerDes; L2, a GPU and its NIC, both labeled, sending to a remote NIC and GPU; L3, two switches linked to all four switches below them; L4, three converging inputs feeding a nearly full queue, with a dashed red arrow labeled PAUSE leaving the queue and pointing back over the inputs; L5, a row of six racks joined by a common bar.
context:
### The five-level model {#sec-network-fabrics-five-level-model}

Provisioning fast NICs or buying a non-blocking switch tier in isolation routinely fails to speed up training: a 400 Gb/s link still stalls if host TCP copies starve the PCIe bus, an unaligned rack layout exhausts the copper link budget, or static ECMP hashing piles two elephant flows onto one spine port. Tracing why a collective slows down requires following the packet across five coupled layers, from serializer/deserializer (SerDes) signaling and copper or optical reach at Level 1 to the integration of a production cluster at Level 5 (@fig-network-five-level-model). Each level is developed at the point where its physical or protocol limit becomes the binding constraint.

title: From NRZ to PAM4 Signaling
caption: **From NRZ to PAM4 Signaling**: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric's fixed $\MessageStartupLatency$ latency.
alt: Two waveform panels with six equal symbol slots marked by dashed vertical lines. Left, NRZ: a square wave switching between levels 1 and 0, with one tall shaded band between the two levels and an arrow labeled full swing; below, a strip of six cells holds the bits 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, labeled 6 bits. Right, PAM4: a stepped wave among four levels labeled 00, 01, 10, and 11, with three thin shaded bands between adjacent levels and an arrow labeled one-third swing across one band; below, a strip of twelve cells grouped in pairs holds two bits per symbol, labeled 12 bits.
context:
```

The price is noise margin. With four levels packed into the same voltage swing, the gap between adjacent levels in PAM4\index{PAM4 signaling!voltage levels} shrinks to one third of the NRZ gap (@fig-pam4-vs-nrz), making the link highly susceptible to noise. Consequently, high-speed links operate near the physical limits of reliable detection and require **forward error correction (FEC)**\index{Forward error correction!definition}\index{FEC!definition} at the physical layer, commonly using Reed-Solomon RS(544,514)-family codes in high-speed Ethernet designs [@anslow2016rsFec; @ethernetAlliance2025roadmap]. FEC processing is an implementation-dependent latency term; IEEE 802.3df operator material treats roughly 100 ns of host-side FEC with the RS(544,514) code (called KP4 in the standard) and hundreds of nanoseconds of end-to-end module latency as meaningful at AI/HPC fabric timescales [@yin2022fecRequirements]. Because each switch on a path decodes and re-encodes the signal, the FEC cost accumulates with the number of switches a packet traverses. A path's length is its **hop count**\index{Hop count!definition}, counted as switch traversals or as inter-switch links; where the two counts differ, each example states which one it uses. A packet that traverses three switches, the leaf-spine-leaf route of a two-tier fabric, incurs a scenario budget of `{python} FECLatency.three_hop_low_ns_str`--`{python} FECLatency.three_hop_high_ns_str` of one-way FEC latency, or `{python} FECLatency.round_trip_low_ns_str`--`{python} FECLatency.round_trip_high_ns_str` for a round trip. Against the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient of the 175B job, a few hundred nanoseconds are negligible, because bulk transfers are governed by bandwidth. The cost lands instead on small, latency-bound messages, such as the control handoffs that coordinate pipeline stages, and on collectives whose many sequential steps each pay it. This physical-layer latency sets a floor on the fabric's fixed startup latency, formalized in @sec-network-fabrics-performance-model as the $\MessageStartupLatency$ term, that no software optimization can remove.

title: GPUDirect RDMA Data Path
caption: **GPUDirect RDMA Data Path**: Without GPUDirect (dashed), a sending node first writes the $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and the NIC then reads it back out, about $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of host-memory traffic per payload. With GPUDirect RDMA (solid), the NIC reads GPU memory directly over the PCIe peer-to-peer path, so the host-memory bounce disappears.
alt: A sending node drawn as its board layout: host memory with a registered buffer and the CPU root complex along the top, a wide PCIe switch in the middle, and GPU memory holding an n-byte payload beside the RDMA NIC along the bottom. A solid green path climbs from GPU memory into the PCIe switch and drops straight down to the NIC, which sends to the fabric. A dashed gray path climbs from GPU memory through the switch to the CPU, then into host memory, labeled 1, write n, and back out, labeled 2, read n, before descending through the switch to the NIC; a note under host memory reads about 2n bytes of bus traffic. A key labels the solid path GPUDirect RDMA and the dashed path staged via host memory.
section: │ Context: Transport — NDR line rate in TCP/RDMA discussion.
context:
RDMA bypasses the kernel data path. Offloading transport logic to the NIC allows applications to read and write registered remote memory without per-message kernel intervention. For ML, GPUDirect RDMA\index{GPUDirect RDMA!accelerator memory},[^fn-gpudirect-rdma-bypass] the path that dense nodes pair with one NIC per GPU (@sec-compute-dense-nodes), extends this principle to accelerator memory [@nvidia2026gpudirectRdma]. Within a sending node (@fig-gpudirect-data-path), GPUDirect RDMA routes an $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload (what one participant sends, not the model-wide gradient state) along the solid green peer-to-peer path through the PCIe switch straight to the RDMA NIC, bypassing host memory entirely. Without this direct memory access (DMA) bypass, the dashed gray staging path must first copy $\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and subsequently read $\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes out to the NIC, generating roughly $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of redundant host-memory bus traffic. The network still transfers the payload, and the PCIe path may comprise multiple DMA transactions; the optimization removes staging copies rather than collapsing the transfer into one transaction.

[^fn-gpudirect-rdma-bypass]: **GPUDirect RDMA**\index{GPUDirect RDMA!zero-copy}: Introduced by NVIDIA for Kepler-class GPUs and CUDA 5.0, GPUDirect RDMA enables a direct PCIe path between GPU memory and third-party peer devices such as network interfaces [@nvidia2026gpudirectRdma]. Before GPUDirect, every gradient transfer had to stage through host memory, consuming CPU memory bandwidth that competes with data loading. Eliminating this bounce path is one reason overlapping communication with backward-pass computation is feasible at scale.

title: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA Verbs Stacks
caption: **Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA Verbs Stacks**: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC's transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. With RDMA verbs over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 (right), the collective library posts work requests from user space, the kernel stays off the data path, and the RDMA NIC runs the reliable transport in hardware, reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect instead of staging a host copy.
alt: Two panels, each divided by dashed lines into user space, kernel, and hardware bands. Left, TCP/IP sockets: training framework in user space, then socket API, TCP/IP stack, and NIC driver in the kernel, then the Ethernet NIC; beside the stack, three payload tiles marked n attach to the framework, the socket API, and the NIC driver and are labeled user buf, socket buf, and TX ring; dashed arrows labeled copy 1 and copy 2 join them, and a thin solid arrow labeled DMA read carries the TX ring into the Ethernet NIC; the footer reads CPU copies data and runs the transport. Right, RDMA verbs: NCCL above the verbs API in user space, then a single amber arrow straight through the empty kernel band, labeled kernel not on the data path, to the RDMA NIC with transport in hardware; a GPU memory box beside the NIC holds a single payload tile and feeds the NIC through a short green arrow; the footer reads NIC reads GPU memory directly (GPUDirect).
context:
The InfiniBand\index{IB|see{InfiniBand}}[^fn-infiniband-protocol-origin] row reflects a protocol heritage that favors hardware-managed losslessness over Ethernet compatibility, and this architectural choice is visible at the protocol boundary. @Fig-ib-roce-stack partitions the protocol stack across user-space, kernel, and hardware bands, contrasting traditional socket overhead against direct verbs hardware offload. The conventional copied TCP/IP path on the left uses two software copies across kernel buffer boundaries and runs the protocol in software. The RDMA stack on the right traces a single amber bypass arrow from the collective communication library (such as the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, or NCCL) and the user-space **verbs API**\index{Verbs API!definition} straight to the RDMA NIC, which keeps the operating system off the active data path.

[^fn-infiniband-protocol-origin]: [offset=-32mm] **InfiniBand**\index{InfiniBand!origin}: Formed in 1999 from the merger of two competing server I/O standards (Future I/O and NGIO), InfiniBand was originally designed to replace PCI as a general-purpose system interconnect. Its pivot to HPC networking preserved the credit-based, hardware-managed flow control that server I/O demanded, and that heritage is why InfiniBand provides native losslessness without the PFC fragility of Ethernet-based RDMA fabrics.

title: The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ Crossover
caption: **The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ Crossover**: Modeled transfer time as a function of message size for an NDR InfiniBand path and a 100 Gb/s RoCE baseline using the scenario parameters in the text. Small messages are latency dominated (flat region), while large messages are bandwidth dominated (linear region); on the InfiniBand path the dotted asymptotes show the knee sitting where the two terms are equal. Measured crossover points vary with the end-to-end path.
alt: Log-log modeled transfer time vs. message size for one NDR InfiniBand scenario and one 100 gigabit per second RoCE scenario, with each crossover point marked by a dot and a label giving its message size, and latency-dominated and bandwidth-dominated regions labeled. Each series is labeled with its startup latency and bandwidth, the Ethernet label above its plateau and the InfiniBand label below. For the InfiniBand path, two dotted asymptotes, a horizontal startup floor alpha and a diagonal transmission line n over beta, meet directly beneath its crossover point.
section: │ How: RoCE alpha on a 400 Gb/s Ethernet link, same messages as NetworkAlphaBeta.
context:
In the 175B training job, a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small_kb_str` control message, such as the notification that tells a pipeline stage its next microbatch is ready, costs $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_small_ib_us_str`, with bandwidth contributing only `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.small_bw_pct_str` of the total. Faster links therefore offer little benefit for this handoff. A `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large_grad_mb_str` gradient shard, roughly the share of the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient that each of the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_str` owns when a reduction partitions it across the whole cluster, costs $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_large_ib_ms_str`; doubling bandwidth to `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.doubled_beta_gb_per_s_str` would approximately halve its transfer time.

Across the full range of message sizes, each path traces a flat latency-dominated plateau that bends into a linear bandwidth-dominated regime (@fig-alpha-beta-crossover). On the modeled NDR path, the knee at `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_ib_kb_str` marks where transmission time overtakes the `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_alpha_us_str` startup latency; the `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_beta_gbit_per_s_str` RoCE path sits on a higher floor of `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_alpha_us_str` and bends near `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_eth_kb_str`. The exact positions reflect the assumed $\MessageStartupLatency$ and $\LinkBandwidth$ scenario parameters rather than invariant protocol constants. On both paths, startup latency governs sub-kilobyte control handoffs, whereas multi-megabyte gradient shards sit well inside the bandwidth-bound regime.

title: Measured AllReduce Time against the Two-Parameter Model
caption: **Measured AllReduce Time against the Two-Parameter Model**: NCCL AllReduce time on one node of eight H100 GPUs over NVLink for message sizes from 8 bytes to 16 GB, on logarithmic axes (points), with the two-parameter model built from the measured small-message floor and the largest message's delivered bandwidth (solid line) and its two asymptotes (dotted). The model is close at both ends; between roughly 1 MB and 1 GB the measurement runs above it. One early small-message point is a timing outlier. Data from @nvidia2026exemplarnccl; whether NVLink SHARP was enabled for this run is not stated.
alt: Log-log plot of AllReduce time in microseconds from about 10 to 60,000 against message size from 8 bytes to 16 gigabytes. Measured points lie flat near 17 microseconds up to about 512 kilobytes, then rise and become linear for large messages. A solid model line follows the flat floor, bends near 5 megabytes, and joins the linear asymptote; between about 1 megabyte and 1 gigabyte the measured points sit above the line by up to about 1.7 times. Dotted lines mark the floor and the bandwidth asymptote.
context:
```

A measured collective shows both regimes and where the two-parameter model needs care. NVIDIA publishes the full output of the standard NCCL AllReduce benchmark on one node of eight H100 GPUs connected by NVLink, sweeping message sizes from 8 bytes to 16 GB [@nvidia2026exemplarnccl]. The two-parameter model can be built from two summary values of that sweep, the median time of the small messages as $\MessageStartupLatency$ and the delivered rate of the largest message as $\LinkBandwidth$, and set beside the measured time (@fig-nccl-allreduce-measured). The small messages sit on a floor of about `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.floor_us_str` µs regardless of size, and the largest messages approach `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.bw_str` of algorithm bandwidth (`{python} MeasuredAllReduce.peak_busbw_str` of bus bandwidth, the benchmark's hardware-normalized rate). Between the two, the model places the knee near `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.knee_mb_str` MB, but the measured time runs up to `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.mid_ratio_mult_str` the model's prediction for messages of 8 to 128 MB, where the delivered bandwidth is still ramping toward its peak. The model is therefore close at the two ends and optimistic in the middle, and that middle range is where the gradient buckets of data-parallel training often fall.

A three-tier radix-4 fabric ($\SwitchRadix=4$) shows the non-blocking structure at a scale small enough to draw (@fig-fat-tree-detail), with four core switches interconnecting four dashed pod modules. ### Rail-optimized topology {#sec-network-fabrics-rail-optimized}

Rail-optimized topology\index{Rail-optimized topology!cabling architecture} begins from the communication pattern rather than from a generic switch hierarchy. Dense accelerator nodes partition GPUs by local slot position into independent horizontal rails (@fig-rail-optimized-cabling). In this physical cabling scheme, high-bandwidth internal NVSwitch planes bind the GPUs within each node, while external network ports route by slot position: GPU 0 in every node connects strictly to the Rail 0 switch, GPU 1 connects to Rail 1, and so on across the cluster.

title: A PFC Deadlock from a Cyclic Buffer Dependency
caption: **A PFC Deadlock from a Cyclic Buffer Dependency**: Four switch queues form the cycle of @eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle. Follow the solid arrows clockwise: each full buffer holds packets that need space in the next. The dashed PAUSE frames run counterclockwise, so each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while awaiting space in its downstream successor, and no queue can drain until a watchdog drops packets.
alt: Four switch boxes arranged as a ring, switch 1 at the top, 2 at the right, 3 at the bottom, and 4 at the left, each containing a full red four-slot queue labeled b1 to b4 and the words queue full. Solid dark arrows curve clockwise around the outside of the ring from switch 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 and back to 1, labeled b1 to b2, b2 to b3, b3 to b4, and b4 to b1. Dashed red arrows labeled PAUSE curve counterclockwise around the inside of the ring between the same switches, and the center of the ring reads deadlock.
section: The graph mechanics of buffer-dependency deadlocks {#sec-network-deadlock-graph}
context:
$$\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \dots \to \PacketBuffer_k \to \PacketBuffer_1$$ {#eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle}

When each buffer in the cycle fills beyond its configured pause threshold, each port asserts a PFC PAUSE frame to its predecessor. Because no buffer can advance a packet into a paused successor, no buffer can drain, and no port can de-assert its PAUSE signal. The entire cycle freezes permanently. A four-switch ring whose queues ($\PacketBuffer_1$ through $\PacketBuffer_4$) are completely full shows this mutual protocol interlock (@fig-pfc-credit-deadlock). Solid gray arrows trace packet forwarding dependencies advancing clockwise ($\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \PacketBuffer_3 \to \PacketBuffer_4 \to \PacketBuffer_1$), while dashed red PAUSE frames propagate counterclockwise. Each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while waiting for its downstream successor to drain, permanently freezing all four queues until an external watchdog intervenes to drop frames.

title: A True Incast Burst
caption: **A True Incast Burst**: This deliberately worst-case fan-in scenario sends `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.n_senders_str` sources at `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.sender_bw_gb_per_s_str` toward one `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.port_gbit_per_s_str` (`{python} IncastCascadeFigure.port_gb_per_s_str`) egress with a `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.buffer_mb_str` buffer. The `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.offered_tb_per_s_str` offered load oversubscribes the destination egress by `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.oversub_mult_str`. Flat aggregation or synchronized reads can create this pattern; bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce does not, because each rank exchanges point-to-point chunks.

The port's 32 MB buffer is drawn as a row of full red cells marked drops or PAUSE upstream, and a dashed red PAUSE arrow runs from the switch back to the top of the sender column. A thin 400 Gb/s arrow leaves the port to one receiver. Below, two bars drawn to the same scale compare rates: a long bar labeled offered, 12.8 TB/s, and a sliver labeled egress, 50 GB/s, with the note 256 times oversubscribed.
context:
:::

In the deliberately worst-case incast above, $\EgressPortUtilization$ is `{python} IncastBurst.oversubscription_mult_str`, so the `{python} IncastBurst.buffer_mb_str` buffer fills in about `{python} IncastBurst.overflow_us_str`. Once full, that buffer represents `{python} IncastBurst.buffer_hold_us_str` of egress waiting time. By contrast, the bandwidth-delay product\index{Bandwidth-delay product!buffer distinction} for the `{python} IncastBurst.port_gbit_per_s_str` egress and an illustrative `{python} IncastBurst.feedback_rtt_us_str` feedback round trip is only `{python} IncastBurst.bandwidth_delay_product_kb_str`; it measures data in flight on the path, not the buffering needed to absorb an arbitrary fan-in burst. ECN\index{ECN!reaction window} must mark early enough for feedback to arrive before exhaustion; PFC can prevent a drop, but its backpressure can spread congestion. A larger buffer extends the reaction window at the cost of a larger tail-latency bound.
