title: Parallel File System Architecture
caption: **Parallel File System Architecture**: A client makes one metadata request (MDS $\to$ MDT) to learn a file's stripe map, then reads the stripes directly from the object storage servers (OSS $\to$ OST) in parallel. Each OST holds every Nth stripe of the file in round-robin order, so consecutive stripes (dark) sit on different servers and one client reads them at once. The shared data path lets every client draw on every OSS, so aggregate bandwidth grows with the number of servers while metadata traffic stays on a separate path.
alt: Architecture diagram with compute clients on the left, a metadata server and a column of object storage servers in the middle, and storage targets on the right. A violet line labeled lookup runs from client 1 to the metadata server, whose target holds a stripe map listing OSTs 1 through N. Green lines join every client through a shared vertical bus to every object storage server. Each object storage target holds stripe tiles of one file: OST 1 holds 0, N, 2N; OST 2 holds 1, N+1, 2N+1; and so on to OST N, with the first tile of each target filled dark green.
context:
:::

A Lustre-style parallel file system decouples metadata lookups from bulk data movement (@fig-storage-pfs-architecture), separating two concerns that traditional file systems handle together [@schwan2003lustre]. Metadata servers (MDS)\index{Metadata server!namespace management}\index{MDS|see{Metadata server}} manage the namespace (persisting file layouts and attributes on metadata targets, or MDTs): file creation, directory listings, permission checks, and lock management. Object storage servers (OSS)\index{Object storage server!data block striping}\index{OSS|see{Object storage server}}[^fn-oss-pfs-disambiguation] manage the actual data blocks, each serving a stripe of every large file. When a client opens a 10 GB training shard, the MDS tells the client which OSS nodes hold which stripes, and the client reads from all of them in parallel. A Lustre[^fn-lustre-parallel-origin] deployment with 100 OSS nodes, each providing 10 GB/s, delivers an aggregate 1 TB/s.

(b) Median throughput per emulated accelerator for each workload and accelerator, on a logarithmic axis. ```

MLPerf Storage measures these profiles on production storage systems. Each submission emulates a set of accelerators that consume samples with a fixed per-sample compute time, so the storage system, not a real GPU, sets the pace, and reports the read throughput the system sustained while keeping the emulated accelerators at least 90 percent busy (70 percent for CosmoFlow) [@mlcommons2024storage; @devarajan2021dlio]. Across the `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.result_count_str` passing results of the closed division in the 2024 round, sustained throughput grows in proportion to the number of emulated accelerators, as the $\InputConsumerAcceleratorCount$ term of @eq-pipeline-throughput predicts (@fig-mlperf-storage-demand, panel a). Per accelerator, the median demand differs about `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.workload_spread_mult_str` across workloads, and ResNet-50, although demanding among image-classification jobs, is the lightest of the three because its samples are small 2D images while 3D U-Net reads whole medical volumes. An emulated H100 needs about `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.unet_h100_str` for 3D U-Net on medical volumes, `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.cosmo_h100_str` for CosmoFlow, and `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.resnet_h100_str` for ResNet-50 (@fig-mlperf-storage-demand, panel b). Emulating H100s instead of A100s raises every workload's demand by `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.gen_ratio_mult_range_str`, because the faster accelerator shortens $\IronLawComputeTime$ while the bytes per batch stay the same. A storage tier sized for one accelerator generation is therefore undersized for the next, even when the dataset and the model do not change.

title: Pipelined Data Loading
caption: **Pipelined Data Loading**: Both panels share one time scale, with illustrative stage durations. Sequential loading (a) leaves the GPU idle while each batch is read and prepared. Pipelined loading (b) reads and prepares batch $\BatchIndex+1$ while the GPU trains on batch $\BatchIndex$, so four batches finish in about the time sequential loading needs for two (dashed line). The shaded column marks one instant with three batches in flight. The overlap hides storage latency only while delivery keeps pace with compute and the prefetch buffer is deep enough to absorb variance.
alt: Two timelines with storage, CPU, and GPU lanes on a shared time axis. Panel a: read, prep, and train blocks run one after another for two batches, with dashed red GPU idle blocks on the GPU lane. Panel b: four back-to-back reads, four prep blocks, and four back-to-back train blocks after one initial idle block, spanning about the same length as panel a; a dashed vertical line carries the end of panel a down into panel b and lands as a tick on its time axis just before the end of train 4, and a shaded column over read 4, prep 3, and train 2 is labeled 3 in flight.
context:
### Pipelining and prefetching {#sec-storage-pipelining}

When a data loader waits until the GPU finishes batch $\BatchIndex$ before reading and decoding batch $\BatchIndex+1$, the accelerator sits idle across the entire storage read and CPU preparation window on every step, as panel (a) of @fig-data-pipeline-vol2 shows. Pipelining\index{Pipelining!data loading} removes that synchronous stall by staging and preparing batch $\BatchIndex+1$ on host resources while the GPU trains on batch $\BatchIndex$, turning the sum of input and compute time into their maximum (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-dam-coordination-sum-max). When delivery keeps pace and enough prepared work sits in host memory to absorb latency variation, four batches finish in about the time sequential loading needs for two (panel (b)); at fleet scale, the open question is how deep that buffer of prepared work must be.

title: Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage Path
caption: **Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage Path**: Both panels draw the same node: CPU and host DRAM above a PCIe switch, NVMe and GPU below it. Green routes are DMA transfers of payload bytes. In the buffered path (a), payload climbs into host DRAM and comes back down, and the CPU copies every payload from the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer before the accelerator's DMA can start. In the GDS path (b), NVMe transfers directly into GPU memory, and the dashed CPU link shows the submission and completion work that remains.
alt: Two panels with the same layout: a CPU and a host DRAM box on top, a PCIe switch bar in the middle, and an NVMe SSD and a GPU containing HBM at the bottom. Panel a: a green route labeled DMA 1 runs from the NVMe SSD through the switch up into a kernel buffer in host DRAM; a gray copy arrow joins the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer, with the CPU attached by a link labeled copy; a second green route labeled DMA 2 runs from the pinned buffer down through the switch into HBM. Panel b: one green route labeled DMA runs from the NVMe SSD through the switch into HBM without entering host DRAM, and a dashed gray arrow labeled control runs from the CPU to the NVMe SSD.
section: GPUDirect Storage and the CPU Data-Copy Bypass {#sec-storage-gds}
context:
The software layers in the traditional I/O path contribute control overhead as well as payload-copy work. Direct I/O and pinned buffers can avoid some copies even without GDS. The correct baseline is therefore the actual data path rather than a fixed number of copies for every read. The direct path changes the payload route without eliminating the software control path. The application registers a GPU memory region for direct DMA (through the cuFile API\index{GPUDirect Storage!cuFile direct DMA} in NVIDIA's implementation), and later reads move payload from NVMe into GPU memory without an intermediate system-memory buffer. The file system and kernel storage drivers still handle submission and completion.

The benefit from GDS matters when host payload movement is a limiting stage after other pipeline work is accounted for. In @fig-gds-path, the conventional path takes two DMA hops through intermediate host-DRAM bounce buffers, while GDS takes a single direct DMA transfer. The direct path eliminates the CPU payload-copy stage, but the dashed control link shows that the host CPU still orchestrates transfer submission and completion.

title: The Complete Data Path
caption: **The Complete Data Path**: Columns are storage tiers, ordered from the durable object store (left) to accelerator memory (right). Training data moves right and bypasses the parallel file system in this running example; checkpoints return left through it. Solid arrows mark copies the training loop waits on; dashed arrows mark copies that run once per job or in the background. The dashed outline is one GPU node: every copy the training loop waits on stays inside it.
alt: Five tier columns headed object storage, parallel file system, local NVMe, host DRAM, and GPU HBM; a dashed outline labeled one GPU node encloses the last three, and the first two are labeled shared services. Training data row: a dataset in object storage, a dashed arrow labeled stage once across the empty parallel file system column to a staged copy on local NVMe, then solid arrows to a prefetch box in host DRAM and a batch in GPU HBM, plus a thinner optional GDS bypass arrow from NVMe over host DRAM to HBM. Checkpoints row: a solid arrow from model state in HBM to a local shard on NVMe labeled local save (pause), then dashed arrows to a durable copy on the parallel file system labeled async copy and to a retained copy in object storage labeled retain selected. A key distinguishes solid and dashed arrows.
context:
At the end of the training job, the final model checkpoint is promoted from the parallel file system to object storage for long-term retention. The local NVMe copies are deleted during job cleanup. If the model is deployed for inference, it is loaded from object storage into the serving cluster's HBM, completing the lifecycle of data movement through the hierarchy.

The total number of data copies in this lifecycle is instructive. Each training sample traverses: object storage $\to$ NVMe (staging), NVMe $\to$ host DRAM (read), host DRAM $\to$ GPU HBM (transfer). Each checkpoint traverses: GPU HBM $\to$ NVMe (local save), NVMe $\to$ parallel file system (async copy), parallel file system $\to$ object storage (long-term retention). Every copy consumes bandwidth and contributes latency. The engineering goal is to minimize copies on the critical path (the training loop) and tolerate additional copies on noncritical paths (staging and archival). Both lifecycles cross the same tiers in opposite directions, with synchronous critical-path copies drawn solid and asynchronous background transfers drawn dashed in @fig-storage-complete-data-path. For training inputs moving rightward, the active loop waits only on local promotion into HBM (or the optional GDS bypass); for checkpoints flowing leftward, the exposed pause is confined to the local NVMe save while parallel-file-system replication and archival retention proceed off the critical path.

title: Two-Phase Checkpoint Staging
caption: **Two-Phase Checkpoint Staging**: Read the lanes left to right. Training pauses only for the local NVMe write ($\TimeInstant_0$ to $\TimeInstant_1$); the copy to the parallel file system overlaps later training steps, and the coordinator publishes the manifest last ($\TimeInstant_3$). Between $\TimeInstant_1$ and $\TimeInstant_3$ the new generation exists only as staged shards, so the previous committed generation remains the restore point.
alt: Timeline with four horizontal lanes labeled training, local NVMe, parallel FS, and coordinator above a time axis marked t0 through t3. A short red paused block in the training lane lines up with a local write block; long blocks show training continuing, an asynchronous copy to the parallel file system, checksum verification, and manifest publication. Brackets below the axis mark the span from t1 to t3 as staged and the span after t3 as restorable.
context:
:::

The exposed pause and the durability boundary therefore fall at different moments, as the four concurrent lanes of @fig-storage-checkpoint-staging align them. Training pauses only during the local NVMe shard write ($\TimeInstant_0$ to $\TimeInstant_1$), resuming on live state while the parallel file system absorbs the asynchronous copy ($\TimeInstant_1$ to $\TimeInstant_2$) and the coordinator validates checksums before publishing the manifest last ($\TimeInstant_3$).

title: The Acknowledgment Gap at a Commit Boundary
caption: **The Acknowledgment Gap at a Commit Boundary**: A worker stores the output row for event e42 and crashes before it records the commit, so its replacement cannot tell whether the row exists and must replay the event. (a) Appending the replayed row duplicates it, and the click counts twice in every training set built from the table. (b) Writing under the stable key (feature_version, e42) makes the replay an overwrite of the same row, so at-least-once replay produces an effectively exactly-once result.
alt: Schematic with two lanes. Worker lane: a gray read e42 box, an arrow to a green write row box labeled output stored, a red X labeled crash, and a dashed violet record commit box labeled never reached; a red bracket under the crash and the commit box is labeled acknowledgment gap, written but not committed. Replacement lane: a gray replay e42 box labeled commit unknown, branching to two panels. Panel a, append the row: a white row e42 click first write above a red row e42 click replay marked duplicate, with the note the click counts twice. Panel b, write under a stable key: one green row (feature_version, e42) click, with the notes replay overwrites the same row and the click counts once.
section: Replay and commit boundaries in data pipelines {#sec-storage-distributed-transformation-semantics}
context:
:::

The two replays differ only in how the output is addressed. An append gives every attempt its own row, while a write under a stable key sends every attempt to the same row, so reprocessing uncertain work leaves the stored result unchanged (@fig-storage-commit-boundary).

title: Data-Movement Accounting Boundaries
caption: **Data-Movement Accounting Boundaries**: Successively broader paths involve different storage and communication components. The schematic identifies what an energy estimate must include; it assigns no universal distance law or fixed energy multiplier. Compare energy per transferred byte only after specifying endpoints, interfaces, switches, and utilization.
alt: One data path drawn left to right through physical components joined by amber links: a local SRAM cell grid, a stack of HBM dies, an intra-node crossbar, a SerDes chip, an optical transceiver, switches, and a remote node. At the crossbar a short branch rises to a peer GPU die, which ends that branch. Three brackets below all start at the SRAM: Package ends after HBM, Node ends after the crossbar and its peer GPU branch, and Fabric path ends at the remote node; the dark part of each bracket spans the components that boundary adds.
context:
:::

Moving data consumes energy across storage arrays, interfaces, serializers, transceivers, and switches. A transfer that starts in local SRAM can stay on-package in high-bandwidth memory (HBM)\index{HBM}\index{High-bandwidth memory|see{HBM}}, cross to an intra-node peer GPU, or traverse intermediate switches to a remote node. Each step widens the physical accounting boundary\index{Energy consumption!data movement hierarchy} that an energy estimate must include (@fig-data-movement-hierarchy). Each boundary activates distinct physical components: on-package links, intra-node crossbars, serializers, optical transceivers, and switch fabrics. Distance alone does not determine energy per bit, and an endpoint-only estimate cannot be compared directly with a complete fabric-path estimate. Locality remains useful because it can avoid transfers and active interfaces; the energy saving must be evaluated under the same workload, utilization, and accounting boundary.

title: Four Central Collective Primitives
caption: **Four Central Collective Primitives**: Standardized patterns for group communication in distributed systems. In each panel the four rows are ranks 0 to 3, read left to right from each rank's input, through the collective, to what each rank holds afterward. (1) AllReduce: all aggregate and all receive the result. (2) AllGather: all send to all and concatenate. (3) ReduceScatter: all aggregate and results are distributed in shards. (4) AllToAll: every process sends unique data to every other process. The two foundational primitives Broadcast (rank 0 sends to all) and Reduce (all aggregate to rank 0) compose the patterns shown here and are defined in the surrounding prose.
alt: Four panels, AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, and AllToAll, each with rows for ranks 0 to 3. Each row shows the rank's input buffer as small tiles, an amber collective band, and the output buffer. AllReduce: four chunks a to d per rank become four green sums on every rank. AllGather: one chunk per rank becomes four chunks a to d on every rank. ReduceScatter: four chunks per rank become one green sum per rank, sum a on rank 0 through sum d on rank 3. AllToAll: rank i's chunks a_i to d_i are transposed so rank 0 holds a0 to a3, rank 1 holds b0 to b3, and so on. Chunk a has a bold outline in every panel.
context:
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating a non-blocking collective as complete when its initiation call returns. The returned request or stream event represents work in flight. A dependent consumer must wait for completion, and a late rank can extend that dependency even though the collective is not a barrier.

:::

title: Ring AllReduce Data Flow
caption: **Ring AllReduce Data Flow**: Four GPUs in a logical ring, each gradient split into chunks A to D; the wrap-around link closes the ring from GPU 3 back to GPU 0. (a) After the $\DeviceCount-1$ ReduceScatter steps, in which every GPU sends one chunk to its neighbor and adds the chunk it receives, each GPU holds one fully reduced chunk. (b) After $\DeviceCount-1$ AllGather steps that forward those finished chunks around the same ring, every GPU holds the full sum. Every link carries data in every step, so each GPU sends $2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\CollectivePayloadSize$ bytes in total, while the $2(\DeviceCount-1)$ steps each pay one startup latency $\MessageStartupLatency$.
alt: Two rows of four GPU cards linked left to right by amber arrows, with an amber wrap-around link from GPU 3 back to GPU 0. Each GPU holds four chunk tiles A to D. Row a, after ReduceScatter: each GPU holds one green fully reduced chunk, a different one per GPU, and its other tiles are partially filled in gray to show how many ranks' contributions they hold. Three small tiles ride on each link, naming the chunk that link carries at steps 1, 2, and 3, with fill growing step by step. Row b, after AllGather: every GPU holds all four chunks as green full sums, and the tiles on each link are green.
context:
```

Across the $2(\DeviceCount-1)$ send/receive rounds each rank moves $\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount$ bytes per round, for $2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount$ bytes sent and the same received. The bandwidth term therefore reaches the information-theoretic lower bound, while the latency term grows as $2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency$. On a four-GPU ring with wrap-around links, the state progresses in two phases (@fig-ring-allreduce). In row (a), $\DeviceCount-1 = 3$ ReduceScatter steps circulate gradient chunks A through D until each GPU holds exactly one fully reduced partition (green $\Glyph{\Sigma} \Glyph{A}$ through $\Glyph{\Sigma} \Glyph{D}$). In row (b), $\DeviceCount-1 = 3$ subsequent AllGather steps forward those finished shards around the ring until every device holds the complete sum.

title: Halving-Doubling Partners across a Node Boundary
caption: **Halving-Doubling Partners across a Node Boundary**: The ReduceScatter phase of recursive halving-doubling on 8 GPUs placed four per node. In round $\PartnerBitIndex$, GPU $\RankIndex$ exchanges with GPU $\RankIndex \oplus 2^{\PartnerBitIndex}$ and sends half of the region it still holds, so the exchanged volume halves each round. (a) and (b) The first two rounds pair GPUs inside a node and use NVLink. (c) The last round pairs every GPU with one on the other node, so the round with the smallest message is the only one that crosses the slower fabric. Which round crosses depends on how many ranks each node holds.
alt: Three panels side by side, each showing Node 0 above Node 1 with four GPU cards per node, GPUs 0 to 3 and 4 to 7. Panel a, round k equals 0, partner i XOR 1, sends M over 2: solid amber brackets join GPU 0 with 1 and 2 with 3 inside each node, and 4 with 5 and 6 with 7. Panel b, round k equals 1, partner i XOR 2, sends M over 4: solid brackets join 0 with 2 above the cards and 1 with 3 below, and likewise 4 with 6 and 5 with 7. Panel c, round k equals 2, partner i XOR 4, sends M over 8: four dashed amber vertical links join GPU 0 to 4, 1 to 5, 2 to 6, and 3 to 7 across the two nodes. A key marks solid amber as NVLink inside a node and dashed amber as InfiniBand across nodes.
context:
The partner distance is where topology enters. Consider the ReduceScatter phase for 8 GPUs placed four per node on two nodes, GPUs 0--3 on the first and GPUs 4--7 on the second, which proceeds in $\log_2(8) = 3$ rounds. In round $\PartnerBitIndex=0$, each GPU $\RankIndex$ partners with GPU $\RankIndex\oplus 1$, pairing neighbors: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7). They exchange half their data and reduce. In round $\PartnerBitIndex=1$, the distance doubles: GPU $\RankIndex$ partners with GPU $\RankIndex\oplus 2$, creating pairs (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7). In round $\PartnerBitIndex=2$, the distance doubles again: GPU $\RankIndex$ partners with GPU $\RankIndex\oplus 4$, creating pairs (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7).

Physical placement determines the cost of these logical pairings (@fig-butterfly-rounds). Rounds $\PartnerBitIndex=0$ and $\PartnerBitIndex=1$ pair GPUs within a node, but in round $\PartnerBitIndex=2$ every GPU on the first node exchanges with one on the second, so that round crosses the node boundary. On eight-GPU nodes the same crossing would appear one round later, at $\PartnerBitIndex=3$ in a 16-rank group. In a separate 1,024-rank example, the final ReduceScatter round pairs GPU $\RankIndex$ with GPU $\RankIndex\oplus 512$. If the two rank halves occupy different racks, those exchanges share the inter-rack fabric. The algorithm's logarithmic rounds and optimal byte volume therefore do not establish its runtime advantage; placement, shared paths, and the changing chunk size in each round must enter the comparison.

title: Complementary Roles in a Double Binary Tree
caption: **Complementary Roles in a Double Binary Tree**: Two reduction trees over eight ranks, each carrying half of the tensor toward its root. (a) The first tree places the odd ranks at its interior and the even ranks at its leaves. (b) The second tree shifts every rank by one, which swaps the roles. The strip below shows the result: every rank is an interior node in exactly one tree and a leaf in the other, so it forwards one combined half and sends one half of its own, about $\CollectivePayloadSize$ in the reduce phase. The broadcast phase runs the same trees in the opposite direction.
alt: Two tree panels side by side. Panel a, tree 1, carries the first half M over 2: rank 7 at the top, rank 3 below it, ranks 1 and 5 below that, and leaves 0, 2, 4, and 6 at the bottom, with amber arrows pointing upward from each child to its parent. Interior ranks are blue cards and leaves are white cards. Panel b, tree 2, every rank shifted by one, carries the second half: rank 0 at the top, then 4, then 2 and 6, with leaves 1, 3, 5, and 7. Below, a two-row strip lists ranks 0 to 7: in the tree 1 row the odd ranks are blue, and in the tree 2 row the even ranks are blue. A key reads interior adds its children and forwards one partial sum; leaf sends its own contribution.
context:
NCCL can use a double binary tree\index{Double binary tree}\index{Double binary tree!complementary trees}\index{NCCL!double binary tree} for many message sizes and topologies, which addresses the bandwidth inefficiency of a standard binary tree while allowing topology-aware tree placement [@jeaugey2017nccl; @nvidiaNcclUserGuide]. The idea is to construct two independent binary trees with complementary interior-node roles, then run both trees simultaneously, each carrying half the data.

The complementary-tree construction balances endpoint work by making ranks that act as interior nodes in one tree act as leaves in the other. With eight ranks, build the first tree by labeling the nodes of a binary tree in the order of an in-order traversal (left subtree, then node, then right subtree). In a balanced seven-node tree labeled from 0, in-order traversal puts the leaves at the even ranks 0, 2, 4, and 6 and the interior nodes at 1, 3, and 5. In one simple construction, the eighth rank, 7, joins as one more interior node above that tree. The odd ranks 1, 3, 5, and 7 thus form the first tree's interior and the even ranks are its leaves. The second tree shifts every rank by one position, so the even ranks become its interior and the odd ranks its leaves (@fig-double-binary-tree). Each tree carries half the tensor, $\CollectivePayloadSize/2$, and the two halves never meet.

title: Algorithm Crossover in Collective Communication
caption: **Algorithm Crossover in Collective Communication**: Below about 1 MB the simple tree's fewer startup rounds make it faster than the ring; above that size the ring's smaller byte volume wins, and the double binary tree tracks the faster of the two across most sizes. The curves are modeled AllReduce times for a 256-GPU group on a 200 Gbps interconnect with $\MessageStartupLatency = 1\\ \MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$, over messages from 1 KB to 10 GB. The double binary tree curve applies modest latency and bandwidth overhead factors (1.2$\times$ and 1.05$\times$) to its ideal cost, so it illustrates the model rather than a measured library result.

A dotted vertical line and an open marker at about 1 MB mark where Ring and Tree cross. The region left of the crossover is tinted green and labeled Tree beats Ring; the region to the right is tinted violet and labeled Ring beats Tree, comparing only those two curves.
context:
| **Double Tree** | $\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\MessageStartupLatency$ |               $\approx\frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}$               |      Near-optimal      |      Complementary tree construction       |

: **AllReduce Algorithm Comparison**: Each algorithm occupies a different point in the latency-bandwidth trade-off space. Ring and Butterfly achieve bandwidth optimality with different latency characteristics, while Double Binary Tree combines logarithmic depth with a near-optimal byte term. The Tree row refers to the simple full-message model, not every tree implementation. {#tbl-allreduce-comparison}

title: Hierarchical AllReduce
caption: **Hierarchical AllReduce**: Three-phase decomposition that exploits the intra-node/inter-node bandwidth gap. Phase 1 performs intra-node aggregation over NVLink (an NVLink ring acting as a ReduceScatter that leaves each GPU holding a node-shard partial sum), leaving a payload of $\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorsPerNode$ on each of the $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ GPUs per node. Phase 2 runs an AllReduce across corresponding GPUs using InfiniBand. Phase 3 completes intra-node distribution over NVLink (the AllGather that returns each GPU to the full result). The schematic shows two representative ranks per node; the same decomposition applies to $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ ranks.
alt: Three panels for the three phases, each showing Node 0 above Node 1, each node holding GPU 0 and GPU 1 cards with two shard tiles. Thick NVLink bars join the GPUs inside a node and dashed InfiniBand links join corresponding GPUs across nodes; in each panel only the links in use are amber and the others are light gray. Phase 1, ReduceScatter: NVLink lit, each GPU holds one half-filled node partial sum. Phase 2, Shard AllReduce: InfiniBand lit, one half-filled shard tile rides each inter-node link, and each GPU ends with one green full sum. Phase 3, AllGather: NVLink lit, every GPU holds both green full sums.
context:
On a DGX H100 node, each GPU's local NVLink capacity is `{python} CommInfraScenario.nvlink_perdir_gb_per_s_str` per direction (the `{python} CommInfraScenario.nvlink_h100_bw_gb_per_s_str` datasheet figure is the bidirectional total), while its one inter-node port provides `{python} CommInfraScenario.ib_ndr_bw_gb_per_s_str` over InfiniBand. These are endpoint capacity budgets, not a promise of uniform achieved rate to every peer. Intra-node connectivity and simultaneous traffic still matter. That hierarchical network\index{Hierarchical network} motivates a schedule that assigns work to each tier according to its usable capacity.

A flat ring whose ordering repeatedly crosses node boundaries can leave local NVLink capacity unused while loading scarce inter-node links. Hierarchical AllReduce\index{Hierarchical AllReduce}\index{Hierarchical AllReduce!three-phase decomposition} explicitly partitions the global operation into three stages that align communication volume with the fabric tiers (@fig-hierarchical-allreduce).

title: Dimension-Ordered Reduction on a Torus Topology
caption: **Dimension-Ordered Reduction on a Torus Topology**: In a 2D torus mesh ($4 \times 4$ node grid representing a simplified TPU pod slice), AllReduce proceeds sequentially along orthogonal dimensions. Phase 1 (orange) executes four parallel horizontal rings across the X dimension ($2(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps). Phase 2 (slate) then executes four parallel vertical rings across the Y dimension ($2(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps) on the row-aggregated partial sums. Dashed stubs mark the torus wrap-around links, each leaving one edge of the grid and re-entering at the opposite edge. This dimension-ordered decomposition needs 12 startup rounds against 30 for a 16-rank 1D global ring, a $2.5\times$ reduction, but each axis processes the full message, so its bandwidth time is $3\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth$ for this grid.
alt: Two 4 by 4 grids of nodes with x and y indices 0 to 3. Panel a, Phase 1: horizontal links in each row are amber arrows with dashed wrap-around stubs at both row ends, vertical links are light gray, and every node is a quarter-filled row partial sum. Panel b, Phase 2: vertical links in each column are slate arrows with dashed wrap-around stubs, horizontal links are light gray, and every node is green. Below, a strip of 12 blocks, six amber and six slate, labeled 12 startup rounds for the 2D torus sits above a strip of 30 gray blocks for a 1D ring, drawn to the same scale.
context:
```

On a `{python} TorusRoundCounts.grid_math` 2D torus grid of `{python} TorusRoundCounts.n_ranks_str` ranks, the dimension-ordered schedule runs in two phases (@fig-torus-reduction)\index{Torus topology!dimension-ordered reduction}. In Phase 1 (orange solid paths), each row executes an independent `{python} TorusRoundCounts.x_ranks_str`-rank Ring AllReduce across the horizontal X dimension using dashed wrap-around boundary links to close the ring (`{python} TorusRoundCounts.x_rounds_math` steps). Once row partial sums are established, Phase 2 (slate solid paths) executes orthogonal `{python} TorusRoundCounts.y_ranks_str`-rank vertical Ring AllReduces down the Y dimension (`{python} TorusRoundCounts.y_rounds_math` steps). These phases use direct nearest-neighbor links without multi-hop routing within a logical ring edge. They reduce the startup count from `{python} TorusRoundCounts.flat_rounds_math` rounds on a flat `{python} TorusRoundCounts.n_ranks_str`-rank ring to `{python} TorusRoundCounts.torus_rounds_math` rounds, a `{python} TorusRoundCounts.reduction_mult_str` reduction in the modeled startup term. In this simple form each axis still processes the full message, so the round-count saving comes at a byte cost that the partitioned dimension-wise schedule removes.

title: Endpoint and In-Network Reduction
caption: **Endpoint and In-Network Reduction**: The upstream half of a reduction over four GPUs. (a) Switches only forward packets, so every full gradient tensor crosses the upper links and converges on one reducer GPU, which does all the arithmetic. (b) Aggregation-capable switches add their inputs, so each upper link carries one partial sum and the root switch finishes the reduction; the result then travels back down the same tree. A software reduction tree also aggregates along its path, but performs arithmetic at endpoints rather than switches. The diagram compares where arithmetic happens, not measured speedup.
alt: Two panels, each a tree of four GPU cards at the bottom, two switches in the middle, and one box at the top, with arrows pointing upward and each GPU holding its gradient tile g0 to g3. Panel a: gray switches labeled forwards only each send two parallel arrows carrying separate tiles g0 and g1, or g2 and g3, to a blue Reducer GPU that adds all and holds the green full sum. Panel b: amber switches labeled adds each send one arrow carrying a single half-filled tile g0+g1 or g2+g3 to an amber root switch that adds and holds the green full sum.
context:
Hierarchical and dimension-ordered schedules redistribute work across links, but their software reduction stages still require endpoint GPUs to receive and combine contributions. NVIDIA's Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol (SHARP)\index{SHARP!in-network reduction}[^fn-sharp-innetwork-aggregation] moves that intermediate aggregation into the network. Instead of routing each partial sum through a GPU for arithmetic, an aggregation-capable InfiniBand switch combines contributions as packets pass through it.

A centralized endpoint reduction and in-switch aggregation send different data up the switch tree (@fig-sharp-innetwork)\index{In-network computing!switch aggregation}. In the endpoint tree of panel (a), intermediate switches merely forward raw packets, forcing all four full gradient tensors ($\LocalGradient_0$ through $\LocalGradient_3$) across the upper links into a single Reducer GPU that executes every addition. In panel (b), SHARP offloads arithmetic to aggregation-capable switch application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)\index{ASIC}\index{Application-specific integrated circuit|see{ASIC}}: each intermediate switch computes partial sums ($\LocalGradient_0+\LocalGradient_1$ and $\LocalGradient_2+\LocalGradient_3$) in-flight, leaving only the combined shards for the root switch to finalize. Moving reduction into the network fabric halves the upper link traffic and relieves accelerator endpoints from coordinating arithmetic steps.

title: Communication-Computation Overlap
caption: **Communication-Computation Overlap**: The backward pass runs from the last layer to the first, and each layer's gradient AllReduce launches as soon as that layer finishes, so it runs on the network while the GPU computes the next layer's gradients. The first layer finishes last and has no computation left to hide behind, so its AllReduce is exposed before the optimizer step. Overlap succeeds only when the nonoverlappable overhead ($\SymmetricMessageOverhead$) is small, leaving the bulk transfer free to proceed concurrently. Durations are schematic.
alt: Two-lane timeline over a time axis. The compute lane shows Backward L4, L3, L2, and L1, each followed by a thin solid amber slice labeled o, then a dashed GPU idle box, then an Optimizer block. The network lane shows AllReduce L4, L3, and L2 each starting when its o slice ends and running beneath the next backward block, then AllReduce L1 beneath the idle box. A bracket marks the first three AllReduces as hidden behind backward compute, and a shaded band labeled exposed covers the last o slice and AllReduce L1. A key notes that o is nonoverlappable overhead that occupies the GPU.
context:
Gradient computation during the backward pass proceeds layer by layer, from the output layer back to the input layer. The gradient for layer $\ell$ is available as soon as that layer's backward pass completes, even while layers $\ell-1, \ell-2, \ldots$ are still computing. That ordering lets the gradient for layer $\ell$ start communicating immediately while the GPU computes the gradient for layer $\ell-1$. Over a four-layer backward pass, the transfers for layers 4 through 2 run beneath later backward work, and only the transfer for layer 1, which becomes ready last, is left exposed before the optimizer step (@fig-comm-compute-overlap).

In PyTorch's `DistributedDataParallel`\index{DistributedDataParallel}, this overlap is implemented through gradient hooks\index{Gradient hook}\index{DistributedDataParallel!gradient hooks}. Each parameter registers a hook that marks its gradient ready. Once all required gradients in a bucket are ready, the reducer can launch an asynchronous AllReduce\index{AllReduce!asynchronous execution}, preserving the same collective order across ranks. Meanwhile, the backward pass continues computing gradients for earlier layers. A transfer is hidden only if it completes before its result is needed; queued communication can consume part of that window, and the last bucket's transfer remains exposed (@sec-communication-overlap-limits).

title: The Memory Wall
caption: **The Memory Wall**: Accelerator memory capacity plotted against the memory a state-of-the-art model needs to train. Capacity climbs steadily while demand climbs faster, and the widening gap is why weights, gradients, and optimizer state must be split across devices rather than merely compressed. Training memory assumes 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam state; parameter counts are from @epochai2026notable and capacities are vendor specifications.
alt: Log-scale line chart from 2012 to 2024. A dashed blue series of single-accelerator memory rises from 12 GB (K80) to 180 GB (B200). A red series of the memory needed to train frontier models rises far faster, crossing above accelerator memory between GPT-2 (2019) and GPT-3 (2020), and a light red band labeled split across devices shades the widening gap through Llama 3 in 2024. GPT-3 is circled and annotated as the first plotted model beyond one accelerator, about 35 times the largest of its year. Arrows at the right span the growth of each series, about 15 times in capacity and about 4 orders of magnitude in demand. The two series are labeled directly rather than with a legend.
section: Plotted models: (label on the figure, name in the Epoch notable-models series).
context:
```

The first signal, memory exhaustion, has a long history, traced in @fig-memory-wall-trend. Over the plotted span, single-accelerator memory grew about `{python} MemoryWallTrend.gpu_growth_mult_str` from the `{python} MemoryWallTrend.first_gpu_str` to the `{python} MemoryWallTrend.last_gpu_str`, while the memory needed to train a state-of-the-art model grew by roughly `{python} MemoryWallTrend.demand_orders_str` orders of magnitude. Among the plotted models, the curves cross in `{python} MemoryWallTrend.crossover_year_str` at GPT-3, whose training state exceeded the largest accelerator then available by about `{python} MemoryWallTrend.crossover_gap_mult_str`. GPT-3 marks where the gap passed an order of magnitude, and every later plotted frontier model also sits far above the capacity curve. For those models, spreading state beyond one device's memory is a precondition for training at all rather than a way to train faster.

title: The 3D Parallelism Cube
caption: **The 3D Parallelism Cube**: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism ($\TensorParallelDegree$, intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism ($\PipelineParallelDegree$, sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism ($\DataParallelDegree$, batch replication). Each cell is one accelerator, identified by its $(\DataParallelDegree, \PipelineParallelDegree, \TensorParallelDegree)$ coordinate, so the cube holds $\DeviceCount = \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree$ devices. A feasible point must jointly satisfy model divisibility, per-device memory limits, and the network hierarchy that carries each axis's traffic.
alt: Cube divided into a four-by-four-by-four grid of cells, one cell per GPU, with the tensor axis along the width (within a layer, fast domain), the pipeline axis along the height (stages, activations), and the data axis along the depth (replicas, gradients). The front bottom right cell is solid navy and marked as one GPU. The cells it communicates with are tinted: the rest of its bottom row is labeled tensor group, the rest of its column is labeled pipeline group, and the cells behind it along the depth are labeled data group. A label reads N equals N DP times N PP times N TP.
context:
[^fn-nvlink-intranode-interconnect]: **NVLink**\index{NVLink!distributed training}: NVIDIA's point-to-point GPU interconnect delivers `{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_a100_gb_per_s_str`--`{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str` per-direction bandwidth, roughly `{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_hdr_ratio_low_mult_str`--`{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_hdr_ratio_high_mult_str` InfiniBand\index{InfiniBand}\index{IB|see{InfiniBand}} HDR per port. This bandwidth gap is why tensor parallelism, which requires AllReduce on every layer, favors the fast NVLink domain, while pipeline and data parallelism can tolerate slower links when their traffic budgets fit. NVLink Switch systems can extend that fast domain beyond one server.

The leap to multi-node training adds network communication overhead, fault tolerance requirements, and cluster orchestration\index{Cluster orchestration!distributed training}. Because each stage compounds the previous one's bottlenecks, single-GPU performance must be optimized before scaling out, so inefficiency does not multiply across the fleet. The resulting design space decomposes onto a three-dimensional grid, $\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree$, that partitions cluster execution across tensor parallelism ($\TensorParallelDegree$, intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism ($\PipelineParallelDegree$, sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism ($\DataParallelDegree$, batch replication). Each cell of the grid is one accelerator coordinate (@fig-3d-parallelism-cube).

title: Data Parallelism Implementation Pipeline
caption: **Data Parallelism Implementation Pipeline**: The five-stage workflow for data-parallel training: (1) partition the global batch, (2) assign sharded mini-batches to individual GPUs, (3) compute independent forward and backward passes to produce local gradients $\MinibatchGradient_i$, (4) execute an AllReduce collective across the cluster to obtain the average gradient $\GlobalBatchGradient$, and (5) update parameters identically across all devices. This strategy preserves the mathematical semantics of single-device SGD while distributing the compute burden.
alt: Five-stage data-parallel workflow across four GPU swimlanes. A green global batch of B equals 128, drawn as sixteen sample tiles in four groups, sends one group of 32 samples to each GPU. Each GPU card holds an identical four-layer model replica and runs forward and backward passes, producing a small signed bar vector g0 to g3 whose bars differ from lane to lane. All four vectors enter one tall amber AllReduce block labeled g global equals one over N times the sum of g i, ring. Every lane then shows the same averaged bar vector g global feeding an update theta card, with the note identical theta on every GPU.
context:
### Data parallelism implementation {#sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-data-parallelism-implementation-fa03}

The implementation details matter because the SGD equivalence only holds when each phase preserves the intended aggregate sampling and weighting, complete local gradient contributions, and a single synchronized update. The concrete workflow follows the dataflow from assigning local batches to synchronizing the computed gradients. The five-stage execution pipeline in @fig-dist-train-data-parallelism follows four GPU swimlanes. Identical model replicas ingest disjoint batch shards and compute local gradients ($\MinibatchGradient_0$--$\MinibatchGradient_3$). They then synchronize through a ring AllReduce collective before applying uniform parameter updates.

title: Communication Patterns and Their Costs
caption: **Communication Patterns and Their Costs**: Ring AllReduce and a parameter server illustrate two ways to aggregate updates. AllToAll instead routes distinct data to each peer; the complete graph shows logical destinations, not a requirement for dedicated physical links. A switched fabric can carry this traffic, with cost determined by message size, routes, and contention.
alt: Three panels. Ring AllReduce: four GPUs, each holding its gradient as four chunk cells, pass one numbered chunk to the next neighbor around a ring, with equal-weight arrows on every link, labeled 2 times N minus 1 over N times M per GPU, load spread over all links. Parameter server: four workers exchange data with a shared bus that feeds one thick red trunk into a highlighted red server NIC beneath the server, labeled 2M per worker, all traffic through one NIC. Logical AllToAll: four GPUs with four chunk cells each, joined by twelve directed arrows, one per ordered pair, labeled N times N minus 1 messages, logical pairs rather than physical wires.
context:
:::

Across the wider design space, @fig-coll-comm compares three synchronization topologies. The bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce circulates chunks along neighbor links ($2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount$ volume). The centralized parameter server is constrained by network interface card (NIC) saturation at the server node. The dense mesh of logical AllToAll peer traffic requires $\DeviceCount(\DeviceCount-1)$ messages. In dense synchronous data-parallel settings, ring AllReduce avoids a single reducer bottleneck by distributing traffic evenly across participating links, as Baidu's implementation illustrates [@gibiansky2017baidu].

title: Distributed Synchronization Models
caption: **Distributed Synchronization Models**: The timelines compare three synchronization strategies. Top: bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) forces all workers to wait at a global barrier every step. Middle: stale synchronous parallel (SSP) allows workers to proceed up to $\StalenessBound$ steps ahead of the slowest worker. Bottom: asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier while allowing gradient staleness; communication and resource contention can still delay progress.
alt: Timeline diagram with three panels of four worker rows, in which worker W3 takes longer per iteration than the others. Top, BSP: after every iteration the faster workers sit in red-hatched wait blocks until W3, labeled slow in red, reaches a global barrier. Middle, SSP with s equal to 1: the faster workers run freely until they would lead W3 by more than one iteration, then pause briefly. Bottom, ASP: every worker runs without waiting, so the faster workers finish eight iterations while W3 finishes six.
context:
:::

Execution traces for four workers with one straggler make the differences visible (@fig-sync-model-timeline). Under BSP, global barriers force the faster workers into idle wait blocks while straggler W3 completes. Under SSP, bounded slack ($\StalenessBound=1$) lets them run ahead and throttles the drift with brief pauses. Under ASP, asynchronous updates remove the global barrier without imposing a finite staleness bound, although communication and resource contention can still leave workers waiting.

title: ZeRO Memory Reduction
caption: **ZeRO Memory Reduction**: Standard data parallelism (DDP) replicates all model states across every GPU. ZeRO progressively partitions these states: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 adds gradient sharding, and ZeRO-3 shards the parameters themselves; each dashed outline marks the replicated stack a stage no longer holds. ZeRO-3 achieves linear memory scaling, enabling models with 100B+ parameters to fit on accelerators that could not hold the replicated state.
alt: Stacked bar chart of per-GPU memory for optimizer state, gradients, and weights, shaded from darker to lighter blue, under DDP, ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3. Totals fall from 112 GB to 29.3, 15.5, and 1.75 GB; a red dashed line at 80 GB accelerator memory, with the region above it washed light red, shows that only DDP exceeds it. Behind each ZeRO bar a dashed gray outline at the 112 GB DDP height marks the replicated state that stage no longer holds on the GPU.
section: Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP {#sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-memoryefficient-data-parallelism-zero-fsdp-0e69}
context:
:::

ZeRO reaches that result in stages, and the intermediate stages matter because each one buys memory with a different communication pattern. Optimizer sharding alone (ZeRO-1) already brings the replicated footprint of the same model under the accelerator ceiling, because optimizer state is three-quarters of it. Gradient sharding (ZeRO-2) and parameter sharding (ZeRO-3/FSDP) continue toward the fully sharded figure (@fig-zero-memory). Each stage also changes which collectives the update uses (@tbl-zero-stages).

title: ZeRO State Partitioning across GPU Ranks
caption: **ZeRO State Partitioning across GPU Ranks**: Which copy of each training state every GPU holds, for 4 workers. A filled full-width tile is a replicated copy; a quarter-width segment inside a dashed outline is that GPU's shard, stepping one quarter per rank. ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state ($\OptimizerStateMemory/4$), ZeRO-2 adds gradients ($\GradientMemory/4$), and ZeRO-3 shards parameters too ($\WeightMemory/4$). The footers give per-worker communication volume relative to DDP: only ZeRO-3 pays more, for the parameter AllGathers.
alt: Four panels, DDP, ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3 / FSDP, each with four GPU rows and three columns, W, G, and O, drawn in light to darker blue. A replicated state is a filled full-width tile; a sharded state is a dashed outline with only one quarter filled, at the first quarter for GPU 0 through the last quarter for GPU 3, forming a staircase down the rows. DDP fills every tile; ZeRO-1 shards O; ZeRO-2 shards G and O; ZeRO-3 shards W, G, and O. Footers read communication volume 1, 1, 1, and 1.5 times.
section: Segment labels where the segments are tall enough to hold text.
context:
Building on that owner-update contract, ZeRO-2\index{ZeRO-2!gradient sharding} also shards gradients by replacing the full reduction with a ReduceScatter that leaves each GPU with only its $1/\DeviceCount$ shard of reduced gradients. Each worker updates its $1/\DeviceCount$ parameter partition using the corresponding optimizer state, and an AllGather then restores the updated parameter replicas. In the ideal ring accounting, each phase transfers $\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount$ elements per worker, for $2\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount$ across both phases, matching DDP's byte volume ($1\times$) when gradient and parameter communication widths match. Replicated parameters avoid forward parameter gathers, although model operations may still communicate. Under the FP16-gradient convention, gradient storage falls from $2\DeviceCount$ bytes per parameter across $\DeviceCount$ workers to $2$ bytes per parameter in total, or $2/\DeviceCount$ per GPU, apart from transient buffers.

At the deepest stage, ZeRO-3\index{ZeRO-3!parameter sharding} and FSDP\index{FSDP!parameter sharding} partition the parameters as well, leaving each GPU with a $1/\DeviceCount$ persistent slice of all three training states. The full-shard schedule considered here gathers each unit before forward computation, releases its unsharded parameters, and gathers them again for backward, before a ReduceScatter distributes the completed gradients for local shard updates. Across four ranks (@fig-zero-partitioning) and under matching communication widths, ZeRO-1 ($\OptimizerStateMemory/4$) and ZeRO-2 ($\OptimizerStateMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4$) retain baseline $1\times$ communication volume. ZeRO-3 ($\WeightMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4, \OptimizerStateMemory/4$) adds the second parameter gather, which yields $1.5\times$ the baseline volume in this accounting.

title: FSDP Parameter Lifetimes
caption: **FSDP Parameter Lifetimes**: One rank executes a sharding unit under a policy that reshards parameters after forward computation. Gathered parameters disappear between forward and backward, while saved activations remain until backward consumes them. Dashed cells show optional prefetch of another unit; these allocations can coexist with the current unit. The cells describe logical lifetimes, not byte totals or operation durations. Implementations may alias shard storage or reuse buffers.
alt: Six phase columns show parameter and optimizer shards present throughout. Gathered parameters are live during the forward and backward gather and compute phases. Saved activations span forward through backward; the gradient buffer changes from full during backward to a shard during reduction and update. Dashed prefetch cells appear beside forward and backward compute.
section: Segment labels where the segments are tall enough to hold text.
context:
Full sharding adds parameter-readiness dependencies that replicated DDP avoids. With one sharding unit per layer, the forward pass needs an AllGather\index{AllGather!FSDP parameter prefetch} to reconstruct parameters ($\LayerParameterPayload$ bytes). Resharding after forward requires another gather before backward ($\LayerParameterPayload$ bytes), followed by a ReduceScatter\index{ReduceScatter!FSDP gradient reduction} for gradients ($\LayerParameterPayload$ bytes under equal communication precision). For a model with $\LayerCount$ layers, this schedule performs about $3\LayerCount$ collective operations per step. DDP instead AllReduces gradient buckets as they become ready. At large worker counts, the ideal per-worker transfer volumes approach $3\ParameterPayload$ bytes versus $2\ParameterPayload$ for DDP. Here $\ParameterPayload$ is the model's parameter bytes at the communication precision, not full training state, and it equals $\GradientPayload$ when parameters and gradients travel at the same width. These volumes do not determine elapsed time alone. While layer $\LayerIndex$ computes, layer $\LayerIndex+1$ can prefetch parameters, subject to memory headroom and fabric contention.

The allocation lifetimes in @fig-fsdp-parameter-lifetime separate persistent ownership from the temporary buffers needed to execute one sharding unit.

title: Speedup under a Fixed Residual
caption: **Speedup under a Fixed Residual**: Effective speedup $\DeviceCount/(1+(\DeviceCount-1)\SerialFraction)$ against GPU count on log-log axes, for illustrative fixed residual fractions $\SerialFraction$ of baseline step time. Ideal scaling (dashed) is linear. Each curve bends away from it and flattens near $1/\SerialFraction$: at 512 GPUs, $\SerialFraction$ = 0.1 percent still delivers about two-thirds of ideal speedup, 1 percent about one-sixth, and 10 percent under 10$\times$ in total. Darker curves carry larger $\SerialFraction$.
alt: Log-log line chart of effective speedup against GPU count from 1 to 512. A dashed diagonal marks ideal linear speedup. Three curves for r of 0.1, 1, and 10 percent bend below it and flatten, the darker curves flattening earlier and lower. Dotted horizontal lines mark the ceilings 1 over r equals 10 and 100 that the 10 percent and 1 percent curves approach, and a pale amber band between ideal and the 10 percent curve is labeled speedup lost at r equals 10 percent.
context:
That baseline fraction is not the synchronization share a profiler reports for a distributed step (the distributed Amdahl pitfall of @sec-vol2-introduction-fleet-law), because the compute share has been divided by $\DeviceCount$ while the residual has not. A residual of `{python} AmdahlObservedShare.r_pct_str` of the single-device step occupies about `{python} AmdahlObservedShare.share_pct_str` of each step on `{python} AmdahlObservedShare.n_str`. Reading the observed share as $\SerialFraction$ would therefore overstate the residual many times over and predict a far lower speedup ceiling than the model implies.

Plotted on log-log axes up to 512 GPUs, the same fixed-residual model shows how much speedup each residual fraction gives up (@fig-scaling-tax)\index{Amdahl's law!fixed residual fraction}, complementing the scaling efficiency bound (principle \ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}). In this illustrative model, a small baseline fraction ($\SerialFraction= 0.1\%$) stays closer to ideal scaling than a larger fraction ($\SerialFraction= 1\%$). A residual equal to a tenth of baseline time ($\SerialFraction= 0.10$) limits asymptotic speedup to $1/\SerialFraction= 10\times$. Actual collective and coordination costs can change with worker count, so predicting a training run requires the full step-time accounting of @eq-distributed-training-scaling-efficiency-fleet.

title: Statistical Cost of Larger Batches
caption: **Statistical Cost of Larger Batches**: A normalized illustration of the gradient-noise trade-off model, with batch size divided by the fitted critical batch. Optimization steps approach a lower limit as batches grow, while total examples processed increase. The crossover is not a hardware-throughput optimum or a measured threshold for a particular model [@mccandlish2018empirical].

Both curves equal two at batch divided by critical batch equal to one, marked as the crossover. The region above the critical batch is shaded light gray; labels name the two regimes, steps falling almost proportionally with few extra samples below the critical batch, and steps flattening toward the minimum while samples keep climbing above it. section: Critical batch size and diminishing returns {#sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-critical-batch-size-parallelism-hurt-4961}
context:
The gradient-noise model separates statistical efficiency from hardware efficiency. Well below $\CriticalBatchSize$\index{Critical batch size!scaling regimes}, increasing batch size can reduce optimization steps almost proportionally while preserving similar total sample use. Near $\CriticalBatchSize$, the trade-off between fewer updates and more samples becomes material. Above it, step count approaches a lower limit while sample use continues to increase. Neither maximum samples per second nor minimum training time necessarily occurs at $\CriticalBatchSize$: those objectives also depend on device utilization, communication, and the validated learning-rate schedule.

On log-log axes, the gradient-noise trade-off appears as a divergence between optimization step count and total sample consumption (@fig-critical-batch-size). Below the critical threshold ($\BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize< 1$), increasing batch size yields near-linear reductions in optimization steps with negligible sample waste. Past the crossover point at $\BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize= 1$ (where both normalized costs equal 2), the step count curve asymptotically flattens toward 1 while total examples processed climb steeply along the $1 + \BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize$ trajectory.
