title: Layer-Wise Model Parallelism
caption: **Layer-Wise Model Parallelism**: (a) A 16-layer transformer placed four consecutive layers per GPU, cutting each GPU's weight footprint to one-quarter of the model. Forward activations cross each stage boundary left to right; gradients return right to left. (b) Without microbatching, one batch visits the stages in turn, forward (F) and then backward (B) in reverse, in equal schematic time slots, so each GPU works in only 2 of 8 slots. The microbatched schedule in @fig-pipeline-parallelism fills much of that idle time.
alt: Panel a: an input box, four GPU cards holding layers 1 to 4, 5 to 8, 9 to 12, and 13 to 16, and a loss box, joined by solid gray forward-activation arrows and dashed gray gradient arrows. Panel b: a four-row, eight-slot timeline in which a single light-blue forward cell steps diagonally down from GPU 0 to GPU 3 and a single darker-blue backward cell steps back up, leaving every other cell idle and hatched red. A small bar beside each row splits into 2 busy and 6 idle segments, labeled busy 2 of 8.
context:
Assigning consecutive blocks of layers to separate GPUs cuts each device's weight footprint in proportion to the number of stages, but a single batch passing through those stages in sequence leaves every other GPU waiting for its turn. Where ZeRO-3 met the capacity limit by sharding storage while every worker still executed every layer, layer-wise model parallelism\index{Memory wall!model parallelism} gives each device a *unique* fraction of the model to compute. With `{python} FrontierModelParallelPipelineRecap.model_parallel_ways_str`-way partitioning, the `{python} FrontierTrainingContext.frontier_params_b_str`-parameter model's `{python} FrontierModelParallelPipelineRecap.weights_gb_str` of FP16 weights fall to approximately `{python} FrontierModelParallelPipelineRecap.weights_per_gpu_gb_str` per GPU. That is only the weights budget; activations, gradients, and optimizer state still need sharding, offload, or pipeline scheduling, the composition developed in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-hybrid-parallelism-12a0.

Layer-wise partitioning is the least invasive model cut. It saves memory by assigning consecutive layers to separate devices, but it preserves the model's sequential dependence. In transformer architectures, this translates to specific devices managing defined sets of attention and feed-forward blocks. For a 16-layer transformer on four GPUs (@fig-dist-layers-blocks), panel (a) maps the weight footprint reduction to one-quarter per device alongside forward activation and backward gradient transfers across stage boundaries. Panel (b) charts the resulting execution timeline, which shows that each GPU remains idle for six of eight time slots without microbatch pipelining.

title: Pipeline Parallelism Schedule
caption: **Pipeline Parallelism Schedule**: A 4-stage pipeline processes 4 microbatches with all forward passes (F) before any backward pass (B), as in GPipe. Rows are pipeline stages and columns are equal time slots. Each backward pass enters a stage only after the next stage has produced that microbatch's gradient, so every stage idles $\PipelineParallelDegree-1$ slots in the forward phase and $\PipelineParallelDegree-1$ in the backward phase, 6 of 14 slots in all.
alt: Pipeline schedule grid with four GPU rows and fourteen time slots. Light blue forward cells for microbatches 1 to 4 step diagonally down and right; darker blue backward cells in reverse microbatch order step diagonally up and right from the last stage; the idle bubble cells that fill the rest of the grid are hatched red, forming triangles at the start and end of the schedule and a diamond in the middle, with the fill slots t1 to t3 and drain slots t12 to t14 bracketed below. At the right, a small bar per stage splits into 8 busy and 6 idle segments, labeled 6 of 14 idle. A legend identifies forward, backward, and idle cells.
context:
:::

In the GPipe schedule of @fig-pipeline-parallelism, a four-stage pipeline processes four microbatches ($\PipelineParallelDegree=4, \MicrobatchCount=4$). Dividing the global batch into discrete microbatches allows forward passes to overlap diagonally across stages before backward passes unfold in reverse order. While microbatching raises hardware utilization above naive sequential placement, pipeline fill ($\PipelineTimeSlot_1$--$\PipelineTimeSlot_3$) and drain ($\PipelineTimeSlot_{12}$--$\PipelineTimeSlot_{14}$) bubbles still leave each device idle for 6 of 14 time slots.

title: One-Forward-One-Backward (1F1B) Pipeline Schedule
caption: **One-Forward-One-Backward (1F1B) Pipeline Schedule**: Four stages process eight microbatches in equal schematic slots. After a warm-up of forward passes, each stage alternates one backward pass with one forward pass, then drains its remaining backward passes. Fill and drain still idle every stage for 6 of 22 slots, the bubble fraction $(\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)$, but each stage releases a microbatch's activations as soon as that microbatch's backward pass runs. The bars at the right count the most microbatches whose activations a stage holds at once, four at stage 0 and one at the last stage, against the eight an all-forwards-first schedule would hold (dashed).
alt: Schedule grid with four GPU rows and twenty-two equal time slots. Light blue forward cells and darker blue backward cells are numbered by microbatch, 1 to 8. GPU 0 runs forwards 1 to 4, idles three slots, then alternates backward 1, forward 5, backward 2, and so on, ending with backwards 6, 7, and 8 separated by idle slots. Each lower stage starts one slot later and begins alternating sooner, and GPU 3 alternates forward and backward from its first microbatch. Idle slots are hatched red, and a red note reads each stage idle 6 of 22 slots. At the right, a row of eight small boxes per stage, headed peak live activations, fills 4, 3, 2, and 1 boxes in blue for 1F1B from GPU 0 down to GPU 3, with the remaining boxes dashed for GPipe.
context:
```

Run on four stages with eight microbatches, the schedule gives each stage a short warm-up of forward passes, a steady state that alternates one backward with one forward, and a drain of the remaining backward passes (@fig-pipeline-1f1b). The warm-up and drain phases still leave a bubble of roughly $(\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)$, 6 of 22 slots here. Interleaving backward work in the steady state, however, frees each activation as soon as its backward consumes it. Stage 0 never holds more than four microbatches' activations where an all-forwards-first schedule would hold all eight, so peak activation memory grows with the stage count rather than the microbatch count. That is the gain over GPipe-style all-forward-then-all-backward scheduling\index{GPipe!bubble overhead}, and it lets the system raise $\MicrobatchCount$ until activation memory, recomputation, or the global-batch constraint becomes the next limit.

title: Matrix Partitioning under Tensor Parallelism
caption: **Matrix Partitioning under Tensor Parallelism**: A Megatron-LM layer pair on two GPUs, read left to right. The first layer (for example, QKV or the first feed-forward layer) is split by columns, $\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix = [\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_1 \mid \ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each GPU computes its own slice $\LayerOutputMatrix_i$ of the replicated input's output. The second layer is split by rows, $\RowParallelWeightMatrix = [\RowParallelWeightMatrix_1 ; \RowParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each slice feeds its matching shard on the same GPU without communication. The only collective is the amber AllReduce that sums the partial outputs $\RowParallelOutputMatrix_1 + \RowParallelOutputMatrix_2$, leaving the full result on both GPUs.
alt: Two GPU lanes, each written as a matrix equation with rectangles drawn to shape. On each lane a replicated input matrix X multiplies weight matrix A, of which the GPU holds only one column half, A1 or A2, the other half dashed. The result is one column slice, Y1 or Y2, which multiplies the matching row half of B, B1 on top for GPU 0 and B2 below for GPU 1, giving a full-size partial sum Z1 or Z2; a note between the lanes reads no communication. Both partial sums enter one amber AllReduce bar spanning the lanes, which outputs the full Z on each GPU.
context:
Each GPU computes its partition independently. The concatenation in the equation is logical, because when the next operation is row-parallel, each output shard remains on its producing device and feeds the matching weight shard without an AllGather. The row-parallel half\index{Tensor parallelism!row-parallel linear layer} of the pattern splits weights along rows, $\WeightMatrix= \begin{bmatrix} \WeightMatrix_1 \\ \WeightMatrix_2 \end{bmatrix}$:
$$\LayerOutputMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix\WeightMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix_1 \WeightMatrix_1 + \LayerInputMatrix_2 \WeightMatrix_2$$
Each GPU computes a partial sum, and the system pays one AllReduce to combine the partial outputs.

title: Ring Attention Rounds
caption: **Ring Attention Rounds**: Context parallelism of degree four on four GPUs. Each GPU keeps its query chunk and, in each round, attends to the key/value tile it currently holds while sending that tile to the next GPU in the ring; dashed arrows close the ring from GPU 3 back to GPU 0. After four rounds every query chunk has seen every tile, so each GPU's attention output for its own queries is complete. The transfer hides behind the block computation only when chunks are long enough, the overlap condition derived next.
alt: Grid with four GPU rows. At the left each GPU holds a blue query box, Q0 to Q3. Four amber columns labeled round 1 to round 4 show the key/value tile each GPU holds: GPU i holds tile i in round 1, tile i minus 1 in round 2, and so on, wrapping modulo four, so GPU 0 holds K0V0, K3V3, K2V2, and K1V1. Amber arrows run diagonally from each tile to the next GPU's tile in the following round, and dashed amber arrows wrap from GPU 3 back to GPU 0, labeled to GPU 0. At the right each GPU has a blue output box, O0 to O3, under the heading output complete.
section: Context parallelism with ring attention versus Ulysses {#sec-distributed-training-context-parallelism-ring-ulysses-8b1f}
context:
Increasing sequence length $\SequenceLength$ can exhaust the remaining activation budget after sequence parallelism and checkpointing. Context parallelism of degree $\ContextParallelDegree$ distributes the sequence across $\ContextParallelDegree$ accelerators. Attention then needs exchanges across sequence partitions. Ring-based point-to-point transfers and AllToAll transpositions provide two ways to supply that information, and can also be combined hierarchically. The ring method relies on an online softmax, which keeps a running maximum and a running sum of the attention scores seen so far. Each arriving key/value tile can then be folded into the partial result, with the earlier contribution rescaled whenever the maximum changes, so no device ever stores the full attention matrix.

Ring Attention\index{Ring Attention!systolic point-to-point} [@liu2023ringAttention] organizes devices in a logical ring where each GPU holds a query chunk $\AttentionQueryMatrix_i$ of length $\SequenceLength/\ContextParallelDegree$ and an initial key/value chunk $(\AttentionKeyMatrix_i, \AttentionValuesMatrix_i)$. Computation proceeds in $\ContextParallelDegree$ rounds along the ring. In each round, GPU $\ContextParallelRankIndex$ computes block attention between its stationary $\AttentionQueryMatrix_i$ and resident $(\AttentionKeyMatrix_j, \AttentionValuesMatrix_j)$ tiles using an online softmax accumulator. At the same time, it asynchronously transmits $(\AttentionKeyMatrix_j, \AttentionValuesMatrix_j)$ to ring neighbor $(\ContextParallelRankIndex+1) \bmod \ContextParallelDegree$ and receives $(\AttentionKeyMatrix_{j-1}, \AttentionValuesMatrix_{j-1})$ from $(\ContextParallelRankIndex-1) \bmod \ContextParallelDegree$. After $\ContextParallelDegree$ rounds every query chunk has attended to every key/value tile, yet no device ever stores the full key/value sequence (@fig-ring-attention-rounds).

title: Ulysses Ownership Transpose
caption: **Ulysses Ownership Transpose**: A schematic with four ranks, four tokens, and four attention heads labels each token–head tile by its owning rank. The first AllToAll changes ownership from token rows to head columns. Each rank computes attention across the full sequence for its head, then the inverse AllToAll restores token ownership for subsequent layers. The head dimension is omitted. This example assumes ordinary multihead attention with compatible divisibility; it does not depict KV-head replication under grouped-query attention.
alt: Three token-by-head grids. In the first, each token row belongs to one rank. An AllToAll arrow leads to a grid in which each head column belongs to one rank. A local attention box and inverse AllToAll arrow lead to the output grid with the original row ownership.
context:
DeepSpeed Ulysses\index{DeepSpeed!Ulysses context parallelism}\index{Context parallelism!AllToAll transpose}\index{DeepSpeed Ulysses|see{DeepSpeed}} [@jacobs2023deepspeed] exploits the independence of attention heads rather than circulating tiles along a ring. Each head attends over the whole sequence without reading any other head's scores, so the attention work can be split by heads instead of by tokens. Outside the attention core, activations are sharded along the sequence dimension ($\SequenceLength/\ContextParallelDegree$ tokens, all $\AttentionHeadCount$ attention heads). Before computing self-attention, an AllToAll collective transposes the tensor from sequence-partitioned `[S/c, h, d_head]` to head-partitioned `[S, h/c, d_head]`. Each GPU now holds the full sequence length $\SequenceLength$, but only a subset $\AttentionHeadCount/\ContextParallelDegree$ of attention heads. Each device computes standard local FlashAttention across the full sequence for its heads; each rank owns complete heads, while the kernel handles causal masking locally. A second AllToAll collective transposes the attention output back to `[S/c, h, d_head]`. Ulysses is conceptually clean and reuses single-GPU attention kernels, but requires that the head count be divisible by the context degree ($\AttentionHeadCount \ge \ContextParallelDegree$). Under Grouped Query Attention (GQA)\index{Grouped-query attention!KV cache reduction}, where the key-value head count $\KvHeadCount$ is smaller, a direct head-sharding implementation requires compatible divisibility and $\ContextParallelDegree\le \KvHeadCount$. Replicating KV heads changes that limit and its communication budget.

The ownership map in @fig-ulysses-ownership-transpose makes this transpose explicit. Unlike the stationary query chunks in @fig-ring-attention-rounds, a Ulysses rank receives every token for its assigned heads.

title: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) AllToAll Routing
caption: **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) AllToAll Routing**: Expert parallelism on four ranks, one expert per rank, read left to right and drawn for top-1 routing with one token traced. Each rank's gate picks the top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ experts for its tokens; the first AllToAll dispatches every token to the rank that hosts its expert, the experts compute, and a second AllToAll returns the results so each rank can form the gate-weighted sum for its own tokens. In both exchanges every rank may send to every other rank, which is why the pattern stresses the fabric's bisection bandwidth.
alt: Five columns over four rows. On the left, ranks 0 to 3 each hold four token chips lettered a to p. An amber dispatch band carries one line per token to the blue expert box on the rank its gate chose, so Expert 0 holds tokens b, g, i, p, Expert 1 holds d, e, k, n, Expert 2 holds a, h, j, o, and Expert 3 holds c, f, l, m, one token from every rank. A second amber return band carries each token back to its home rank, where the four chips reappear in their original order shaded blue. The route of token a, from rank 0 to Expert 2 and back, is drawn heavier.
context:
Scaling a dense model's parameter count increases its per-token compute cost in lockstep, because every token must multiply through every weight matrix in the network. MoE\index{MoE!routing}\index{Mixture of experts|see{MoE}} architectures [@shazeer2017outrageously] break that lockstep through conditional computation, and expert parallelism\index{Expert parallelism!conditional computation} distributes the resulting capacity across devices. In an MoE layer, the feed-forward block contains $\ExpertCount$ independent feed-forward networks ("experts"), and a gating network selects only a small subset—often top-1 or top-2—for each token. Adding more experts while holding each expert's shape and the selected count fixed expands stored parameters without increasing expert FLOPs per token, trading dense matrix work for routing and all-to-all communication.

In a distributed setting, experts are partitioned across workers, with each rank hosting a disjoint subset of expert networks. One routing cycle across four ranks shows the sequence (@fig-moe-all-to-all-routing). After top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ gating selects destination experts, an AllToAll dispatch shuffles tokens across the fabric to the hosting ranks. Expert FFNs then compute locally, and a second AllToAll return routes the processed activations back to the originating ranks to form the gate-weighted sum. The backward pass repeats both exchanges in reverse order, sending output gradients to the ranks hosting the experts and returning input gradients to the ranks that own the tokens. The primary advantage is decoupling model size from per-token compute, which lets parameter count grow within feasible hardware budgets. The primary constraint is the AllToAll\index{AllToAll!expert parallelism} communication, which is bandwidth-intensive and sensitive to load imbalance.

title: Embedding Sharding Strategies
caption: **Embedding Sharding Strategies**: Row-wise sharding places complete embedding vectors on specific servers based on entity ID, requiring a network gather for lookup. Column-wise sharding splits each vector across all servers, allowing parallel local lookups followed by an AllGather, which is efficient for popular \"hot\" embeddings. Hybrid sharding combines these approaches, using replication or column sharding for hot items and row sharding for the \"cold\" long tail to balance load and memory.
alt: Three panels, each drawing an embedding table as a grid of rows (one row per ID, numbered 0 to 7 at the left) and columns (dimensions). Panel a, row-wise: server 1 holds whole rows 0 to 3 and server 2 holds whole rows 4 to 7, labeled IDs split, AllToAll, whole vectors. Panel b, column-wise: server 1 and server 2 each hold a tall block of columns spanning all rows 0 to 7, labeled dimensions split, AllGather, slices of each vector. Panel c, hybrid: both servers hold the same shaded hot rows 0 and 1, while server 1 holds cold rows 2 to 4 and server 2 holds cold rows 5 to 7, labeled hot rows replicated, AllToAll, cold tail only.
context:
: **Embedding Sharding Strategies**: Comparison of row-wise, column-wise, and hybrid embedding placement strategies, balancing lookup locality against network communication collectives and memory load balancing. {#tbl-embedding-sharding}

The trade-off is locality against load balance. Row-wise sharding keeps each embedding vector whole on one device, while column-wise sharding spreads its dimensions across devices. Both require returning the pieces each consuming computation needs, but placement alone does not prescribe a collective; the runtime can use shard RPCs or collectives according to where inputs and outputs reside. A row-wise layout commonly realizes its lookups as an AllToAll of whole vectors, and a column-wise layout as an AllGather of slices of each vector (@fig-embedding-sharding). Hybrid placement can replicate or column-partition hot embeddings while row-sharding the cold tail, trading additional storage and communication against concentrated lookup load.

title: One PPO-Style RLHF Step
caption: **One PPO-Style RLHF Step**: The policy generates responses to a batch of prompts. The frozen reference model supplies log-probabilities for the KL penalty, the frozen reward model supplies a scalar score, and the trained value model supplies value estimates. The penalized reward and value estimates form advantages, which update the policy and value models. Blue cards carry gradients and optimizer state; slate cards run forward passes only and hold weights alone, as each card's weight, gradient, and optimizer-state strip shows; strip widths follow the 2, 2, and 12 bytes per parameter of mixed-precision Adam, unlike the equal-width columns of @fig-zero-partitioning. That asymmetry drives placement.
alt: Flow diagram. Prompts feed a blue Policy card, whose responses fan out to three cards: Reference (slate, log-probs for KL), Reward model (slate, scalar score r), and Value model (blue, value estimates). Each card carries a strip of weight, gradient, and optimizer-state tiles sized 2 to 2 to 12: the blue Policy and Value cards fill all three tiles, while the slate Reference and Reward cards fill only the weight tile and show gradients and optimizer state as dashed empty outlines. The three scoring outputs merge into an Advantages box labeled r minus beta KL, GAE, and a blue return line labeled PPO update feeds gradients back to the Policy and Value cards only.
context:
### The multi-model coordination problem {#sec-distributed-training-rlhf-coordination}

Holding four models in accelerator memory at once multiplies the static state budget before a single prompt is even decoded, and only two of those models ever run a backward pass. In PPO\index{Proximal policy optimization!model asymmetry}\index{PPO|see{Proximal policy optimization}} [@schulman2017proximal], as used in InstructGPT-style systems [@ouyang2022instructgpt], the four roles differ sharply in execution mode and memory burden (@tbl-rlhf-model-coordination-roles). In @fig-rlhf-ppo-step, the policy $\Policy$ generates responses for scoring by the frozen reference and reward models and evaluation by the value model $\CriticModel$. The penalized reward ($\ResponseReward- \KlPenaltyCoefficient\,\text{KL}$) subtracts a Kullback–Leibler divergence penalty, weighted by a coefficient $\KlPenaltyCoefficient$ unrelated to link bandwidth $\LinkBandwidth$, to discourage drift from the reference. Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) combines rewards and value estimates to judge how much better a response was than expected. Those estimates guide policy updates; the value model learns to predict returns, the cumulative discounted reward that follows each generated token. Reference and reward models remain forward-only in this loop, and shared-backbone implementations can combine roles without changing their distinct responsibilities.

title: Parallelism Strategy Decision Framework
caption: **Parallelism Strategy Decision Framework**: A selection guide that begins with memory fit. For a model that fits on one device, evaluate data parallelism against the throughput target and input-delivery budget; the complete dataset need not fit in accelerator memory. A model that does not fit is routed by the structure that breaks the budget, with sequential depth leading to pipeline parallelism, an oversized single layer to tensor parallelism, and otherwise sharded data parallelism (FSDP/ZeRO). Combine parallelism axes when the workload requires them. Peak memory, global batch, bandwidth, and workload imbalance constrain every candidate.
alt: Decision tree flowchart. From the workload profile, diamonds ask whether the model fits on one GPU, whether one GPU meets the target, whether the layer stack is deep, and whether a single layer is too large. Outcomes are single device, data parallel, pipeline parallel, tensor parallel, or sharded data parallel (FSDP, ZeRO), each with a small glyph of layer bars inside GPU frames: one full stack for a single device, three full copies for data parallel, two frames holding upper and lower layer groups for pipeline parallel, two frames each holding one half of every layer for tensor parallel, and three frames each holding a different one-third slice of every layer, the rest dashed, for sharded data parallel. Dashed lines from the four parallel outcomes lead to a box that combines axes as TP times PP times DP.
context:
: **Parallel Training Strategies**: Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism form the canonical 3D core. Sequence/context parallelism extends the partition along token positions, while expert parallelism extends it across sparse model capacity. Strategy selection remains an engineering feasibility test: identify the binding constraint, the communication primitive it creates, the placement decision it forces, and the measurement that proves the strategy is helping. {#tbl-parallelism-compare tbl-colwidths="[15,22,20,23,20]"}

A decision path condenses the table, starting from memory fit and then asking which structure breaks the budget (@fig-parallelism-flowchart). Before accepting any branch, check peak memory, global batch, communication service time, and load balance together; bandwidth is a feasibility constraint throughout the decision, not an afterthought.

title: Published Failure Rates from Production Clusters
caption: **Published Failure Rates from Production Clusters**: Measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta's RSC clusters [@kokolis2025] plotted with Llama 3 training measurements [@dubey2024llama] against the theoretical 1/N curve. At 16,384 GPUs, the Kokolis projection and the Llama 3 empirical measurement bracket a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours (the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement), confirming that fault tolerance is a mathematical necessity, not an edge case. Data sources: Kokolis et al., arXiv:2410.21680; Meta, arXiv:2407.21783.
alt: Log-log scatter plot of mean time to failure in hours versus GPU count with a dashed theoretical 50,000 hours over N line. Filled blue dots mark measured Meta RSC values at 8 and 1,024 GPUs, hollow blue dots mark projections at 16,384 and 131K GPUs, and a dark diamond marks the Llama 3 measurement of 3.1 hours. A short light red band at 16,384 GPUs spans 1.8 to 3.1 hours, labeled failure every 2 to 3 h. Dotted gray reference lines mark 1 day, 1 week, and 3 months.
context:
```

Production measurements confirm the $1/\AcceleratorCount$ trend of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling and show that the GPU-only line is optimistic. Plotted on log-log axes, measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta's clusters follow the slope of the $50{,}000\,\text{h}/\AcceleratorCount$ line across more than three orders of magnitude in job size but sit below it. The gap arises because a job can be interrupted by far more than its GPUs (@fig-published-failure-rates). The @kokolis2025 study of Meta's Research SuperCluster reported measured MTTF values for observed RSC job sizes and projected a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` MTTF for `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU jobs. That projection lands next to the Llama 3\index{Llama-3!failure report} run previewed in @sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment (war story \ref{ws-fault-tolerance-llama3-failure-cadence} follows its recovery). That run recorded `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_interruptions_str` unexpected interruptions across a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_days_str`-day snapshot on `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str` H100 GPUs, which gives an observed MTTF of about `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_str`. Together, the measured Llama run and Kokolis projection put `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU training on a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours, bracketed by the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement. This evidence turns the idealized $1/\AcceleratorCount$ relation into an engineering constraint that determines checkpoint frequency, recovery architecture, and infrastructure investment.

context:
```

Production logs show which of these failures a large run actually meets. During a `{python} InterruptionCauses.days_str`-day period of Llama 3 405B pretraining on `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpus_str` H100 GPUs, Meta traced each of `{python} InterruptionCauses.total_str` unexpected interruptions to a root cause [@dubey2024llama]. Grouped by cause in @fig-llama3-interruptions, GPU components account for `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpu_count_str` of them, about `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpu_share_pct_str`, led by `{python} InterruptionCauses.faulty_gpu_str` faulty GPUs and `{python} InterruptionCauses.hbm_str` HBM memory failures. Software bugs caused `{python} InterruptionCauses.software_str`, network switches and cables `{python} InterruptionCauses.network_str`, and the remaining host hardware, from NICs to power supplies, `{python} InterruptionCauses.host_str` between them. Only `{python} InterruptionCauses.sdc_str` interruptions were attributed to silent data corruption, and that count includes only corruption that was caught. Most fault-tolerance effort therefore goes to frequent, detectable accelerator failures, while the rare silent ones demand a different kind of defense.

title: Fail-Stop vs. Byzantine Failures
caption: **Fail-Stop vs. Byzantine Failures**: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which a timeout flags as suspect without distinguishing a crash from delay or isolation. In the Byzantine model (right), a failed worker continues to participate but sends incorrect data (for example, corrupted gradients reported as valid), which can poison the global model state if not detected by redundant validation.
alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line, each showing four worker message streams along a time axis with a liveness column at the right. Left, fail-stop: W1, W3, and W4 emit regular violet heartbeat ticks and get green checks; W2's ticks stop at a red X, a bracket labeled silence runs to a violet diamond labeled timeout, and W2 gets a red X for liveness. Caption text reads silence is the evidence. Right, Byzantine: W5 to W8 send amber gradient squares on the same schedule and all four get green checks, but partway along W6's row its squares turn red. Text reads on time, but wrong.
context:
Where a fail-stop component ceases to participate, a value-corrupting component can keep running while returning incorrect results. A GPU may return wrong gradients without raising an error, a link may deliver a corrupted packet whose error pattern the CRC happens not to cover, or a worker may compute different results for identical inputs and state. Byzantine failures\index{Byzantine failure!classification} allow arbitrary behavior, including inconsistent messages to different participants [@lamport1982byzantine]. ML systems can encounter this broader failure model through silent data corruption\index{Silent data corruption!mechanism} or adversarial corruption. Numerical instability\index{Numerical instability!Byzantine failure} and determinism violations\index{Determinism!violation} also require validation when they break the execution contract, but ordinary rounding differences or intentionally stochastic outputs are not themselves evidence of a faulty worker. The recovery concern is a participant whose accepted contribution can corrupt shared state without a visible crash.

The two models leave different evidence (@fig-failure-types). A fail-stop worker such as W2 falls silent, and its missing heartbeats make it suspect. A Byzantine worker such as W6 keeps sending messages on schedule, so it passes every liveness check while the values it sends are wrong.

caption: **Hierarchy of Failure Domains**: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. A node failure affects `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs. A rack switch failure affects 32--64 GPUs (each rack is drawn with only two of its four to eight nodes). A power distribution unit (PDU) failure may affect multiple racks. The red rack shows one such correlated failure: a single top-of-rack switch fault removes every GPU it contains, while the neighboring rack is untouched, which is why replicas must span independent domains (for example, different racks or rows).

: **Failure Domains in ML Infrastructure**: Understanding failure domain boundaries enables placement of redundant components across independent domains, preventing correlated failures from defeating redundancy strategies. {#tbl-failure-domains}

title: The ML Failure Spectrum
caption: **The ML Failure Spectrum**: Hardware faults ordered by how long they persist. A transient fault leaves nothing to repair, an intermittent fault returns under the load that exposed it, and a permanent fault repeats on every retry. Persistence decides the fleet response, from retry through quarantine to replacement, and fault tolerance engineering must handle all three to keep a fleet making progress.
alt: An arrow labeled fault persistence runs from clears on its own to lasts until repaired above three panels: transient, intermittent, and permanent. Each panel shows a row of eight attempt squares over time, green when an attempt completes and red when it faults. Transient: one red square among greens. Intermittent: gray load bars above the row, and the two attempts under the tallest load bars are red. Permanent: two green squares then all red. Below each row are a typical cause (particle strike, cracked solder joint, stuck-at fault or wear-out) and a response box (retry or roll back, drain and stress-test, replace and restore).
section: Fault persistence and the fleet response {#sec-ft-fault-persistence-response}
context:
### Fault persistence and the fleet response {#sec-ft-fault-persistence-response}

Each persistence class from the taxonomy maps to a different fleet action, from retry for a fault that leaves nothing to repair, through quarantine for one that returns under load, to replacement for one that repeats on every attempt (@fig-fault-tolerance-failure-spectrum). A transient fault\index{Transient fault!fleet response}, as @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-transient-failures-57b4 established, leaves no lasting defect from that event, so the fleet's question is only whether its effect escaped. A single-event upset, a voltage droop on an unstable power path [@reddi2013], a timing violation, or a soft error in combinational logic [@mukherjee2005] can corrupt a tensor, packet, or instruction. Detection and correction can prevent propagation; affected state may otherwise require rollback. During training, an undetected error in weights or gradients can compromise convergence and contaminate subsequent checkpoints [@he2023]. During stateless inference, an activation error can remain confined to one request [@mahmoud2020]. If that activation enters retained state such as a KV cache, later outputs can also depend on it.

title: The Bathtub Curve
caption: **The Bathtub Curve**: Hardware failure rates $\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)$ vary over time. (1) Infant mortality: high failure rate initially due to manufacturing defects. (2) Useful life: constant, low failure rate where random failures dominate. (3) Wear-out: increasing failure rate as components age. Burn-in testing aims to filter out infant mortality failures before deployment.
alt: Line graph of failure rate versus component age from days to end of life, showing a bathtub shape across three shaded regions separated by dashed lines: (1) infant mortality in red with a falling rate from manufacturing defects screened by burn-in, (2) useful life in green with a constant rate whose flat floor is highlighted and labeled h equals 1 over MTTF, with MTTF about 50,000 hours, and (3) wear-out in red with a rising rate from electromigration and thermal fatigue.
section: Hardware lifecycle and the hazard rate {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-bathtub-curve-hardware-lifecycle-7d8a}
context:
As components age, they enter the wear-out\index{Bathtub curve!wear-out} phase, where failure rates increase due to accumulated wear. For GPUs, wear mechanisms include electromigration in circuits, thermal cycling stress on solder joints, and degradation of thermal interface materials. The onset of wear-out depends heavily on operating conditions; components operated at high temperatures or with frequent thermal cycling enter wear-out earlier.

The practical implication for ML systems is that fleet-wide failure rates can depend on age distribution. Under the bathtub model, a new cohort passes through elevated early-life risk, a relatively stable period, and eventual wear-out. Screening, operating conditions, and replacement policy determine how much of that pattern appears in field data. Mixed-age fleets combine cohorts at different stages, so their aggregate hazard need not follow the curve of a single cohort.

title: Silent Data Corruption Propagation
caption: **Silent Data Corruption Propagation**: A hardware bit flip moves left to right from one wrong tensor value through the backward pass and the weight update, surfacing only at the final stage as degraded model quality. The two timelines below contrast a detected error, which traps within milliseconds and restarts from the last checkpoint, with silent corruption, which is saved into checkpoints for hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a rollback; the gap between the two is the cost of silence.
alt: Top, a left-to-right chain linked by red arrows: an 8-bit word with one red bit under a lightning mark labeled bit flip in memory or ALU; a 5 by 5 tensor grid with one red cell labeled wrong value in one tensor entry; a gradient grid where the red cell's row and column are tinted red, labeled backward pass taints gradients; a weight grid whose whole row and column are red, labeled weight update commits to weights; and a small plot whose rising quality curve turns red and falls, labeled quality drops seen at evaluation. Below, two timelines share a time axis marked t equals zero, milliseconds, and hours to days. Detected error: a fault dot, a trap dot, then a green restart from checkpoint box. Silent corruption: a fault dot, a long red dashed span labeled corrupt state saved containing three crossed-out checkpoint squares, an alert dot, then a green roll back box.
context:
Digital hardware implements *deterministic* operations, but physical fault occurrence requires a *probabilistic* reliability model. Two mechanisms illustrate the distinction. Single-event upsets (SEUs)\index{SEU!mechanism}\index{Single-event upset|see{SEU}}, the particle strikes introduced with transient failures, create fleet exposure that grows with device count and operating time even when the per-device rate is low. Manufacturing variances\index{Manufacturing variance!silicon margin} can leave "marginal" chips that pass initial QA but fail under particular inputs or operating conditions. Voltage and temperature margins matter, including supply disturbances during rapid current changes ($d\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent/d\TimeInstant$). These defects can produce repeatable errors, so a probabilistic fleet model does not imply that every individual fault is random.

Facebook documented a pervasive SDC issue where a hardware fault caused a valid file to be reported as "size zero" during decompression [@dixit2021silent]; the system "worked" without crashing, but data was silently deleted. In ML, the same failure manifests as valid-looking but numerically corrupted gradients. The pipeline trace in @fig-sdc-example follows a single ALU or memory bit flip as it corrupts an individual tensor entry, taints gradient reduction during the backward pass, commits into weights, and finally surfaces as degraded quality at evaluation. The comparative timelines beneath contrast this silent latency with a standard detected error. A hardware trap halts within milliseconds to restart cleanly from the last checkpoint, whereas silent corruption commits contaminated state into checkpoints over hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a costly rollback.

title: Silent Data Corruption at Scale
caption: **Silent Data Corruption at Scale**: Jeff Dean presents on silent data corruption (SDC) at MLSys 2024, arguing that at the scale of large ML training jobs hardware errors occur routinely, and that incorrect computations from one buggy chip can propagate and infect an entire training run. Source: Jeff Dean, MLSys 2024 keynote (Google).
alt: Photograph of Jeff Dean giving a keynote at MLSys 2024. On stage he stands at a podium; a projected slide titled 'Silent Data Corruption errors (SDCs)' explains that ML-scale hardware errors can propagate and infect the entire training system.
context:
:::

Telemetry from production training fleets shows this corruption is routine rather than anomalous. At modern training scales, hardware bit flips occur regularly, and erroneous computations from a single malfunctioning accelerator can propagate into the global model state, as Jeff Dean documented in his MLSys 2024 keynote on silent data corruption [@dean2024mlsys] (@fig-sdc-jeffdean).

title: Gradient Norm Deviation
caption: **Gradient Norm Deviation**: Transient hardware faults, such as silent data corruption (SDC), can disrupt optimization by causing abrupt changes in gradient norms. Google's production examples show SDC anomalies surfacing as visible gradient-norm spikes. Source: [@dean2024mlsys].
alt: Line graph of gradient norm over training time showing smooth baseline with sudden spike anomaly caused by silent data corruption event.
context:
:::

In the Google training telemetry presented by @dean2024mlsys, @fig-sdc-training-fault identifies an abrupt gradient-norm anomaly as an SDC event. The plot shows the symptom without identifying the damaged bit or circuit. Corrupting a floating-point exponent is one mechanism that can greatly change a tensor value and subsequent updates. Gradient clipping can limit update magnitude, but it does not reconstruct the correct gradient; an anomaly detector must trigger validation or recovery before suspect state is accepted.

title: Hot-Spare Failover
caption: **Hot-Spare Failover**: An $\DeviceCount+1$ pool of four active GPUs and one standby spare. When loss or gradient sanity checks flag a suspect GPU and replay implicates it, the job drains that device and resumes on the spare from the last known-good state; the device goes to repair and a healthy unit refills the spare slot. Google's data-center examples use this reactive pattern to keep training moving despite hardware faults, in contrast to running every computation on two or three redundant units and comparing results [@dean2024mlsys]. The standing cost is the idle spare.
alt: Three panels left to right, each a row of five GPU slots. Panel 1: G0, G1, and G3 active in blue, G2 outlined in red and labeled suspect, and a dashed green spare S. Panel 2: G2 dashed gray and labeled isolated, and S solid blue and labeled active. Panel 3: a new dashed green spare S prime occupies the G2 slot, labeled new spare, with G2 sent to repair.
context:
Full replication protects a broader computation path at a correspondingly high resource cost. Dual modular redundancy\index{DMR!fleet contrast} runs every computation twice and compares the results, and triple modular redundancy\index{TMR!fleet contrast} runs it three times and takes a majority vote. These schemes pay 100 and 200 percent hardware overhead, respectively, to detect or mask a fault within a single control deadline [@sheaffer2007; @arifeen2020]. These guarantees depend on the replicas avoiding a shared fault. The price is justified in safety-critical embedded control, such as a vehicle's onboard computers, where one wrong output can endanger people and the replicated hardware is a small computer. For fleet training, duplicating every step of a run on `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str` doubles the compute devoted to those steps, before comparison and coordination costs. When corruption is rare and rollback can recover valid state, selective redundancy can protect useful progress at lower cost. Screening removes suspect devices, statistical checks run continuously, standby pools absorb drained nodes, and periodic or triggered recomputation checks selected execution paths.

Google's reactive hot-spare protocol shows how those pieces combine in three stages (@fig-sdc-controller). When runtime monitors flag an anomalous gradient and replay implicates a suspect accelerator (G2), the scheduler isolates that device and promotes a standby hot spare (S) into the active ring. It then provisions a replacement spare (S') while the suspect unit undergoes hardware diagnostics [@dean2024mlsys]. The fleet pays in advance for one idle device per pool rather than for a duplicate of every computation, and the protocol shifts the burden of correctness from unverified hardware to system-level auditing. Even so, these hardware checks reduce only the risk of an unreliable physical substrate; they do not protect against faults that the software stack introduces itself, bugs that look like valid computation while corrupting the ML pipeline.

title: The Checkpoint Trade-Off
caption: **The Checkpoint Trade-Off**: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter's 175B running example on its `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, with a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_s_str` checkpoint write and a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h_str` full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal.
alt: Plot of share of wall time wasted against checkpoint interval in minutes. A dashed blue save-overhead curve falls hyperbolically, a dashed red expected-rework line rises linearly, and a solid dark total curve has a shallow minimum marked with a green dot at about 14 minutes and 5.9 percent wasted. A dotted dropline from the minimum passes through an open circle where the two dashed terms cross, labeled terms equal. The background left of the optimum is tinted blue and labeled writes dominate; the background to the right is tinted red and labeled rework dominates. Each curve carries a direct label.
context:
:::

The result connects measured or estimated interruption rates to checkpoint policy. At this interval, saving and expected replay together consume approximately `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.overhead_pct_str` of training time in the first-order model, half from writes and half from replay, because at the square-root optimum the two terms of @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste are equal. Plotting those two terms for this cluster shows how forgiving the optimum is (@fig-checkpoint-tradeoff). Write overhead falls hyperbolically and expected rework climbs linearly, so their sum has a shallow floor around `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. An interval slightly off the optimum costs little, while one several times too short or too long costs far more, which is why a rough MTBF estimate still yields a usable schedule. How far the estimate itself can be trusted depends on the simplifying assumptions behind it.

title: Checkpoint-Recovery Timeline
caption: **Checkpoint-Recovery Timeline**: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.
alt: Top, a horizontal timeline: blue compute, green save, blue compute, green save, a red-hatched block labeled lost that ends at a red vertical line, a red recover block, and a final blue compute block. A bracket above the lost and recover blocks reads cost of one failure; brackets below label T ckpt, T write, rework, and T recovery. Bottom, a progress line on the same time axis rises during compute and stays flat during each save, with green dots marking durable progress at the end of each save. During the lost block the line rises in red, then at the failure a red dashed arrow drops it back to the last durable level, it stays flat through recovery, and it climbs again.
section: Young-Daly optimum: green dot with a dropline; the two dashed terms cross on the dropline
context:
:::

Along an execution timeline, a training run alternates productive compute intervals ($\CheckpointInterval$) with synchronous save barriers ($\CheckpointWriteTime$), and a failure charges two distinct penalties (@fig-checkpoint-recovery-timeline). Uncheckpointed progress is discarded as lost rework, and the restart latency ($\FailureRecoveryTime$) of job scheduling\index{Recovery procedure!job scheduling delay}, checkpoint loading, and pipeline warmup\index{Warmup!recovery overhead} follows before useful work resumes. Recovery latency therefore matters as much as write duration. Restart adds scheduling and warmup to reading the saved state back, so total restart time can exceed the checkpoint write time. It belongs in the total-waste and service-level objective (SLO) budgets as a per-failure term (perspective \ref{psp-fault-tolerance-young-daly-formula-assumptions}) rather than inside the per-checkpoint write term.

title: Distributed Checkpoint Architecture
caption: **Distributed Checkpoint Architecture**: Centralized vs. sharded checkpoint writes. In the centralized pattern (left), every worker funnels its shard through one coordinator, whose ingress bandwidth and buffering constrain the write path and whose failure halts the save. In the distributed pattern (right), each worker writes its own shard to local NVMe in parallel and a background process drains the shards to remote object storage, so the local blocking write time can remain roughly constant with fixed shard sizes and sufficient staging bandwidth; shared drain capacity still limits completion.
alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line. Left, centralized: four workers send red arrows that merge into one coordinator box labeled ingress limit, which writes to shared storage; beneath, a timing strip shows the four workers' green shard writes in a staircase, one after another, with a red bracket reading blocking write grows with workers. Right, distributed: each of four workers writes with a green arrow to its own NVMe drive, and dashed arrows drain the drives to an object store labeled background; beneath, the four green shard writes start together and end together under a green bracket labeled blocking, followed by dashed gray bars under a bracket labeled drain in background.
context:
#### Distributed checkpointing {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-checkpointing-5dcc}

Distributed checkpointing eliminates this coordinator funnel by having each worker persist its own shard directly. @Fig-distributed-checkpoint-architecture contrasts the dataflow topologies: the centralized pattern concentrates traffic at the coordinator's ingress, while the distributed pattern writes in parallel to local NVMe and drains the shards to remote object storage in the background. With fixed per-worker shard sizes and sufficient independent staging bandwidth, adding workers need not lengthen the local write pause. Shared drain capacity and completion coordination can still limit scaling. A coordinator signals when to checkpoint and confirms completion, but state flows directly from workers to storage without aggregation.

title: Training Failure Signatures
caption: **Training Failure Signatures**: Common patterns of model loss over time that indicate underlying system or algorithmic failures. (A) Normal training. (B) Gradient explosion. (C) Loss plateau. (D) NaN divergence, ending where a nonfinite-value check halts the run; without such a check the process can keep running on NaN values rather than crash. Identifying these signatures automatically is essential for rapid recovery in autonomous training pipelines. The curves are synthetic illustrations of each pattern, not logs from a training run.
alt: Four loss-versus-steps panels in a two-by-two grid on a shared loss axis. (A) Normal training: a green curve descending smoothly. Panels B to D repeat that healthy curve as a faint green reference line behind each pathology. (B) Gradient explosion: a descending curve with a red spike segment midway that then rejoins the healthy reference, labeled healthy. (C) Loss plateau: a curve that flattens early, with the gap between it and the healthy reference shaded red and labeled gap to healthy. (D) NaN divergence: a curve that pulls away above the healthy reference, oscillating with growing amplitude, then climbs steeply to a red X labeled NaN check halts run.
context:
Container orchestration health checks\index{Health check!orchestration layer} provide a third layer. Kubernetes, the container orchestration system, offers liveness probes\index{Liveness probe!container orchestration} (verifying that a process still responds and makes progress) and readiness probes\index{Readiness probe!container orchestration} (verifying that a process is ready to handle requests). Slurm, the batch scheduler common on HPC-style training clusters, instead runs a periodic node health-check program that can drain a node whose GPUs, links, or file systems fail their tests. Both operate independently of the training framework, catching failures that application-level heartbeats might miss; a liveness probe that tests forward progress rather than mere process existence can catch a process that is alive but deadlocked.

Loss spike\index{Loss spike!failure anomaly} detection exposes an anomaly, not its cause. @Fig-training-failure-signatures contrasts an idealized healthy loss trend with gradient explosion, a premature plateau, and NaN divergence. Real stochastic training need not decrease monotonically, so a transient rise alone does not establish failure, and nonfinite values need not crash the process. Silent hardware corruption can produce an abrupt loss or gradient-norm spike, but so can a bad batch, an optimizer instability, a data-ordering defect, or a distributed-state mismatch. Robust systems therefore pause before the suspect update commits, preserve the input and worker evidence, and replay the step on known-good hardware. The system drains hardware only after that evidence implicates the device; otherwise, it repairs the data, optimizer, or synchronization path that produced the same symptom.

title: Epoch Fencing during Recovery
caption: **Epoch Fencing during Recovery**: When the old worker's lease expires, the coordinator starts epoch 8 and advances the epoch the checkpoint store enforces before the replacement begins writing. The replacement's writes carry token 8 and are accepted; when the old worker resumes from its pause or partition, its write still carries token 7 and the store rejects it. The lease decides ownership, and the fence at the store enforces that decision even against a worker that never learned it lost ownership.
alt: Swim-lane timeline with four lanes: coordinator, replacement, old worker, and checkpoint store, with time running left to right. The coordinator lane shows epoch 7 then epoch 8, split at a mark labeled lease expires. A dashed violet arrow labeled advance fence runs from the epoch boundary down to the store, whose bar changes from accepts epoch at least 7 to accepts epoch at least 8. The replacement lane begins after the boundary with a bar labeled token 8, and a green arrow from it to the store is labeled write, token 8: accepted. The old worker lane shows a token 7 bar, a dashed gray line labeled paused or partitioned, and a bar labeled resumes, from which a red arrow ends at a red X labeled write, token 7: rejected.
context:
Recovery validation tests whether the restored job behaves consistently with its recorded state. Parameter shapes, dtypes, and shard identities must match the manifest. A short replay or validation workload then checks loss and gradient statistics under the expected numerical tolerance; different batches need not reproduce the last prefailure loss. Immediate divergence is evidence to investigate the checkpoint, data state, and execution configuration, not proof that the snapshot is corrupt. Falling back to an earlier validated generation is appropriate when the newest state cannot be trusted.

Recovery must also prevent the failed ownership epoch from returning. A coordinator grants each worker-group incarnation a monotonically increasing epoch (a membership counter, unrelated to a training epoch over the dataset) and associates membership with a renewable lease. Every state-changing write carries that epoch as a fencing token. Before replacement writes proceed, the recovery protocol advances the enforced epoch at each protected resource, which rejects writes carrying an older token (@fig-epoch-fencing). The old worker then cannot publish a checkpoint or update job progress, even if it resumes after a long pause; rendezvous likewise admits only the current membership. A lease alone is insufficient because expiration changes the coordinator's ownership decision, not the old worker's ability to reach storage. Fencing enforces that decision at the resource boundary [@kleppmann2017designing].

title: Elastic Training Recovery
caption: **Elastic Training Recovery**: Read the three phases top to bottom. Rather than restoring the original worker count before resuming, elastic training pauses when a node fails, reloads the last consistent checkpoint, re-forms the ring over the $\DeviceCount-1$ survivors, and redistributes the failed node's data shards among them. The job resumes at reduced throughput (75 percent here, assuming an unchanged per-worker rate), turning a hard failure into a temporary slowdown.
alt: Three stacked phase panels joined by downward arrows, each with a ring of nodes at left, columns of data-shard tiles in the middle, and a throughput bar at right. Phase 1: nodes N0 to N3 in an amber ring, three shard tiles per node, throughput bar full at 100 percent. Phase 2: N3 is red, the ring links touching it are red and dashed, N3's three shard tiles are red, a violet box over the surviving columns reads rendezvous plus reload, and the empty throughput bar reads paused. Phase 3: N0, N1, and N2 form a three-node ring, each column holds four tiles with the new top tile in green, a label reads plus 1 shard each (plus 33 percent), N3's column is an empty dashed outline, and the throughput bar is three-quarters full at 75 percent.
context:
:::

A small example shows the lifecycle in three phases (@fig-elastic-flow). Execution begins with a balanced four-node AllReduce ring at full throughput. When Node 3 drops out, the survivors pause at a rendezvous barrier and reload the last consistent checkpoint. The group then contracts into a three-node ring in which each worker takes a one-third larger data shard, resuming productive training at 75 percent throughput if the per-worker rate remains unchanged.

title: Serving Redundancy Strategies
caption: **Serving Redundancy Strategies**: Active-active (left) splits traffic across three replicas, each carrying about one-third, which uses every device but requires enough headroom for the survivors to absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive (right) sends all traffic to one primary and keeps a warm standby with weights already loaded, which simplifies failover at the cost of capacity that serves nothing while the primary is healthy.
alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line. Each replica card holds a blue weights bar and a load gauge whose green fill shows traffic served. Left, active-active: a load balancer splits requests along three violet arrows labeled one third to replicas 1, 2, and 3; each gauge is one-third full, and a bracket under the empty part of the first gauge reads headroom absorbs a failed share. Right, active-passive: a load balancer sends a solid arrow labeled all traffic to a primary whose gauge is full and labeled traffic, and a dashed arrow labeled on failure to a dashed warm standby whose weights are loaded but whose gauge is empty and labeled idle; text below reads loaded, serves nothing.
context:
#### Replication strategies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replication-strategies-aaa2}

The availability equation says how much redundancy can help; the replication topology determines how that redundancy behaves under normal execution and sudden hardware loss. Two fundamental designs make opposite bets (@fig-serving-redundancy). Active-active replication splits ingress traffic evenly across live replicas, one-third each for three, which keeps every device busy but requires spare headroom so the survivors can absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive replication sends all traffic to a designated primary and keeps a pre-warmed standby whose weights remain loaded in accelerator memory, which makes failover fast at the expense of a device that serves nothing while the primary is healthy.

title: The Three Pillars of Observability
caption: **The Three Pillars of Observability**: Diagnosis of fleet failures can combine three signal types. Metrics reveal *when* and *where* a problem occurs (for example, GPU utilization drops). Logs provide the *what* through event context (for example, an out-of-memory exception). Traces expose the *request path* by linking events across the distributed lifecycle (for example, identifying the request that triggered the memory spike). A single signal can justify immediate mitigation; joining signals on shared identifiers strengthens diagnosis without proving the cause.
alt: Three panels draw each signal in its native form. Metrics, labeled when and where: a GPU utilization time series that runs level and then drops sharply in red. Logs, labeled what happened: a stream of gray log lines with one red monospace line reading OOM exception. Traces, labeled request path: a waterfall of nested span bars with one long span outlined in red. In each panel a dashed violet connector leaves the red anomaly, the end of the utilization drop, the end of the OOM line, and the end of the red span, and runs down as an arrow into a bar reading correlate on shared identifiers, listing request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment, which leads to a recovery action box: shed load, restart, roll back, or degrade.

title: Jobs versus GPU Time by Job Size
caption: **Jobs versus GPU Time by Job Size**: Cumulative share of GPU jobs (gray) and of GPU time (red) against the number of GPUs each job requested, for the Kalos LLM-development cluster from March to August 2023. Almost every job is small, while almost all GPU time goes to jobs of 256 GPUs or more. Data from the AcmeTrace release of @hu2024characterization.

The red curve, cumulative share of GPU time, stays below 5 percent through 128 GPUs, then climbs at 256, 504, 512, and 1,024 GPUs to reach 100 percent. A shaded region marks jobs of 256 GPUs or more.
context:
```

Production traces show that this mix is the normal case rather than a contrived one. In the Kalos cluster that Shanghai AI Laboratory used for language-model development in 2023, `{python} JobSizeMix.single_job_pct_str` of `{python} JobSizeMix.job_count_str` GPU jobs requested a single GPU, yet together they consumed `{python} JobSizeMix.single_time_pct_str` of the cluster's GPU time. Jobs of `{python} JobSizeMix.large_threshold_str` GPUs or more made up `{python} JobSizeMix.large_job_pct_str` of submissions and consumed `{python} JobSizeMix.large_time_pct_str` of GPU time [@hu2024characterization], two distributions that @fig-acme-job-size plots side by side. Counted by jobs, the cluster is a stream of small experiments; counted by GPU-hours, it is a few percent of jobs that hold nearly all the accelerators. A scheduler must serve both views at once, which is why fairness, packing, and preemption policies cannot be judged by either count alone.

title: Scheduling Trade-Offs across Competing Fleet Objectives
caption: **Scheduling Trade-Offs across Competing Fleet Objectives**: A four-way trade-off diamond (Throughput, Latency, Fairness, Cost Efficiency) illustrates the tensions governing cluster scheduling. Throughput favors long, unbroken runs; Latency favors aggressive preemption for interactive jobs; Resource-share fairness can constrain placement to equalize shares; and Cost Efficiency uses discounted, interruptible capacity. Each vertex sketches a four-GPU pool over time as that objective would schedule it and names a possible cost of favoring it; the conflicts depend on workload and available capacity.
alt: Four violet-outlined cards arranged as a diamond and joined by dashed edges, each holding a small strip of a four-GPU pool against time, with strip height standing for GPUs, and a line naming what that objective gives up. Throughput, at top: one large gang block runs unbroken across the whole strip while three small jobs wait stacked in a dashed queue column to its left; gives up small jobs, which starve. Cost efficiency, at left: three spot blocks separated by two red preemption ticks, each tick followed by a red hatched stretch of redone work; gives up preemption overhead. Fairness, at right: team A holds half the pool for the whole period, team B holds the other half briefly and the rest of its share sits idle with a dashed outline; gives up peak utilization. Latency, at bottom: the gang block is cut by two red preemption ticks so short gray jobs can start, leaving the gang in fragments; gives up large gangs, which fragment. The center reads a scheduling policy sets the weights.
context:
Fairness requires an outcome metric rather than an input quota rule alone. For job $\JobIndex$, **slowdown**\index{Slowdown!definition} $\JobSlowdown_j=(\JobQueueWaitTime_j+\IsolatedJobRunTime_j)/\IsolatedJobRunTime_j$ compares its queueing-plus-running time with its isolated runtime $\IsolatedJobRunTime_j$, assuming the running time is unchanged by sharing. A one-hour job that waits nine hours has $\JobSlowdown_j=10$, even if its team eventually receives its nominal GPU share. When contention or resizing changes execution time, the numerator must instead use the observed queueing-plus-running duration while the denominator retains the isolated baseline. A scheduler should report the distribution of slowdown by user and job class, together with the age of the oldest pending feasible job. Dominant-share parity detects unequal resource allocation, slowdown exposes unequal delay, and the maximum feasible wait exposes starvation risk. These metrics separate a policy that is fair in allocated GPU-hours from one that is fair in the time users wait to obtain useful results.

Each of the four objectives, pursued alone, schedules the same pool differently and gives up something the others protect (@fig-fleet-orchestration-scheduling-tradeoffs). Favoring a large unbroken allocation can delay short experiments, while repeatedly admitting short jobs can prevent a large gang from assembling. These conflicts depend on the workload and available capacity; improving one objective does not necessarily worsen every other objective. Resource-share fairness and completion-delay fairness therefore need separate measurements.

title: The Fragmentation Problem
caption: **The Fragmentation Problem**: A snapshot of an 8-node cluster (rows) with 8 GPUs each (columns). Blue blocks mark the slots each active job holds (J1 to J15); dashed white cells are free, and the count at the right of each row gives that node's free slots. Although 19 GPUs, roughly 30 percent of capacity, are free, every node still holds at least one busy slot, so the pending job above the grid, which needs a full node, cannot be placed. Fragmentation, not total capacity, sets what the scheduler can admit.

Each active job, J1 to J15, is a light blue block spanning its slots; free slots are white with dashed outlines, scattered across every row.
