context:
develops it together with the reservation it must protect and the runtime estimates it depends on. A second strategy, periodic **defragmentation**\index{Defragmentation!definition}, migrates or preempts low-priority jobs to consolidate free resources into contiguous blocks, analogous to memory compaction in operating systems. The scheduler identifies nodes where partial allocations leave stranded resources, preempts the jobs occupying those resources, and re-schedules them on nodes where they can be packed more efficiently. The cost includes state transfer and restart, plus replay of work not captured by a valid checkpoint. A graceful checkpoint can preserve recent progress, but still takes time and storage bandwidth. The scheduler must weigh these costs against the benefit of starting large jobs sooner, and low-demand periods reduce the number of competing jobs affected by the move.

A third strategy, **over-subscription**\index{Over-subscription!definition}, admits more demand than a capacity dimension can sustain simultaneously, but only where the resource is divisible and the scheduler can bound interference. Average activity of a GPU's streaming multiprocessors (SMs), its compute units, does not create fractional whole GPUs. A job that reserves device memory, requires an exclusive CUDA context, or belongs to a rigid gang still occupies its assigned device while kernels are idle. Statistical multiplexing can be safe for explicitly shareable CPU, network, storage, or partitioned GPU capacity when tenants have measured, weakly correlated peaks and enforceable limits. It is unsafe to convert 70 percent average GPU utilization into a 1.4$\times$ device overcommit ratio. Whole-device capacity should instead be recovered through preemption, elastic resizing, or an isolation mechanism such as Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) hardware partitioning or NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), which lets several processes' kernels share one device. Either mechanism helps only if the scheduler models its memory, compute, and fault-sharing contract explicitly. Both reappear with the serving workloads they suit best in @sec-fleet-orchestration-resource-isolation.

title: The Distributed Deadlock (Hold and Wait)
caption: **The Distributed Deadlock (Hold and Wait)**: In a non-gang scheduler (left), job J1 acquires half the cluster and waits for the rest, while job J2 acquires the other half and waits for J1 to release its GPUs. Neither can proceed, and 100 percent of the cluster sits idle. Gang scheduling (right) solves this by mandating atomic allocation: a job is either granted its entire $\DeviceCount$-GPU requirement simultaneously or it waits in the queue without holding any resources.
alt: Two panels, each with a queue lane above eight GPU rows against a time axis. Left, partial allocation: J1 holds GPU rows 0 to 3 and J2 holds rows 4 to 7, both drawn as red hatched blocks labeled holds 4 of 8 that extend past the right edge with dashed ends; two curved red arrows form a cycle between them labeled waits, and the panel reads 8 GPUs held, none computing. Right, gang scheduling: a blue J1 block spans all eight rows, then a blue J2 block spans all eight rows after it, each labeled all 8 at once; above them, J2 waits in the queue in a dashed violet box labeled holds 0 until an arrow labeled J1 finishes drops it into the GPUs. The panel reads no partial holds, no deadlock.
context:
### Gang scheduling {#sec-fleet-orchestration-gang-scheduling}

Partial allocation of rigid multi-GPU jobs creates a distributed scheduling failure mode in which two jobs each hold half the resources they need and block each other indefinitely while every allocated GPU sits idle. In the left panel of @fig-gang-scheduling-deadlock, jobs J1 and J2 each hold 4 of the 8 GPUs they require, and the whole pool stalls. Atomic gang scheduling\index{Gang scheduling!atomic allocation} (right panel) instead grants J1 all 8 GPUs as one allocation while J2 waits without holding any, which prevents this allocation deadlock.

title: Backfill under a Reservation
caption: **Backfill under a Reservation**: The head-of-queue gang holds a reservation that begins when the running jobs release their GPUs. Until then, the free GPUs form a backfill window. A short job that ends before the reservation start runs in that window, while a job whose runtime bound would carry it past the start is held, because admitting it would delay the gang. The schematic carries no measured values.
alt: Schematic of GPUs in a pool against time. Running jobs, a blue block, hold the upper GPUs until a vertical violet line labeled reservation start. To the right of the line, a dashed violet block spanning every GPU is labeled reserved for the head-of-queue gang, needs every GPU at once. Below the running jobs and left of the line, a hatched dashed region is labeled backfill window, free until the reservation. Inside it, a green block labeled B1 ends before the start and is admitted. A red dashed block labeled B2 extends past the reservation line into the gang's block and is labeled would delay the gang, held.
context:
[^fn-deadlock-scheduling-cycle]: **Hold-and-wait**\index{Deadlock!Coffman conditions}: One of the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait), all of which must hold for deadlock to occur [@coffman1971]. Gang scheduling removes hold-and-wait through atomic allocation, which is why it prevents this deadlock by construction; the price is reduced packing flexibility.

Naive gang scheduling is wasteful in predictable ways. Atomic allocation means the waiting job holds nothing, yet a large gang will never assemble if every freed GPU goes to a smaller job. The scheduler therefore places a **reservation**\index{Backfill scheduling!reservation} for the job at the head of the queue, draining capacity toward it by declining to start new work on GPUs that the gang will need. If the cluster has `{python} ClusterEconomicsContext.gang_held_gpus_str` free GPUs and that job requests `{python} ClusterEconomicsContext.gang_job_gpus_str`, the reservation keeps the `{python} ClusterEconomicsContext.gang_held_gpus_str` GPUs idle until `{python} ClusterEconomicsContext.gang_missing_gpus_str` more become available, potentially wasting thousands of GPU-hours. Backfill scheduling\index{Backfill scheduling!conservative backfilling}\index{Gang scheduling!backfilling} addresses this by identifying jobs in the queue that can fit within the `{python} ClusterEconomicsContext.gang_held_gpus_str` available GPUs without delaying the large job's expected start time (@fig-fleet-orchestration-backfill-reservation), an idea popularized in the ANL/IBM SP scheduling system [@lifka1995anlibm]. A 128-GPU job with an estimated runtime of 2 hours is a backfill candidate if the `{python} ClusterEconomicsContext.gang_missing_gpus_str` additional GPUs needed by the large job will remain unavailable for at least 2 hours. Protecting the reservation requires an enforced runtime bound or a preemption contract that releases the backfill allocation in time, including any checkpoint and cleanup delay. The estimate identifies an opportunity; the release contract makes the reservation enforceable.

title: Architectural Paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes
caption: **Architectural Paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes**: Slurm (left) uses an imperative batch model where users submit explicit resource requests to a centralized controller (`slurmctld`) providing deterministic atomic allocation. Kubernetes (right) uses a declarative service model where controllers continuously reconcile observed cluster state in `etcd` against desired state specifications.
alt: Two columns. Left, Slurm, drawn as a straight one-way line: a job script with an sbatch command flows down once to slurmctld, then to slurmd on each node, whose connectors end on one dashed violet outline enclosing four nodes; the note reads all nodes granted at once, or the job waits. Right, Kubernetes, drawn as a closed loop: a desired-state file applied with kubectl flows into the API server and etcd, which holds two slots reading desired 4 pods and observed 3. Three violet arrows then form a cycle labeled reconcile loop: watch, from etcd down to the controllers, which act on the gap; recreate, from the controllers to a group of four pods, of which Pod 3 is drawn red and dashed and labeled failed; and status, from the pods back up into etcd. The note reads observed state is reconciled continuously.
context:
A pending gang and a queue of small backfill jobs need both a policy for sharing capacity and a control plane that can enforce it. The policies just developed apply across platforms; the orchestration paradigm determines how the platform represents allocations and recovers when observed state diverges from them. Slurm, shaped by HPC batch systems, favors explicit resource requests and predictable allocation. Kubernetes, shaped by cloud-native service management, favors declared desired state and continuous reconciliation. The choice is therefore not Slurm vs. Kubernetes as products; it is which control model best matches the workload mix, failure behavior, and operational culture of the fleet.

The two platforms embody two control models (@fig-fleet-orchestration-slurm-vs-k8s). Slurm follows an imperative batch model, in which the user states the resources a job needs and the central slurmctld dispatches that allocation through per-node slurmd daemons. Kubernetes follows a declarative model, in which the user states what should be running and controllers reconcile observed state toward that declaration through the API server and node agents. Both platforms accept explicit resource requirements and track execution state, so the useful distinction is which lifecycle the platform manages directly: an allocated batch job or a collection of workloads maintained by controllers. That distinction shapes how ML workloads are admitted, monitored, and recovered from failure, and distributed training still needs framework-level coordination under either model.

title: Physical Topology Hierarchy and Bandwidth Cliffs
caption: **Physical Topology Hierarchy and Bandwidth Cliffs**: Hardware boundaries dictate communication performance across three distinct domains. The example compares a `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str` per-direction NVLink endpoint budget with a `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` per-direction external port. Under balanced load saturating a `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ratio_hi_str`:1 to `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ratio_lo_str`:1 oversubscribed spine, the external per-endpoint share falls to approximately `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str`. A non-blocking spine need not impose this reduction. The bar in each domain's header draws its bandwidth on one shared linear scale.
alt: Nested boxes. A pod of spine switches contains a rack under one leaf switch, which contains a node of eight GPUs, G0 to G7, each wired to an NVSwitch. Beside the rack's node sit three smaller gray nodes labeled more nodes, and beside the rack sit three gray racks labeled more racks, each holding a column of miniature gray nodes drawn like the sibling nodes. Each domain header carries a solid amber bar of its per-direction bandwidth, all starting at the same position on one linear scale: the node bar for NVLink at 450 GB/s is long, the rack bar at 50 GB/s is short, and the pod bar at about 12.5 to 25 GB/s per endpoint, oversubscribed, is a sliver with a dashed extension.
context:
A 64-GPU job within one rack can avoid cross-rack paths that a spread allocation must use. It outperforms the spread allocation only when those paths add exposed latency or bandwidth contention; a non-blocking, uncongested spine need not reduce sustained throughput. The performance difference stems directly from the hierarchical communication analysis in @sec-communication-collective-operations-collective-operations-hierarchical-allreduce-1338: a flat ring AllReduce runs at the speed of the slowest link in the ring, and cross-rack hops introduce both higher latency and increased contention risk. For synchronous training, every iteration waits for the slowest worker to complete its AllReduce, so even occasional cross-rack congestion inflates the Fleet Law's communication term $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ (@eq-fleet-law) on every step it touches.

The scheduler must therefore model the cluster as a hierarchical graph with discrete bandwidth boundaries (@fig-fleet-orchestration-topology-hierarchy). In the illustrated H100 fleet, per-direction bandwidth steps down from `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str` across the NVSwitch inside a node to `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` per port under a leaf switch, and to roughly `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str` per endpoint when balanced traffic saturates an oversubscribed spine. A node boundary can introduce a large bandwidth reduction, but a non-blocking rack or pod boundary need not reduce per-endpoint bandwidth. Oversubscription adds a separate constraint when traffic saturates shared uplinks. Topology-aware placement minimizes the communication cost of the job's actual traffic pattern rather than applying a fixed penalty to every boundary.

Applied to a whole job, the same reasoning ranks placement strategies. The latencies in this comparison are illustrative, not derived. They are constructed to stay above the ring-AllReduce bandwidth bound for the payload, and they show the order in which placement removes delay rather than values a reader could recompute from topology names. For a 0.5 GB gradient synchronization on `{python} TopologyPlacement.n_gpus_str` GPUs, random placement spans multiple racks and spine switches and takes an assumed `{python} TopologyPlacement.random_placement_latency_ms_str`. Each successive strategy removes a source of delay that the previous one leaves. Confining the group to a single rack removes spine hops and reduces latency to `{python} TopologyPlacement.rack_aware_latency_ms_str`. Rail-optimized alignment maps ranks so that every member of each collective group sits at the same local GPU index and therefore on the same network rail (developed in @sec-fleet-orchestration-rail-optimized). Traffic that previously hopped between rails through the spine now stays within one rail's switches, which cuts latency to `{python} TopologyPlacement.rail_optimized_latency_ms_str`. A **hierarchical placement**\index{Hierarchical placement!definition} algorithm applies these constraints from the most restrictive communication domain outward, matching each 3D parallelism dimension to the interconnect tier its traffic can tolerate (@fig-fleet-orchestration-hierarchical-placement). In the illustrated fleet, it places each tensor-parallel group within an NVLink-connected node, where the per-layer activation exchanges run at `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str`. It places consecutive pipeline stages under the same leaf switch, where stage boundaries cross at `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str`. It distributes data-parallel replicas across racks only when the once-per-step gradient synchronization fits the roughly `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str` per endpoint that an oversubscribed spine leaves. This alignment reduces costly boundary crossings, but placement alone cannot reserve the fabric's full bisection bandwidth against other jobs.

title: Elastic Training Worker Lifecycle and State Machine
caption: **Elastic Training Worker Lifecycle and State Machine**: The state machine governing dynamic worker membership. Active training loops on step completion and leaves that state along three paths: idle GPUs trigger scale up, a preemption for higher-priority work triggers scale down, and a host timeout or ECC error triggers worker replacement. Each path rebuilds the communication group and returns to active training (dashed arrows), and a spot reclamation deadline can force a shrinking job straight into replacement. Worker processes may restart during resizing, so recovery requires the application to restore valid training state.
alt: State machine with a central active training state that has a step completion self-loop. Solid arrows lead from it to scale up on idle GPUs, to scale down on preemption, and to replace worker on host timeout or ECC error. Dashed arrows return to active training labeled group rebuilt, ranks released, and spare joined. A red dashed arrow labeled spot reclaim deadline runs from scale down to replace worker.
context:
### The scheduler-framework contract {#sec-fleet-orchestration-elastic-contract}

If a scheduler reclaims four nodes from a running job by abruptly killing their containers, or adds four idle nodes without triggering a new rendezvous, the surviving ranks treat the change as a fatal collective timeout rather than an elastic resize. Resizing a live job without crashing it requires an explicit contract between the scheduler and the training framework. For planned resizing, the scheduler and framework coordinate resource release through defined signals and an agreed adaptation window. Unexpected failures can bypass that window, so the framework must also recover from valid saved state. Its recovery path reconstructs communication groups and either preserves the global batch or applies a validated batch-size and learning-rate policy. The worker-membership lifecycle therefore behaves as a state machine centered on active training (@fig-fleet-orchestration-elastic-state-machine). Idle GPUs trigger scale-up, preemptions trigger scale-down, and host timeouts or ECC errors divert ranks to worker replacement; each path returns to active training once the communication group is rebuilt or a spare node joins.

Efficiency falls, yet quadrupling from `{python} ElasticNodeRange.max_gpus_str` to `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.top_gpus_str` still raises throughput `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.thr_gain_mult_str`, so a lower efficiency is a declining marginal return rather than a slowdown. Panel (b) locates the loss. Tensor-parallel communication shrinks along with each worker's computation, so its share of the step never rises above `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.tp_share_str`. The decline comes instead from pipeline fill and drain and unhidden gradient synchronization, which take roughly fixed time per step while each worker's share of the batch shrinks. The pipeline bubble grows fastest of the three, for a reason the bubble fraction $(\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)$ of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-pipeline-parallelism-8748 makes explicit. A minimum allocation could follow from a completion deadline or the job's declared resource contract. It does not follow from insufficient per-worker computation at smaller scale, since with fixed global work fewer workers generally perform more work each. The upper limit likewise requires comparing additional useful progress with resize cost and the value of serving queued jobs. A real scheduler must obtain those inputs from profiling and the workload's quality target.

title: Capacity Reservation Tiers and Portfolio Optimization
caption: **Capacity Reservation Tiers and Portfolio Optimization**: This constructed portfolio combines reserved physical capacity, on-demand acquisitions, and interruptible workers. Reserved capacity covers the steady 60 percent base, on-demand the next 20 percent, and spot the peak; these shares and the demand curve are scenario assumptions. A discount commitment alone does not reserve capacity, and on-demand admission is not instantaneous. Schedulers map steady-state baseline demand to reserved capacity, diurnal spikes to on-demand instances, and restart-tolerant training to discounted spot pools. Hatching marks reserved capacity that is held while demand sits below it.
alt: Chart of share of peak capacity over one day with three horizontal tiers separated by dashed lines: reserved from 0 to 60 percent, steady base load; on-demand from 60 to 80 percent, bursts that can wait; and spot from 80 to 100 percent, restart-tolerant work. A constructed demand curve starts near 40 percent, peaks near 92 percent inside the spot tier, and settles near 50 percent. The area under the curve is filled with the color of the tier that serves it: blue below 60 percent, yellow between 60 and 80, and green above 80. Inside the reserved tier, the area above the curve is hatched and labeled reserved, idle, while the on-demand and spot tiers stay white wherever demand does not reach them.
context:
: **Cloud Capacity Reservation Tiers**: Capacity tiers trade cost and commitment against availability guarantees and interruption risk, giving the scheduler a price ladder for routing workloads by urgency and restart tolerance. {#tbl-cloud-capacity-reservation-tiers tbl-colwidths="[18,25,27,30]"}

The constructed portfolio in @fig-fleet-orchestration-capacity-reservation divides capacity into a reserved tier covering the steady 60 percent baseline, an on-demand band between 60 and 80 percent, and an interruptible spot tier serving peaks up to 92 percent. An organization with 60 percent steady-state utilization and 40 percent burst demand might reserve capacity for 60 percent of peak need, use on-demand for bursts whose deadlines tolerate admission and startup delay, and use spot for restart-tolerant work. These shares illustrate a policy rather than establish an optimal portfolio. The scheduler must match each workload's deadline and recovery contract to the capacity tier. Reserved capacity can support the steady serving load or a training job's base allocation, while spot can support elastic replicas or independent experiments that tolerate reclamation. A peak in urgent demand cannot automatically be assigned to spot merely because it lies above the reserved band.

title: The Utilization Paradox
caption: **The Utilization Paradox**: As cluster utilization approaches saturation (100 percent), job wait times increase hyperbolically and diverge near saturation, not linearly. The shaded region above 80 percent and the dashed 75 percent target illustrate headroom choices in this toy queue model, not measured GPU-utilization thresholds. Real queue delay also depends on job sizes, gang constraints, and arrival variability.
alt: Semi-log plot of toy-queue wait time vs. offered service load relative to capacity. Three directly labeled curves for small, mixed, and large jobs. Wait times explode near 100 percent. An illustrative high-load region is shaded above 80 percent. A dashed line shows an assumed headroom target at 75 percent.
context:
## Debugging Cluster Utilization {#sec-fleet-orchestration-debugging}

A cluster dashboard shows average GPU utilization stuck at 60 percent, yet developers complain about three-day queue times for small debugging jobs. Hundreds of GPUs sit idle, but no jobs are starting. Explaining the gap requires tracing the interactions among hardware topology, scheduler policies, and user behavior. Part of the paradox is the queueing arithmetic of notebook \ref{nbk-fleet-orchestration-queuing-theory-gpu-clusters}. The $\ServingUtilization/(1-\ServingUtilization)$ factor grows without bound as offered load approaches service capacity, so mean wait rises gently through moderate load and then steeply above 80 percent for small, mixed, and large workloads alike (@fig-utilization-paradox, plotted on a logarithmic scale). The curves use the notebook's exponential reference case ($\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient= 1$), so they are the gentlest version of the effect. A mixed ML queue with the notebook's representative $\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient= 3$ multiplies every curve by the larger variability factor, shifting each one upward without changing where it bends. The curves also describe offered service load rather than allocated or kernel-active GPU percentages, and their 75 percent headroom marker is an illustrative choice rather than a universal cluster threshold. Queueing explains why a busy fleet waits. A fleet whose queue is full while devices sit idle is waiting for a different reason, and finding it requires looking past the dashboard.

title: ML Goodput as a Chain of Three Boundaries
caption: **ML Goodput as a Chain of Three Boundaries**: Capacity-time becomes useful work only by crossing three boundaries in the order a job meets them, and each factor divides what crossed its boundary by what reached it. The dashed slice at the end of each row is the capacity-time lost at the boundary above that row, and the losses beside it are charged there and at no other boundary, so the three factors multiply into the share of offered capacity-time that becomes useful work. Widths are schematic, not measured.
alt: Four horizontal bars stacked top to bottom, each shorter than the one above and separated by dashed boundary lines. The top bar reads capacity-time the fleet offers. A navy chip S labeled complete allocation, held divided by offered, marks the first boundary; the next bar reads held by complete allocations, with a dashed empty slice at its right end and beside it the losses unallocated capacity, partial gangs, and fragmentation. A chip R labeled retained step, retained divided by held, marks the second boundary; the next bar reads time on retained steps, with a dashed slice and the losses startup, input waits, checkpoint pauses, and recovery and rework. A chip P labeled ideal rate, ideal divided by retained, marks the third boundary; the bottom bar is green and reads useful work, with a dashed slice and the losses exposed communication, stragglers, bubbles, memory stalls, and dispatch. Below the bars a line reads useful work equals capacity-time times S times R times P.
context:
$$\MlProductivityGoodput = \SchedulingGoodput \times \RuntimeGoodput \times \ProgramGoodput$$ {#eq-perf-ml-productivity-goodput}

The three factors multiply cleanly because each factor's denominator is the preceding factor's numerator. Scheduling goodput divides held all-allocated time by offered capacity-time, runtime goodput divides retained productive step time by all-allocated time, and program goodput divides predicted ideal time by productive step time. Adjacent numerators and denominators cancel, leaving the ideal-rate time of useful work divided by the total capacity-time the fleet offered (@fig-performance-engineering-goodput-boundaries). MPG is therefore a dimensionless fraction of fleet capacity rather than a raw throughput rate: useful fleet output equals peak capacity multiplied by MPG, and the effective cost per unit of useful work equals the cost of raw capacity divided by MPG. That telescoping cancellation also defines when the product is valid. If two factors include the same lost interval in their denominators, that loss is counted twice; if a gap falls between one factor's numerator and the next factor's denominator, the loss goes uncounted in both.

```

Recording exact software versions in the system-state contract is essential because software upgrades alone can shift delivered throughput by a large multiple on identical silicon. Between September 2023 and April 2025, NVIDIA submitted the same eight-GPU DGX H100 node to four consecutive MLPerf Inference rounds while upgrading its inference stack from TensorRT 9.0 to 10.8 [@reddi2020; @mlcommons2025inference]. Across those four rounds, offline throughput rose `{python} SoftwareGains.gptj_gain_mult_str` on GPT-J, `{python} SoftwareGains.llama_gain_mult_str` on Llama 2 70B, and `{python} SoftwareGains.sdxl_gain_mult_str` on Stable Diffusion XL (@fig-mlperf-software-gains), whereas ResNet-50 and BERT—whose kernels were already mature—remained flat. Any before-and-after experiment that straddles a framework or compiler upgrade therefore confounds the upgrade with the optimization under test.

title: Localizing a Lost Factor
caption: **Localizing a Lost Factor**: The three records are read from the top, cheapest and most complete first, and each settles one factor of goodput. Scheduler records cover every job and settle scheduling goodput, but they see a held allocation only as a closed block. The job timeline settles runtime goodput and shows that retained steps run slower than planned without showing why. Step traces, collected for sampled ranks over a short window, settle program goodput, and their highlighted window expands into the profiling hierarchy of @fig-optimization-hierarchy. Widths are schematic, not measured.
alt: Three rungs stacked top to bottom, each with a navy chip, a name, the losses it shows, a line reading cannot see, and a coverage label on the left, and a small timeline on the right. Chips S, R, and P are joined by downward arrows. Rung S, scheduler records, every job, free: a lane with a hatched queue interval, a hatched partial gang interval with rising gray steps, a marker labeled gang complete, and a long gray block labeled held, contents not visible. Rung R, job timeline, every job, cheap: a lane of gray retained-step blocks broken by tan blocks labeled startup, checkpoint, restart and rework, and checkpoint, with a red cross above the restart; above the lane a wavy step-time line runs above a dashed line labeled plan. Rung P, step traces, sampled ranks, costly: an orange compute lane and a violet comm lane, with dashed empty gaps in the compute lane labeled exposed comm and dispatch. A navy window on each upper timeline opens through a shaded wedge into the rung below, and the window on the step trace opens into a dashed box labeled kernels and counters, the profiling hierarchy.
context:
For these three records to enforce the accounting boundaries of @sec-performance-engineering-goodput-boundaries, their instrumentation must align with those boundaries. If a job timeline logs only total step duration without separating data-loader stalls, every input wait is folded into step time and a runtime goodput loss masquerades as a program goodput loss. Similarly, because a single straggling accelerator stretches synchronous step time across every peer in its collective group, identifying which rank caused the slowdown requires lightweight per-rank step timers inside the job timeline.

Our running Llama 2 70B training job illustrates how the three rungs work together. Suppose that after one week on the shared cluster, the job has retained substantially fewer steps than predicted by a plan that assumed full-week allocation at the single-node step rate. Consulting the scheduler records first reveals that the job held partial node allocations before its full 16-node gang assembled—a scheduling loss quantified in @sec-performance-engineering-scheduling-evidence. Reading the job timeline from that gang-complete timestamp next isolates the initial startup delay, synchronous checkpoint pauses, steps re-executed after failures, and a modest input-stall fraction, which @sec-performance-engineering-runtime-composition composes into runtime goodput. The same timeline also shows that every retained step ran longer than the single-node baseline from day one, proving that part of the shortfall lies in program goodput. Only at that point does the team trigger step traces on one data-parallel group over a brief window. Because per-rank timeline counters show no single outlier rank, the team inspects intervals common to all ranks and finds inter-node gradient collectives extending past the backward pass—the exposed communication analyzed in @sec-performance-engineering-exposed-communication. Each rung answers the exact question that the others cannot (@fig-performance-engineering-localization-ladder).

caption: **Runtime Loss versus Job Size**: Each bar recomputes the five terms of @eq-perf-runtime-loss-composition for the running example at one job size, from `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.n_min_str` to `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.n_max_str` GPUs, holding the 70B checkpoint, the recovery budget, the data stall ratio, the preemption budget, and the week of held time at the running example's values and recomputing the Young-Daly interval at each size. Input waits and preemption stay flat and dominate small jobs, while checkpoint waste and recovery grow with device count, pass input waits near `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.crossover_gpus_str` GPUs (dotted line), and lift the loss from `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.loss_min_pct_str` to `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.loss_max_pct_str`, above the loss of at most `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.llama_loss_pct_str` implied by the effective training time Llama 3 405B reported on its dedicated cluster (hollow bar) [@dubey2024llama].
alt: Stacked bar chart of runtime loss as a percent of held time against job size, with eight bars at 128, 256, 512, 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, 8,192, and 16,384 GPUs. Each bar stacks, from the bottom, input waits in light tan at about 7.7 percent, preemption in light violet at about 1.4 percent, a gray startup sliver too thin to see, checkpoints in medium brown, and recovery in dark brown. The bottom two segments are the same height in every bar, while the two brown segments on top grow from slivers at 128 GPUs to about 4.8 and 4.3 percent at 16,384. Totals above the bars read 10, 10, 10, 11, 11, 13, 15, and 18 percent; the first bar is labeled running example. A dotted vertical line just left of the 16,384 bar is labeled checkpoints plus recovery pass input waits. Beside the last bar a narrow hollow bar reaches 10 percent, labeled at most 10 percent, Llama 3 405B, dedicated, cited. A key at the upper left names the five terms.
context:
Because the overall runtime goodput is already close to what a well-run job achieves, the engineering lesson lies in how the loss is divided. A team consulting only @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability might invest in faster checkpoint writes and warm restarts, yet on this 128-GPU job those levers can recover at most the `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.ckpt_waste_pct_str` and `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.failure_term_pct_str` shares assigned to them by the composition. Meanwhile, the input pipeline sized in @sec-storage-pipeline-equation governs roughly `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.input_vs_failure_mult_str` as much held time. Without a preemption cap, the `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.preempt_unbudgeted_per_day_str` forced preemptions per day that @sec-fleet-orchestration-preemption-cascades models for a low-priority run would consume `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.preempt_unbudgeted_pct_str` of held time—exceeding every other term and breaking the small-loss regime of the first-order sum.

Both job size and job duration reorder these terms. As device count grows, checkpoint waste and failure recovery expand until their combined loss overtakes input waits near `{python} RuntimeLossScaling.crossover_gpus_str` GPUs (@fig-performance-engineering-runtime-scaling). Similarly, the same `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.t_startup_min_str` startup cost that is negligible over a week consumes about `{python} RuntimeGoodputComposition.startup_short_pct_str` of an evaluation job that holds its allocation for only an hour. The composition does not pick a universal winner among these levers; rather, it shows each subsystem owner how much held time their lever can actually reach—a comparison no single subsystem can make in isolation.

title: Iron Law Diagnostic Flowchart
caption: **Iron Law Diagnostic Flowchart**: A triage flow for a job or replica whose retained steps miss their step-time target. Low accelerator activity sends the diagnosis right, toward waits, and high activity sends it down to the roofline. The I/O and CPU branches identify input waits and host preprocessing, which are runtime goodput losses at the input boundary, so a yes on either sends the reader back to @sec-performance-engineering-runtime-goodput rather than to the program. The communication-overhead leaf is exposed communication, a program goodput loss in the Fleet Law's communication term. Only a busy device reaches the roofline panel, whose memory-bound and compute-bound leaves are candidate levers to test, not prescriptions. Fusion and tiling are developed in @sec-performance-engineering-program-goodput, serving precision and speculative decoding in @sec-inference-scale, and expert routing in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-expert-parallelism-mixture-experts-bc45. Every path returns to re-profiling.
alt: Troubleshooting flowchart starting from a box reading Target is missed. A GPU-utilization check sends its yes branch right along an overhead lane: an I/O-bound check whose yes branch leads to a green More DL workers box, then a CPU-bound check whose yes branch leads to a green Offload preprocessing box, and whose no branch ends at a violet Comm overhead box. The utilization check's no branch leads down into a panel titled Intensity greater than ridge, which draws a small roofline: a blue rising slope over a blue memory-bound region meets a flat orange ceiling over an orange compute-bound region at a dot marked ridge. Below the blue region, a blue group holds operator fusion and INT4 or speculative decoding; below the orange region, an orange group holds FP8 math and MoE routing. Every remedy joins a bus into a Re-profile workload box, and a dashed loop labeled iterate until the target is met returns to the start.
context:
:::

Systematic triage of a slow step begins outside the accelerator kernels. If a step misses its duration target while accelerator utilization is low, the bottleneck lies in input stalls, host preprocessing, or exposed communication—because optimizing a kernel cannot speed up a device that is waiting for work to arrive. Only when the accelerator is actively executing kernels does diagnosis turn to whether those kernels are bound by arithmetic throughput or memory bandwidth, evaluated against the roofline's ridge point (the operational intensity where the memory-bandwidth slope meets the compute ceiling). Organized in order of application, these checks form a diagnostic decision tree (@fig-iron-law-flowchart) whose initial branches exit program goodput altogether. A device waiting for its next batch or for host-side preprocessing is losing runtime goodput at the input boundary, which returns the investigation to @sec-performance-engineering-runtime-goodput.

title: From Annotations to Collectives
caption: **From Annotations to Collectives**: The running example's mesh places the model axis of `{python} FleetCapacityOpening.tp_width_str` GPUs inside each node and the data axis across the `{python} FleetCapacityOpening.example_nodes_str`. In one feed-forward block, the column-split gate and up projections need no exchange, and the row-split output projection leaves partial sums that propagation completes with a model-axis AllReduce in every layer, over NVLink and already inside the node baseline. The weight gradients are reduced once per step along the data axis across the fabric (a ReduceScatter and an AllGather when the optimizer state is sharded), and that exchange is the time the fleet step spends beyond the node baseline. Schematic; representative nodes only.
alt: Two panels. Left panel, device mesh: four tall node frames labeled node 0, node 1, node 2, and node 15, with an ellipsis between node 2 and node 15. Each frame holds eight stacked GPU boxes joined by short solid amber links. An upward arrow on the left is labeled model axis, 8 GPUs, NVLink, inside a node; a rightward arrow below is labeled data axis, 16 nodes, network fabric, across nodes. The bottom GPU of node 0 is solid navy; the other GPUs of node 0 and the bottom GPU of each other node are light blue, and the bottom GPUs connect through a dashed amber line running beneath the frames. A legend reads one GPU and GPUs it exchanges with. Right panel, one feed-forward block, top to bottom: a box x, batch split on data axis; two weight glyphs with one highlighted column strip each, labeled W gate and W up, columns, model; a box gated activation, no exchange; a weight glyph with one highlighted row strip labeled W out, rows, model; an arrow labeled partial sums into a solid amber box reading AllReduce, model axis, NVLink, inside a node, every layer, already in the node baseline; an arrow labeled weight gradients into a dashed amber box reading gradient AllReduce, data axis, fabric, across nodes, once per step, time beyond the node baseline.
context:
the mesh has a `model` axis of `{python} FleetCapacityOpening.tp_width_str` devices and a `data` axis spanning the sixteen nodes. The second input is a small set of sharding annotations\index{Sharding annotation!mesh axes} on key tensors, declaring which tensor dimension is partitioned along which mesh axis. The input batch dimension is split along the `data` axis. Within each feed-forward block, the gate and up projection weights are split column-wise along the `model` axis while the output projection weight is split row-wise. The attention projections are split by head along the `model` axis. Every other intermediate tensor in the program remains unannotated.

From those few seeds, the compiler derives the rest of the parallel program through sharding propagation\index{Sharding propagation!inserted collectives}, walking the computation graph to infer the output layout of each operator from the layouts of its inputs. Multiplying an input activation by a column-split weight matrix yields an activation split along its feature dimension; the subsequent element-wise gated activation preserves that layout without communication. Next, multiplying that feature-split activation by a row-split output weight produces a partial sum on each device, prompting the compiler to insert an AllReduce along the `model` axis to complete the projection. The backward pass mirrors this derivation. Each device's weight gradients cover only its local shard along the `model` axis but represent partial sums across the `data` axis, so the compiler automatically inserts a cross-node gradient reduction along the `data` axis (or a ReduceScatter paired with a forward AllGather when optimizer state is sharded). The resulting communication schedule matches the hand-partitioned Megatron-style layer of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-tensor-parallelism-d76e, yet it is synthesized automatically from single-device model code that contains no explicit collective calls (@fig-performance-engineering-device-mesh). Wherever two incompatible tensor layouts meet in the graph, propagation resolves the mismatch by inserting an AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll, or point-to-point permutation.

title: Overlap on a Shared Device
caption: **Overlap on a Shared Device**: One step of three kernels and one collective on a compute stream and a communication stream. Serialized, the collective runs after the kernels and is exposed. Overlapped on a device with resources to spare, it hides completely behind the kernels. Overlapped on a real device, the collective's own kernels take streaming multiprocessors and memory bandwidth from the kernel beside it, which runs longer, so the step ends between the two. Only a measured step shows where between them it ends. Durations are schematic, not measured.
alt: Three timelines stacked top to bottom, each with a compute lane of blue kernel blocks and a comm lane below it, and a dark vertical bar marking where the step ends. Dotted vertical guides run through all three, labeled ideal overlap end and serialized end at the bottom. In panel a, serialized, three kernels run back to back and an amber block labeled exposed follows them on the comm lane, so the step ends at the serialized guide. In panel b, overlapped, no contention, an amber block labeled hidden runs beneath the second kernel, and the step ends at the ideal overlap guide. In panel c, overlapped, shared device, the same hidden amber block runs beneath the second kernel, whose end is extended by a short red block, with the red word contention beside it; the third kernel starts after the red block, so the step ends between the two guides.
section: Inputs are ready on producer_stream; gradients do not alias A or B.
context:
:::

Placing work on separate streams enables concurrency, but it does not partition the underlying hardware resources.\index{SM partitioning!resource contention} Because collective libraries such as NCCL\index{NCCL!communication collectives} launch their own GPU kernels to copy, pack, and reduce buffers across NVLink and network interfaces, an overlapped collective competes directly with concurrent matrix multiplications for streaming multiprocessors (SMs), L2 cache, and HBM bandwidth [@pati2024t3]. In a kernel timeline, successful stream overlap shifts the collective bar underneath the compute kernels, but resource contention stretches the duration of those compute kernels, causing the step to finish later than an idealized contention-free model would predict (@fig-performance-engineering-overlap-contention). Overlapping a collective improves program goodput only if the communication time removed from the critical path exceeds the contention delay added to the concurrent computation—a net balance that only an end-to-end step measurement can verify.

title: Fusion Across the HBM Boundary
caption: **Fusion Across the HBM Boundary**: Separate kernels write each intermediate tensor to HBM and read it back for the next operation. A fused kernel keeps these intermediates in registers or SRAM as it executes the same chain. The diagram isolates intermediate traffic; common input, weight, and final-output transfers remain outside the drawing. The fused schedule assumes compatible operations and enough on-chip storage for the live working set, including normalization state.
alt: Top: separate linear, activation, and normalization kernels connect through two intermediate tensors in an HBM region. Amber arrows mark a write and read for each intermediate. Bottom: the same three operations connect directly inside one registers and SRAM region labeled fused kernel.
context:
Operator fusion\index{Operator fusion!fleet gain} merges a chain of consecutive operations into a single GPU kernel so that intermediate activations remain in registers or shared memory (SRAM) instead of round-tripping through HBM, while replacing multiple host kernel launches with one. It therefore reduces both the memory traffic volume $\DataVolume$ and the host-dispatch portion of $\Latency$. For a linear layer followed by an activation and normalization at the hidden dimension of Llama 2 70B and a batch of `{python} FusionTrafficCalc.batch_size_str` tokens, eliminating the HBM write-and-read of the two intermediates cuts total modeled HBM traffic by a factor of about `{python} FusionTrafficCalc.traffic_ratio_mult_str`. The hardware limit on fusion is register and SRAM pressure: keeping too many live intermediates per thread reduces SM occupancy and can eventually slow the kernel down. In a profile, successful fusion manifests as fewer kernel launches, fewer measured HBM bytes transferred, and a shorter step duration (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-kernel-levers-fusion).

The boundary comparison in @fig-fusion-before-after shows which intermediate transfers fusion can remove.

title: Tiled Attention and Online State
caption: **Tiled Attention and Online State**: For one query tile, the kernel reads relevant key/value tiles from HBM and updates on-chip state after each block. This state contains running row maxima, normalization sums, and output accumulators; the feedback path carries it into the next block. After the last required block, the kernel normalizes and writes the output tile. Score tiles remain temporary on-chip values rather than a sequence-by-sequence HBM allocation. Another query tile can require reading the same key/value tiles again; the diagram does not imply one global read.
alt: An HBM region holds query tiles, key/value tiles, and output. Read arrows enter query and key/value tiles in a registers and SRAM region. Both feed block attention, which updates online state. A feedback arrow returns that state to block attention. The state connects to an output tile with a final write arrow returning to HBM.
context:
Tiling\index{FlashAttention!fleet gain} partitions a computation into blocks sized to fit in on-chip SRAM so that each operand fetched from HBM is reused across many arithmetic operations before eviction. Applied to self-attention (as in FlashAttention [@dao2022]), tiling evaluates attention block by block using online softmax rescaling, avoiding ever materializing the quadratic sequence-by-sequence score matrix in HBM. For a single attention head of our 70B model at a sequence length of `{python} FlashAttentionSavings.seq_len_str` tokens, an idealized traffic bound shows that eliminating the score and probability matrix round-trips reduces HBM traffic by roughly `{python} FlashAttentionSavings.savings_mult_str`. Beyond cutting $\DataVolume$, tiling frees substantial HBM capacity, which training jobs reinvest in longer context lengths or larger microbatches and serving replicas reinvest in larger key-value caches. The trade-off is extra arithmetic for online rescaling and, during backpropagation, recomputing attention scores on the fly rather than storing them. Success is verified by the disappearance of quadratic score-matrix allocations and HBM traffic in the memory trace (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-kernel-levers-tiling).

The working set in @fig-performance-engineering-flashattention-tiling stays local while attention consumes successive key/value tiles.

```

This ratio rule is strongly asymmetric when the factors start at different levels. A program optimization that lifted the running example's program goodput from `{python} GoodputDecomposition.program_str` to its single-node ceiling of `{python} GoodputDecomposition.program_ceiling_str` would increase the product by `{python} GoodputDecomposition.p_ceiling_rel_pct_str`. It would therefore still yield a net gain even if it sacrificed up to `{python} TradeProductRule.runtime_affordable_pct_str` of the job's runtime goodput (@fig-performance-engineering-iso-goodput). A runtime lever has no comparable margin to spend: even if every runtime loss were eliminated, a runtime goodput of `{python} GoodputDecomposition.runtime_str` could rise by at most `{python} TradeProductRule.runtime_headroom_pct_str`. Because a factor already near one has little relative headroom left to offer, a trade that spends runtime goodput to purchase program goodput merits careful measurement, whereas a trade in the opposite direction warrants immediate skepticism.

title: End-to-End Inference Pipeline
caption: **End-to-End Inference Pipeline**: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request's latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute.
alt: Two regions labeled CPU and GPU. In the CPU region, requests flow down through a load balancer and a tokenizer. Token IDs pass right to a prefill box in the GPU region, which writes to a KV cache box. A decode box reads from and appends to the KV cache, loops on itself, and sends generated token IDs left to a detokenize box that feeds a response stream. Below, a horizontal strip divides one request's latency into route, pre, prefill, decode steps, and post segments, the decode segment ticked into per-token steps, with brackets marking time to first token and TPOT times output tokens.

title: Batching Strategies Compared
caption: **Batching Strategies Compared**: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay.
alt: Three stacked timelines labeled (a) no batching, (b) static batching, and (c) dynamic batching. Each shows four request rows R1 to R4 with arrival ticks, gray wait segments, blue forward-pass segments, and hatched padding, above a GPU row. The GPU row shows four single-request passes in (a), one four-request pass in (b), and two two-request passes in (c). Dashed violet lines mark when each batch is dispatched.
context:
### Batching across model architectures {#sec-inference-scale-batching-differs-across-model-types-2026}

Holding arriving requests until a fixed batch fills forces early arrivals to wait and pads shorter inputs with wasted work, whereas running every request immediately leaves later arrivals queued behind one-request passes that underuse the GPU. Batching efficiency depends on how computation scales with batch size relative to memory and communication constraints, and the execution timeline in @fig-batching-strategies separates waiting to form a batch from waiting for the accelerator to become available. Unbatched serving adds no batch-formation delay, but later requests can still queue behind earlier forward passes. Static batching consolidates all four illustrated requests into one pass, adding formation delay and padding to accommodate different input lengths. Dynamic batching closes formation windows at fixed time intervals ($\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$), producing two passes with two requests each in this example. The window limits intentional formation delay; it does not bound total queueing when ready batches arrive faster than the server can execute them.

title: Decode Inherits the Bandwidth Deficit
caption: **Decode Inherits the Bandwidth Deficit**: Peak compute and memory bandwidth for four accelerator generations, normalized to the V100. Compute rises `{python} MemoryWallRatios.compute_mult_str` against bandwidth's `{python} MemoryWallRatios.bandwidth_mult_str`. In weight-bandwidth-bound decode, each iteration loads the active weights and reuses them across its output tokens; at fixed batch size, bandwidth growth constrains the gain. These hardware ratios are not measured workload speedups. Specifications are dense peak rates and bandwidths from the vendor datasheets recorded in the chapter's data file.
alt: Line chart normalized to the V100 across V100, A100, H100, and B200, showing peak compute reaching 18 times and memory bandwidth 8.9 times by the B200, with the widening gap between the two lines shaded and labeled bandwidth deficit.
context:
:::

Recommendation systems shift the bottleneck again: sparse embedding lookup\index{Recommendation system!embedding lookup bottleneck} can limit throughput before dense computation does. Grouping sparse accesses improves locality and distributes lookup work across shards, while batching the dense stages improves matrix multiplication throughput. The serving policy must therefore account for both stages and the communication between them rather than infer the bottleneck from the model category alone.

For every configuration it records the output tokens per second each user receives, called interactivity (the reciprocal of TPOT), and the output tokens per second each GPU delivers across all users. @Fig-throughput-interactivity plots `{python} ServingFrontier.config_count_str` such configurations at FP8 precision and traces, for each accelerator, the frontier of configurations that no other configuration beats on both rates. Every frontier falls as interactivity rises, because a faster stream per user permits fewer concurrent sequences per decode step. The best B200 configuration delivers about `{python} ServingFrontier.b200_peak_str` output tokens per second per GPU when each user receives about `{python} ServingFrontier.b200_peak_tps_user_str` tokens per second. It delivers about `{python} ServingFrontier.b200_at_high_str` when each user must receive at least `{python} ServingFrontier.high_tps_user_str`, a `{python} ServingFrontier.b200_span_mult_str` difference in per-GPU output paid for faster streams. The interactivity target alone moves per-GPU output by that much, so it must be fixed before any two throughput figures can be compared.

The same frontiers separate hardware generations by more than their datasheets do. At `{python} ServingFrontier.target_tps_user_str` tokens per second per user, the best measured H100 configuration delivers about `{python} ServingFrontier.h100_at_target_str` output tokens per second per GPU and the best GB200 NVL72 configuration about `{python} ServingFrontier.gb200_at_target_str`, a `{python} ServingFrontier.gen_mult_str` difference. The benchmark does not apportion the gap, but the candidates lie mostly beyond peak arithmetic, in memory bandwidth and capacity per GPU, a 72-GPU NVLink domain that keeps experts and KV state off slower networks, and platform-tuned serving software. A throughput figure quoted without its latency target therefore says little about either system.

caption: **Static vs. Continuous Batching**: In static batching (a), completed slots cannot be reused until the longest request finishes, although completed responses may already be released. Continuous batching (b) admits waiting requests into freed slots at iteration boundaries, starting each with a prefill step. Over the eight iterations shown, 20 of 32 slot-iterations do useful work under static batching and all 32 under continuous batching; the hatched idle slots are the capacity recovered when arrivals and cache capacity permit.
alt: Two stacked grids of four slots by eight iterations. Top: static batching, where requests R1 to R4 end at iterations 3, 8, 5, and 4, and every later cell in the finished slots is hatched as idle; a note reads 20 of 32 slots busy. Bottom: continuous batching, where requests R5, R6, and R7 enter the freed slots with a dark prefill cell and continue decoding, leaving no idle cells; a note reads 32 of 32 slots busy. Final-token cells are green.
section: Continuous batching for large language model (LLM) inference {#sec-inference-scale-continuous-batching-llm-inference-f8e6}
context:
```

Admitting, completing, and refilling slots on every iteration lets waiting work use capacity released before the longest sequence finishes. The illustrated preemption path adds HBM-to-CPU-DRAM transfers under memory pressure, so recovered capacity must repay both scheduling and state-movement costs. Counted in slot-iterations (@fig-continuous-batching-comparison), fixed membership leaves only 20 of 32 productive, while continuous admission fills all 32 under the illustrated arrival and capacity assumptions. Prefill and decode cells do not necessarily take equal time. Slot occupancy therefore measures the opportunity; the realized throughput gain depends on how much longer the inserted prefill cells take than the decode steps they share an iteration with.

title: Feature-Parallel Batching Pipeline
caption: **Feature-Parallel Batching Pipeline**: Requests are batched by feature type (Users, Items, Context) and dispatched to specialized embedding servers in parallel. The retrieved embeddings are then concatenated and processed by the dense ranking head. This architecture enables scaling to trillions of parameters by decoupling embedding storage from dense compute.
alt: Left to right: a request enters a feature split box, by type, which fans out to three embedding tables labeled user, item, and context embeddings. Each table is drawn as rows split across two side-by-side shards, shard 0 and shard 1, with the one looked-up row filled solid: the user row in shard 0, the item row in shard 1, and the context row in shard 0. Amber lines labeled gather, concatenate carry the three rows into one stacked vector of segments U, I, and C. The vector feeds a ranking head, dense MLP, drawn as three narrowing layers, which produces a ranked output drawn as four green bars of decreasing length.
context:
A single recommendation request may issue thousands of sparse lookups across embedding tables holding billions of entries before the dense ranking head can score a candidate. Grouping requests solely at the dense MLP therefore leaves the service bottlenecked on scattered memory reads and cross-server transfers. While fixed-shape vision inputs allow simple request grouping and autoregressive generation pairs iteration-level admission with KV-cache management (and with prefill-decode scheduling in @sec-inference-scale-prefill-decode), recommendation systems must also batch around the placement of sparse state. *Sparse embedding lookups* can dominate memory access and communication in an embedding-heavy workload even when *dense matrix multiplications* account for much of the arithmetic. Grouping those accesses by feature type and destination—feature-parallel batching\index{Feature-parallel batching}—improves lookup locality at each shard, complementing request batching in the dense stages.

Recommendation batching starts by grouping work around embedding locality rather than request shape. An incoming request splits across user, item, and context feature types to query sharded embedding tables concurrently, after which a gather barrier concatenates the retrieved representations for the dense MLP ranking head (@fig-feature-parallel-pipeline).

While the model fits easily at small context lengths, the KV cache (sloped lines) eventually consumes all remaining HBM. At 128K context, a batch size of 2 is physically impossible on a single GPU (`{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` + `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.batch_example_kv_gb_str` exceeds `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str`), forcing the system to either reduce batch size, change the state representation, or distribute the state across devices.

Sloped lines for batch 1, 2, 4, and 8 rise from the weights line; batches 8, 4, and 2 stop at open circles where they meet the capacity line, batch 8 earliest at about 17K tokens, while batch 1 stays below the line out to 128K tokens.

```

Even when a 4-bit quantized 70B model occupies only `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` of an `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str` H100, admitting a second 128K-token request pushes the combined weight and KV-cache footprint past `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str` and exhausts HBM before execution resources saturate. Increasing batch size in LLM serving therefore hits the KV cache wall\index{KV cache!capacity wall} long before compute binds. @Fig-kv-cache-wall leaves the reference replica to show the wall on a single H100. It combines an idealized `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` weight payload for a quantized 70B model with its full-attention, eight-KV-head GQA state.
