```

Applied to a fixed `{python} RegionalGridCarbon.energy_mwh_str` facility-energy account, regional electricity factors change operational carbon by nearly two orders of magnitude (@fig-carbon-intensity). The assumed factors range from `{python} RegionalGridCarbon.lowest_g_str` for Norway (`{python} RegionalGridCarbon.lowest_t_str` $\text{CO}_2$ for the workload) to `{python} RegionalGridCarbon.highest_g_str` for Poland (`{python} RegionalGridCarbon.highest_t_str` $\text{CO}_2$), producing a calculated `{python} RegionalGridCarbon.spread_mult_str` emissions ratio. These rounded annual-average factors [@iea2023weo], the same ones notebook \ref{nbk-sustainable-ai-geography-carbon} used for Quebec and Poland, illustrate the effect of placement while holding facility energy constant. They are not measurements of the same job run at every site. Actual placement decisions require time-matched grid evidence and must include changes in facility overhead and the energy needed to move or resume the work.

title: The Carbon Lifecycle of an ML System
caption: **The Carbon Lifecycle of an ML System**: Manufacturing contributes embodied carbon, while training and inference contribute operational carbon through energy, facility overhead, and grid intensity. Block widths show timing, not magnitude. The relative size of each term is workload-specific: serving volume, grid factor, and hardware lifetime determine which one dominates.
alt: Three lanes on a shared time axis with a dashed marker for when the hardware enters service and a bracket for service life. Manufacturing is one brown block before the hardware enters service; training is one orange block after it, marked once; inference is a long row of small orange blocks, marked recurs per request, extending to the end of service life. Each lane lists its drivers, and the lifecycle carbon equation below sums the embodied, training, and inference terms.
context:
$$\text{CO}_{2,\text{lifecycle}} = \text{CO}_{2,\text{training}} + \text{CO}_{2,\text{inference}} + \text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied}}$$ {#eq-lifecycle-carbon}

Each term has its own physical drivers (@fig-carbon-lifecycle). The embodied term $\text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied}}$ is fixed before the hardware runs, at roughly `{python} AcceleratorEmbodiedFootprints.a100_kg_str` to `{python} AcceleratorEmbodiedFootprints.h100_kg_str` CO~2~e per accelerator for the devices priced above. The training term $\text{CO}_{2,\text{training}}$ is a one-time cost set by cluster scale, PUE, and checkpoint I/O, while the inference term $\text{CO}_{2,\text{inference}}$ recurs for as long as request traffic and KV-cache residency keep serving replicas powered. Their relative proportions therefore shift over the deployment lifetime, as the worked account in notebook \ref{nbk-sustainable-ai-lifecycle-carbon-estimation} and the serving crossover in @sec-sustainable-ai-inference-energy-costs-aec9 show.

title: The Energy Gap
caption: **The Energy Gap**: US data center electricity consumption more than tripled from `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2014_twh_str` (2014) to `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2024_twh_str` (2024). LBNL projects `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_ref_twh_str` by 2030 in its reference case, within a range of `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_low_value_str` to `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_high_twh_str` [@shehabi2024united; @shehabi2026united], with AI workloads treated as an important driver of growth. At the high end, data centers would consume approximately `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_high_share_str` of US electricity, motivating evaluation of the generation, transmission, and connection capacity needed to serve that projected demand.
alt: Bar chart of US data center electricity: gray bars at 58 TWh in 2014 and 192 TWh in 2024, and a 2030 projection drawn as a hatched bar up to the 521 TWh low bound topped by a dashed outline band that extends to the 843 TWh high bound, with the 649 TWh reference case marked inside the band.
context:
```

The United States alone illustrates how cloud and AI infrastructure can reshape national energy planning. US data center electricity consumption more than tripled from `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2014_twh_str` in 2014 to `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2024_twh_str` in 2024, reaching `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2024_share_str` of national supply, according to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) estimates that @fig-energy-gap plots [@shehabi2024united; @shehabi2026united]. LBNL's reference case projects `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_ref_twh_str` for 2030, about `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_ref_share_str` of US electricity, inside a scenario range of `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_low_value_str` to `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_high_twh_str` [@shehabi2026united]. These scenarios describe possible demand, not a measured capacity ceiling. They motivate evaluating efficiency gains alongside the generation, transmission, and connection capacity needed to serve that demand.

title: Direct and Indirect Water Accounts
caption: **Direct and Indirect Water Accounts**: An evaporative cooling tower (a) rejects heat by consuming water withdrawn from the local watershed, returning only its blowdown. A dry cooler (b) draws no local cooling water but spends more electricity on fans, and generating that electricity consumes water in the power plant's watershed. Water is therefore a separate, location-weighted account traded against energy. The schematic shows which flows exist, not their sizes.
alt: Two panels. In panel a, an orange electricity arrow runs from a power plant box labeled off-site water to a data center box, a gray heat arrow runs to a blue cooling tower box, a brown evaporation arrow rises to a consumed box drawn with a heavy brown outline, a thick blue withdrawal arrow rises from a local watershed band to the tower, and a thinner blue blowdown arrow returns to the watershed. In panel b, a thicker orange arrow labeled electricity plus fan power runs from a power plant box labeled more off-site water to the data center, heat goes to a dry cooler box, a gray warm air arrow rises to an ambient air box, and a dashed gray line labeled no direct draw connects the cooler to the local watershed.
context:
A `{python} CoolingTowerWaterUse.it_load_mw_str` data center with evaporative cooling towers can consume well over 100 million liters of water per year, depending on climate and cooling design, which has become a significant concern in water-stressed regions. At the evaporative WUE of `{python} CoolingTowerWaterUse.wue_str` L/kWh used earlier, continuous operation consumes about `{python} CoolingTowerWaterUse.annual_water_million_liters_str` million liters per year, roughly `{python} CoolingTowerWaterUse.household_years_low_str`--`{python} CoolingTowerWaterUse.household_years_high_str` household-years of water use under the earlier annual household baseline. As ML data centers grow to `{python} CoolingTowerWaterUse.campus_power_mw_str` and beyond, their water footprint becomes a meaningful factor in local resource planning.

Dry coolers use fans to blow air over a radiator without evaporating cooling water. They avoid that direct water consumption, but the added fan electricity carries its own water burden at the generating plant, in a different watershed from the facility (@fig-datacenter-water-accounts). Heat rejection depends on the temperature difference between coolant and ambient air, so hot weather can reduce capacity or require more fan power. Hybrid designs use dry cooling when conditions permit and evaporative assistance when needed, trading water consumption against electrical demand and thermal margin.

The recommendation-model bars divide roughly evenly between training (light and mid orange) and inference (solid orange), while the public open-source baselines report training-only footprints (hatched gray outline), showing that inference serving at scale can rival or exceed training emissions for deployed systems. Meta production models stack a light orange offline training segment, a thin mid orange online training segment, and a solid saturated orange inference segment, all in one orange family; the segments are labeled directly on the RM-1 bar. Public benchmark models are white bars with gray hatching. RM-1 is longest, near 0.85 million kg, and a bracket over its inference segment reads inference rivals training. context:
[^fn-nas-carbon-footprint]: **Neural architecture search (NAS) carbon cost**\index{Neural architecture search!carbon cost}: The ~284,000 kg CO~2~e figure from @strubell2019 represents an unoptimized Evolved Transformer search that drops sharply when accounting for TPU hardware, grid mix, and proxy tasks [@patterson2021carbon]. The systems lesson is boundary discipline: search, tuning, and failed trials belong inside the carbon accounting boundary, but reusable architecture search should be amortized across all downstream deployments.

The GPT-3 calculation in notebook \ref{nbk-sustainable-ai-carbon-cost-training} put one training run at hundreds of trans-Atlantic passenger round trips. Such run-level comparisons convey scale, but they do not by themselves describe the footprint of a deployed service. The operational lesson is that carbon accounting must distinguish training from recurring inference over a declared observation period. Meta's recommendation workloads (RM-1 through RM-5) split operational emissions roughly evenly between training and inference, while inference dominates its language-model example (@fig-meta-analysis). The public baselines, including GPT-3 and BERT-NAS, report training only; their bars do not establish a lifetime training-to-inference ratio. For high-traffic Archetype B deployments (@sec-introduction-archetype-b-dlrm-scale-fa6d), both recurring serving and model updates belong in the account before deciding which phase offers the larger reduction.

The accelerator-only boundary counts active accelerators on the most efficiently used machines; the full-stack boundary also counts host processors and memory, idle machines provisioned for latency and availability, and data-center overhead, across the whole fleet. Hatched segments are components that the accelerator-only boundary leaves out. Data from Table 1 of @elsworth2025measuring.

The accelerator-only bar counts 0.10 for active accelerators, with hatched uncounted segments for host CPU and memory 0.04, idle machines 0.02, and overhead 0.01. The full-stack bar counts active accelerators 0.14, host CPU and memory 0.06, idle machines 0.02, and data-center overhead 0.02, totaling 0.24, labeled 2.4 times the accelerator-only total.
context:
```

A production measurement shows how large that account is. Google instrumented the fleet serving its Gemini assistant and attributed energy to the median text prompt in May 2025 across every component of the serving stack [@elsworth2025measuring]. The full-stack figure is `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.full_energy_str` per prompt (@fig-prompt-energy-boundary), of which the active accelerators account for only `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.accel_share_pct_str`. The host processors and memory that feed them add `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.host_share_pct_str`, and idle machines held for latency and availability together with facility overhead add another `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.idle_overhead_share_pct_str`. Counting only active accelerators on the most efficiently used machines, the boundary many published estimates use, yields `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.narrow_energy_str`, a `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.boundary_ratio_mult_str` understatement of the same workload. The measured prompt also sits at about a quarter of the `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.worked_example_energy_str` per query assumed in the worked example above, a reminder that per-query energy is a property of a specific model, serving stack, and utilization rather than a constant. The same study reports that software and utilization improvements cut the median prompt's energy `{python} PromptEnergyBoundary.year_reduction_mult_str` in a single year, so a per-query figure also carries a date.

title: AI System Lifecycle
caption: **AI System Lifecycle**: Four stages in sequence, each dropping the burden it adds, with a recovery loop from decommissioning back to manufacture. Design decisions fix much of the load the later stages carry; manufacturing adds embodied carbon, water, and chemicals; use adds operational energy at the grid's carbon intensity; decommissioning adds e-waste unless hardware is refurbished or its components recovered.
alt: Four stage boxes left to right: design, manufacture, use, and decommission, each with two activities. Manufacture drops a brown box of embodied carbon, water, and chemicals; use drops an orange box of operational energy times grid intensity; decommission drops a box of e-waste unless recovered. A dashed line from design runs under all three burden boxes, labeled load set at design time. A dashed green loop labeled refurbish or recover returns from decommission to manufacture.
context:
[^fn-lca-hardware-footprint]: **Life cycle assessment (LCA)**\index{Life cycle assessment!ISO 14040 standard}\index{LCA|see{Life cycle assessment}}: Standardized by ISO 14040/14044, LCA traces environmental impact from raw material extraction through disposal [@iso140402006lca; @iso140442006lca]. For AI hardware, LCA separates embodied manufacturing emissions from operational energy use, making hardware refresh cycles and accelerator lifespan extension first-order sustainability levers that operational efficiency alone cannot substitute.

Each of the four lifecycle stages\index{Life cycle assessment!AI system lifecycle} adds its burden through a distinct physical mechanism (@fig-ai-lca). System design fixes much of the lifetime load, manufacturing embeds carbon, water, and chemical burdens during fabrication, operation draws grid electricity for training and serving, and decommissioning produces electronic waste unless hardware is refurbished or its components recovered.

title: Semiconductor Water Cycle
caption: **Semiconductor Water Cycle**: Intake supplies process water; treatment returns part of the flow for reuse. Recycling can reduce freshwater withdrawal, while evaporation and other unreturned flows determine consumption. State the denominator of any reuse fraction.
alt: A watershed band on the left supplies a withdrawal arrow to intake, which flows through ultrapure water treatment to fab processing. Fab processing sends water down to wastewater treatment and loses evaporation to a consumed box on the right, drawn as the focal element with a brown tint and heavy outline. Wastewater treatment sends a green reused flow back to intake, an unreturned flow to the consumed box, and a discharged flow back to the watershed.
context:
Semiconductor fabrication uses ultrapure water for chemical-mechanical planarization, wet etching, and wafer rinsing [@cooper2011].[^fn-fab-water-consumption] Complete environmental accounting requires auditing gross process flow, freshwater withdrawal, recycled volume, and evaporative consumption as distinct quantities, because internal reuse and flows that leave the facility change different totals (@fig-water-cycle). Treatment returns reclaimed water to the intake stream and can reduce freshwater withdrawal, whereas evaporation remains a consumptive loss within the local water account. That classification does not mean the water permanently disappears from the hydrological cycle.

[^fn-fab-water-consumption]: **Semiconductor water scale**\index{Semiconductor water scale!definition}\index{Semiconductor fabrication!water consumption}: A fab water inventory must separate intake, internal reuse, discharge, and consumption. Water per usable die depends on process flow, yield, allocation, and site conditions; a smaller process-node label does not establish a universal per-die multiplier.

title: IoT Device Growth
caption: **IoT Device Growth**: Connected devices worldwide, with historical counts through 2023 (unhatched) and projections from 2024 onward (hatched) [@Statista_2022]. The counts describe the connected-device ecosystem, not the number of AI systems or the amount of e-waste. Waste generation also depends on service lifetimes, repair, reuse, and disposal.
alt: Bar chart showing IoT device growth from 8.6 billion in 2019 to projected 29.42 billion in 2030. Steady annual increases of approximately 2 billion devices per year. Hatched bars mark projected values from 2024 onward, and value labels appear only on 2019, 2023, and 2030.
context:
Memory capacity, bandwidth, and interconnect compatibility can motivate replacement before accelerators physically fail. In tightly integrated systems, a new accelerator generation may require baseboard, networking, or server changes; PCIe-based designs can offer different upgrade options. Evaluate the actual compatibility boundary and reuse path. Replacement does not automatically mean disposal, and a functioning retired node may remain useful for less demanding workloads.

The deployment of **embedded AI**\index{Embedded AI!definition} integrates inference into edge appliances and consumer electronics. The broader connected-device fleet\index{IoT!device growth} (@fig-iot-number) grew from an estimated 8.6 billion devices in 2019 to 15.1 billion in 2023, with 29.4 billion projected by 2030 [@Statista_2022]. These counts indicate the scale of the device ecosystem, not the number of AI systems or the amount of e-waste. Waste generation also depends on service life, repair, and reuse. Adhesive enclosures, nonreplaceable batteries, and proprietary components can make repair difficult, increasing the risk that a limited failure leads to whole-device disposal [@Balde_2017].

title: Interventions and Their Accounting Boundaries
caption: **Interventions and Their Accounting Boundaries**: Work and execution changes affect IT energy; facility overhead converts that energy to a facility total. A chosen grid factor converts electricity to emissions, while hardware lifecycle emissions enter separately. Evaluate the complete configuration at fixed useful work rather than multiplying unrelated improvement factors.
alt: A vertical chain from fixed useful work through IT energy, a multiply-by-PUE node, facility energy, a multiply-by-kg-CO2e-per-kWh node, electricity carbon, an add-embodied node, and the lifecycle account. The first two tiers sit on a band labeled kWh and the last two on a band labeled kg CO2e. Lever boxes on the left point at what each one changes: work reduction and execution efficiency at IT energy, facility overhead at the PUE node, grid factor at the carbon-factor node, and hardware lifecycle at the embodied node.
context:
[^fn-jevons-efficiency-paradox]: **Jevons paradox**\index{Jevons paradox!definition}: @jevons1865coal described how efficiency could stimulate demand enough to increase total coal use. Price reductions alone do not establish either energy factor; measure both unit energy and demand.

Each mitigation lever acts at one accounting tier (@fig-energy-intervention). Work reduction and execution efficiency change IT energy. Facility overhead scales that energy to the facility total. A regional grid factor converts facility kilowatt-hours into operational carbon. Hardware amortization adds embodied emissions at its own boundary. Because these terms carry different units and compound at different layers, isolated efficiency percentages cannot be multiplied into a single composite reduction factor.

title: Jevons Paradox in AI Workloads
caption: **Jevons Paradox in AI Workloads**: A schematic elastic demand curve. When unit cost falls from $\ComputeUnitCost_0$ to $\ComputeUnitCost_1$, demand grows from $\ComputeDemandVolume_0$ to $\ComputeDemandVolume_1$. The green rectangle is the expenditure saved on the original volume; the red rectangle is the expenditure on added volume at the lower unit cost. In this schematic, the red area exceeds the green. These areas represent energy only if unit cost changes proportionally to energy per operation; an emissions comparison also requires carbon intensity.
alt: Demand curve on axes of unit cost versus AI compute volume. Cost drops from P0 to P1 while volume grows from Q0 to Q1. A green rectangle marks savings on base volume, a larger red rectangle marks expenditure on added volume, and a gray rectangle marks retained base volume.
context:
:::

Rebound can cancel a reduction at any of these tiers. On an elastic demand curve ($\DemandPriceElasticity> 1$), a fall in unit cost raises volume enough to outweigh the saving (@fig-jevons-ai). When unit cost falls from $\ComputeUnitCost_0$ to $\ComputeUnitCost_1$, the green shaded area represents the saving on baseline volume $\ComputeDemandVolume_0$. Demand expands to $\ComputeDemandVolume_1$, creating a red area ($\ComputeUnitCost_1 (\ComputeDemandVolume_1 - \ComputeDemandVolume_0)$) that exceeds the original saving in this schematic. With monetary unit cost on the vertical axis, the areas measure expenditure. They represent energy only under an additional assumption that unit cost changes in proportion to energy per operation; an emissions comparison also needs the applicable carbon intensity.

title: A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule
caption: **A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule**: Three constraints share one time axis. The job waits, checkpointed, through the high-carbon hours of the grid signal and runs in the low-carbon window only where cluster headroom exists, finishing with slack before the deadline. The equation below the timeline charges the shift for its checkpoint, idle-wait, and migration carbon, so waiting pays only when the avoided emissions exceed those terms. The curve is schematic, not a measured grid trace.
alt: Timeline with three lanes over a shared time axis. The top lane shows a schematic grid carbon curve with a shaded high-carbon peak and a later low-carbon trough. The job lane shows a dashed waiting arrow, then a green block running under the trough, then a slack block before a red dashed deadline line. The capacity lane shows a hatched busy period followed by available headroom. An equation below sums integrated power times carbon intensity with checkpoint, idle, and migration terms.
context:
Google's carbon-intelligent computing platform\index{Carbon-aware scheduling!results} illustrates this approach by using forecasts and virtual capacity limits to delay flexible work [@radovanovic2021carbonaware]. In the multi-tier accounting cascade of @fig-energy-intervention, temporal load shifting modulates the grid emissions factor applied to facility electricity rather than reducing raw compute FLOPs. That is a carbon intervention, not automatically an energy reduction; checkpointing, transfer, and a different runtime can also change electricity consumption.

Because a scheduler asks how moving a job changes emissions, it needs a marginal signal\index{Carbon-aware scheduling!marginal vs. average emissions} rather than the average factor an inventory uses, and the providers compared above expose signals with different methodologies and coverage. A feasible schedule must satisfy three constraints on one time axis at once, the grid carbon signal $\text{CO}_{2,\text{grid}}(\TimeInstant)$, the job's execution state, and cluster headroom $\ClusterHeadroom(\TimeInstant)$ (@fig-carbon-aware-scheduling). The job waits, checkpointed, through the high-carbon peak, runs for $\JobDuration$ in a low-carbon trough where headroom exists, and still finishes with slack before its deadline. Waiting pays only when the avoided grid emissions exceed the checkpoint I/O, idle standby, and state migration that the wait itself causes.

Renewable generation variability complicates batch training dispatch across power grids. Over one week of November 2023, the European Union's hourly generation mix moved across days as well as within each day (@fig-europe-energy-grid). Demand peaked each day between `{python} EuropeGridWeek.load_peak_low_gw_str` and `{python} EuropeGridWeek.load_peak_high_gw_str`. Nuclear held near `{python} EuropeGridWeek.nuclear_mean_gw_str`, solar contributed midday output, and wind ranged from `{python} EuropeGridWeek.wind_min_gw_str` on `{python} EuropeGridWeek.wind_min_day_str` to `{python} EuropeGridWeek.wind_max_gw_str` on `{python} EuropeGridWeek.wind_max_day_str`. Wind contributes to that variation, but demand, other generation, storage, and electricity exchanges also affect fossil dispatch. Carbon-aware scheduling therefore needs regional grid forecasts rather than a fixed assumption about which hours are cleanest.

title: Ethical AI Concerns
caption: **Ethical AI Concerns**: The distributional concerns raised by AI infrastructure fall into four groups. Environmental justice, intergenerational equity, and resource competition stand on the transparency layer, because each can be assessed only with the per-model energy, carbon, and water records that the transparency gap leaves undisclosed. That layer, drawn with the heavier outline, is the one engineering telemetry addresses most directly.
alt: Three light neutral cards across the top, titled environmental justice, intergenerational equity, and resource competition, each listing its terms: water withdrawal and grid strain; CO2 persistence and long-lived infrastructure; agricultural and municipal claims on land, water, and minerals. Below them a wide band with a heavier dark outline, titled transparency gap and marked as where engineering acts, holds one shared set of per-model records, a single centered row of energy, carbon, and water columns whose dashed cells read undisclosed. A single gray trunk rises from the band, labeled assessed with telemetry, and branches into one arrow up to each of the three cards.
context:
[^fn-siting-environmental-justice]: **Environmental justice in data center siting**\index{Environmental justice in data center siting!definition}: A site-cost model can omit burdens borne by nearby residents, such as competing water demand or changes to local infrastructure. A low financial cost therefore does not establish a low community burden. Site evaluation must identify who benefits, who bears the resource costs, and how affected communities participate in the decision alongside the analysis of grid intensity and water stress.

These distributional concerns fall into four groups (@fig-ethical-ai). Environmental justice concerns local water withdrawal and grid strain. Intergenerational equity concerns atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$ persistence and long-lived infrastructure. Resource competition concerns agricultural and municipal claims on land, water, and minerals. The transparency gap concerns undisclosed per-model energy, carbon, and water records. Engineering acts most directly on the last group, because auditable telemetry is what allows the other three to be assessed at all; the measurement contract of @sec-sustainable-ai-part-ii-measurement-assessment-fb0b supplies that telemetry.

title: Assurance Case Structure
caption: **Assurance Case Structure**: Evidence supports a claim only through an explicit argument and only within stated assumptions. An accountable owner turns the claim into a launch decision, and a material change named by the invalidation rule expires that approval, so the case is a versioned artifact rather than a one-time sign-off.
alt: Inside a light frame labeled assurance case, one stated use and operating envelope, four green evidence tiles (disaggregated results, audit reports, decision logs, documentation) join into one arrow to an argument box, which points to a blue claim box, which points to a violet accountable owner box above a violet launch decision box listing launch, restrict, and reject. A dashed assumptions strip listing population, setting, and suppliers sits beneath the argument and claim, joined to both by dotted lines. Below the frame, a material change box points to a red invalidation rule box, and a dashed red arrow labeled approval expires runs from it up to the launch decision.
context:
Constraint selection needs an explicit division of authority. Domain experts and affected parties identify consequential harms and acceptable uses; policy and legal specialists identify applicable obligations; engineers determine what can be measured and enforced. The accountable launch authority approves the resulting criteria and records unresolved disagreements. A convenient metric or an available implementation does not authorize the engineering team to choose whose errors matter most.

The resulting assurance case is not a single compliance document, but a versioned set of linked artifacts that structure accountability across the system lifecycle. At its foundation sits an explicit *claim* defining the property required for a specified use and operating envelope. An *argument* articulates how operational controls and empirical observations justify that claim, drawing on *evidence* from reproducible evaluations, audits, access logs, documentation, and user research. These claims and arguments hold only under stated *assumptions* regarding environmental, population, supplier, and workflow boundaries. To ensure operational authority, every assurance case specifies an accountable *owner* empowered to block launch, restrict use, or require remediation. An explicit *invalidation rule* governs that authority. It defines the measurable performance change, distribution shift, or operational incident that expires prior approval and triggers reassessment. Evidence reaches the claim only through the argument and only inside the stated assumptions, and the owner's launch decision lasts only until the invalidation rule fires (@fig-assurance-case).

title: Conditional Fairness Trade-Offs
caption: **Conditional Fairness Trade-Offs**: For score-based prediction, calibration within groups and equal mean scores within both outcome classes cannot all hold with unequal base rates and imperfect prediction. Equal base rates or perfect prediction are exceptional cases. This score-balance theorem is distinct from checking equalized odds at one decision threshold.
alt: Two Venn diagrams of three overlapping circles labeled calibration within groups, balance in the Y equals 1 class, and balance in the Y equals 0 class. In panel a, unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, the central region where all three circles overlap is hatched red and marked with the empty-set symbol, labeled all three cannot hold. In panel b, equal base rates or perfect prediction, the same central region is filled green and marked all 3, labeled all three can hold.
context:
\SecondGroupQualifiedFraction$, which differ whenever $\FirstGroupQualifiedFraction\neq \SecondGroupQualifiedFraction$, so demographic parity fails; they match only at $\QualifiedAdmissionRate= 0$. The no-unqualified-admissions rule fixes each group's false positive rate at zero, so equal opportunity here coincides with equalized odds, and parity holds only when each group's true positive rate also falls to zero. That is the definition's condition (true positive rate equal to false positive rate) in concrete form. Relaxing the rule removes the conflict, because admitting some unqualified Group B applicants can raise Group B's overall rate to Group A's. Which constraint to give up is a value judgment about the decision, not a property the model can settle.

The fairness impossibility theorem (principle \ref{pri-fairness-impossibility}) is the canonical result, and it concerns scores rather than decisions. It joins the groupwise calibration of @sec-responsible-ai-calibration-8b73 to score balance, which requires equal average scores across groups among people with positive outcomes and, separately, among people with negative outcomes. With unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, all three requirements cannot hold together [@kleinberg2016inherent]. The admissions conflict concerns decisions and this result concerns scores, so they constrain different criteria. The score result also does not say that a calibrated score can never meet equalized odds at a particular threshold; that is a third, narrower question. Satisfying one criterion may preclude another, so engineers must treat fairness metrics like latency budgets, explicit trade-offs chosen by stakeholders, enforced by the system, and monitored for violation. Determining which metric to prioritize requires careful consideration of the application context, potential harms, and stakeholder values as detailed in @sec-responsible-ai-normative-pluralism-value-conflicts-d61f [@barocas-hardt-narayanan]. Whenever base rates differ and predictions remain imperfect, group calibration, positive-class score balance, and negative-class score balance converge on an infeasible joint state (@fig-fairness-impossibility).

title: Fairness Metric Disagreement Across Thresholds
caption: **Fairness Metric Disagreement Across Thresholds**: Three fairness metrics, demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity, computed on synthetic scores for two groups with differing base rates as the classification threshold varies over a nontrivial operating range. At every evaluated threshold, at least one metric is substantially violated, illustrating practical trade-offs among selection-rate, error-rate, and opportunity criteria. Trivial always-positive or always-negative classifiers fall outside the evaluated range. The shaded region marks the largest of the three violations at each threshold.
alt: Line plot of demographic parity (solid), equalized odds (dashed), and equal opportunity (dash-dot) violations against classification threshold from 0.15 to 0.85. A gray shaded area under the highest curve marks the largest violation at each threshold. A dotted horizontal line marks the lowest value of that envelope, an open circle at the right end labeled smallest worst-case gap sits on it, and a hatched band between zero and that line is labeled as a band the worst-case gap never falls into.
context:
:::

The conflict persists as the classification threshold moves. For two groups with unequal base rates, every threshold from 0.15 to 0.85 leaves at least one of demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity substantially violated (@fig-fairness-metric-disagreement). A threshold that reduces one measured gap need not minimize the others, so the policy must specify which criterion governs the decision and evaluate the remaining gaps.

Errors fell after the disparity was published. In August 2018, about six months after the Gender Shades results were published, @raji2019 repeated the audit on the same benchmark. Each of the three companies that had been named had reduced its error on darker-skinned women: IBM from `{python} GenderShadesReaudit.ibm_before_str` to `{python} GenderShadesReaudit.ibm_after_str` percent, Face++ from `{python} GenderShadesReaudit.facepp_before_str` to `{python} GenderShadesReaudit.facepp_after_str`, and Microsoft from `{python} GenderShadesReaudit.msft_before_str` to `{python} GenderShadesReaudit.msft_after_str` (@fig-gender-shades-audit). title: Threshold-Dependent Fairness
caption: **Threshold-Dependent Fairness**: Varying classification thresholds across subgroups allows equal true positive rates but introduces complexity in model serving and requires access to sensitive attributes at inference time. Achieving fairness requires careful consideration of subgroup-specific performance, as a single threshold may disproportionately impact certain groups, highlighting the tension between accuracy and equitable outcomes in machine learning systems.
alt: Two stacked panels, each with a blue band for Subgroup A and an amber band for Subgroup B holding plus markers for qualified applicants and open circles for defaults along a 0 to 1 score axis, with the approval region at or above each threshold shaded darker. Panel a draws one dashed threshold at 0.75 across both bands and lists TPR 75 percent for Subgroup A and 25 percent for Subgroup B. Panel b draws a threshold at 0.75 in the Subgroup A band and at 0.45 in the Subgroup B band and lists TPR 75 percent for both.
context:
:::

A separate illustrative loan scenario partitions applicants into Subgroup A (higher score distribution, blue band) and Subgroup B (lower score distribution, amber band), and the summary panels of @fig-fairness-example contrast two operating regimes. Applying a single global threshold ($\ClassificationThreshold = 0.75$) approves qualified applicants in Subgroup B at only 25 percent TPR compared to 75 percent for Subgroup A, a threefold opportunity disparity. Conversely, shifting to group-adapted thresholds ($\FirstGroupClassificationThreshold= 0.75$ for Subgroup A and $\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold= 0.45$ for Subgroup B) equalizes true positive rates at 75 percent. That policy requires the authorized decision component to access the relevant group attribute and log the governing threshold. Neither the attribute lookup nor the policy decision must run on the client, but the system must preserve evidence explaining why identical scores receive different decisions.

title: Production Responsible AI Architecture
caption: **Production Responsible AI Architecture**: The request path performs access controls, minimization, and inference. Bounded evidence collection feeds asynchronous fairness monitoring and explanation services. Delayed outcomes support label-dependent metrics; a governed update path returns approved changes to serving.
alt: Two lanes. The synchronous request path, labeled inside the serving SLO, runs request, access control and minimization, inference, and response. Inference writes one green tile per decision into an evidence log of bounded records. Beneath it a row of delayed-label tiles is filled for older decisions, marked outcome known, and dashed for recent ones, marked pending. In the asynchronous governance lane, the evidence log feeds explanations and parity metrics, the known labels feed error-rate metrics, and all three feed a release gate with a named owner, from which a dashed approved-update arrow returns to inference.
context:
#### Real-time fairness monitoring architecture {#sec-responsible-ai-realtime-fairness-monitoring-architecture-15ee}

Implementing responsible AI principles in production systems requires architectural patterns that integrate fairness monitoring, explainability, and privacy controls directly into the model serving infrastructure. The infrastructure separates into two decoupled tiers (@fig-responsible-ai-architecture). A synchronous request path enforces access control, data minimization, and low-latency inference, while an asynchronous governance tier ingests bounded execution evidence and delayed labels to drive fairness auditing, post-hoc explanations, and owner-governed release gates.

title: Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training
caption: **Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training**: Each protection holds only at its own boundary. Raw records stay on clients, secure aggregation protects individual updates under its protocol assumptions, and central differential privacy bounds the released model relative to the specified privacy unit, provided the curator is trusted. Neither implies a universal ordering of privacy strength.
alt: Three client cards, each holding a grid of raw-record tiles that stay on the device and a small bar chart of update values clipped at a dashed clip line. Each client sends its update into a secure aggregation region, where the updates appear as uniformly hatched masked bars that merge into a summation node; the region is labeled bounded collusion, dropout. The sum enters a dotted trusted curator region, where an aggregate bar chart gains gray noise segments and a privacy accountant meter shows some budget segments spent per release. Only an arrow to the released model crosses a dashed vertical line marked public.
context:
The constraint the table cannot show is that privacy claims must name their boundary. Differentially private training bounds training-data leakage through the released model; ordinary inference on fixed weights remains within that post-processing guarantee. It does not protect new private inputs copied into service logs or unrelated private-data accesses. Interface design, retention rules, rate limiting, and access control address those separate exposures. Opaque data collection can also violate user expectations, making consent surfaces and clear disclosure part of the privacy architecture.

Federated training draws three such boundaries (@fig-privacy-risk-flow). Raw records stay on the client, secure aggregation hides individual updates only under its collusion and dropout assumptions, and central differential privacy bounds what the released model reveals only if the curator that adds the noise is trusted. Each protection covers a different quantity against a different observer, so a claim about one says nothing about the others. The privacy unit, clipping rule, protocol assumptions, and composition across rounds define each guarantee [@bonawitz2017; @dwork2014].\index{Privacy!preserving machine learning pipeline}

title: Model Update Strategies
caption: **Model Update Strategies**: Three approaches to removing a data point's influence. Full retraining gives exact unlearning at the highest cost; gradient ascent provides an approximate update by maximizing loss on the forget set; and SISA training partitions data into shards so only the affected shard is retrained. The accompanying cost model quantifies the full-retraining and SISA cases.
alt: Three panels, each showing the same grid of training-data tiles. Full retraining: every retained tile is shaded as recomputed and the two forget-set tiles are dashed as removed, feeding train from scratch on retained data; guarantee exact, recompute whole model. Gradient ascent: only the two forget-set tiles are shaded as recomputed, feeding an ascent step theta plus eta times the gradient of the loss; guarantee approximate, recompute forget-set passes. SISA sharding: the grid splits into shards S1, S2, and S3; only S3, which held the removed forget-set tiles, is shaded and retrained while S1 and S2 are kept; guarantee exact, recompute one shard, serving by shard vote. A key below names recomputed, untouched, forget set, and forget set removed.
context:
Privacy preservation does not end at training time. In many real-world systems, users may have rights to revoke consent or request deletion of their data, even after a model has been trained and deployed [@gdpr2016; @california2023ccpa]. When the approved response requires removing training influence, the architecture must support the chosen method and its verification. An endpoint without sufficient data, training state, or compute may need a replacement model trained elsewhere; a device with the required resources may perform the work locally. Placement follows those requirements rather than the deployment label alone.

Full retraining requires access to the permitted remaining training data and a defined training procedure. Three update strategies differ in what they recompute and what removal they guarantee (@fig-machine-unlearning). Retraining from scratch on the retained data, the training set with the forget set $\ForgetDataset$ removed, supplies a reference for exact removal relative to that procedure. Gradient ascent on the forget set increases its loss through updates of the form $\ModelParameters + \LearningRate \nabla \LossFunction$, but increased loss alone does not demonstrate removal. Sharded, isolated, sliced, and aggregated (SISA) training partitions data into isolated shards $\SisaTrainingShard_1, \SisaTrainingShard_2, \SisaTrainingShard_3$ and aggregates their predictions. A deletion affects the constituent model trained on its shard; saved states before the affected slice can reduce the retraining work.

title: Model Interpretability Spectrum
caption: **Model Interpretability Spectrum**: A heuristic ordering by model family. Small linear models and shallow decision trees can offer transparent reasoning, while neural networks typically require post-hoc explanation techniques; size, feature meaning, and audience can move any model along the spectrum. This distinction guides model selection based on application needs, prioritizing transparency in regulated domains or when stakeholder trust is important. The label under each family names the handle an explanation typically uses.
alt: Six model families in a row above a double-headed axis running from more interpretable to less interpretable, each with a small structural sketch whose explanation handle is drawn dark. Sparse linear models: a few nonzero coefficient bars, coefficients. Small decision trees: one highlighted split path, split paths. Prototype and concept models: an input linked to its matching exemplar, exemplars. Tree ensembles: six small trees, each with one dark root-to-leaf path, TreeSHAP. Deep neural networks: dense layers with shaded input nodes, gradients and SHAP. Foundation models: a deep layer stack with a probe reading one layer, probing. Brackets group the first two as interpretable by design, the third as hybrid, and the last three as needing post-hoc explanation.
context:
Inherently interpretable models\index{Inherently interpretable model!transparency by design} expose a decision structure that the intended audience can inspect. Small decision trees, short rule lists, and sparse linear models with meaningful features can support this goal; a large tree or high-dimensional linear model may not. Nearest-neighbor comparisons likewise require an understandable similarity metric and representative examples. Interpretability therefore depends on structure, features, and audience, not merely the model-family label. In high-stakes applications, model selection should evaluate whether a sufficiently accurate, inspectable model meets the task before assuming that post-hoc explanations are necessary [@rudin2019].

Six common model families fall along an interpretability continuum in three groups (@fig-vol2-interpretability-spectrum). Sparse linear models (explained via coefficients) and small decision trees (via split paths) are interpretable by design. Prototype and concept models are hybrid architectures explained via exemplars. Tree ensembles (via TreeSHAP), deep networks (via gradients and SHAP), and foundation models (via probing) require post-hoc explanation. While this ordering provides a structural heuristic across model families, dimensionality and scale can shift boundaries; a million-node decision tree or dense linear regression can prove just as opaque as a deep neural network. This distinction is central to choosing an appropriate model for a given application, particularly in settings where regulatory scrutiny or stakeholder trust is essential.

title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline
caption: **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline**: The top lane carries the policy from a pretrained model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and proximal policy optimization (PPO) to the aligned policy. The bottom lane turns human judgment into an objective: raters compare sampled SFT outputs, and those comparisons train a reward model whose score drives PPO. The SFT model also serves as the KL reference that limits how far PPO moves the policy, so every human preference reaches the weights only through the learned reward model.
alt: Two lanes. Policy lane: pretrained model, supervised fine-tuning, RL fine-tuning with PPO, and aligned policy, joined by arrows, with a dashed arrow labeled KL reference running over the top from supervised fine-tuning to PPO. Human judgment lane: a stack of human raters feeds a stack of preference pairs, each showing outputs y1 and y2 with y1 preferred, which trains a reward model r of x and y drawn as the one dark filled box. Only two arrows cross between lanes: a dashed arrow labeled sampled outputs from supervised fine-tuning down to the preference pairs, and a heavy arrow labeled reward signal, the only path to weights, from the reward model up to PPO.
context:
control surfaces {#sec-responsible-ai-responsibility-generative-era-3c3e}

A binary loan classifier has two possible outputs to audit. A large language model (LLM) such as Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), by contrast, can be steered by a user prompt or a poisoned retrieved document into generating defamatory claims, leaking personal data, or refusing benign requests from one dialect more often than another. Generative AI does not replace core fairness, privacy, and explainability concerns; it changes the control surface. Instead of only auditing labels or feature attributions, operators must govern prompts, retrieved context, reward models, and open-ended outputs. Fairness remains concerned with how quality, refusals, errors, representation, and access are distributed across people and groups, but open-ended outputs make those quantities harder to define and sample. Alignment introduces a separate problem, which is keeping stochastic outputs and actions consistent with intended objectives and policies across a combinatorial range of prompts. The two questions differ in kind. Fairness asks how benefits, errors, and burdens are distributed among affected people; alignment asks whether an optimizing system pursues the objective its designers and legitimate stakeholders intended. An aligned system can implement an unfair objective faithfully, and a statistically fair classifier can still optimize the wrong social goal, so production systems need both fairness evaluation and behavioral alignment rather than relabeling one as the other. A common multi-stage alignment pipeline runs in two coupled lanes (@fig-rlhf-pipeline). An upper execution path advances the policy from pretraining through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to proximal policy optimization (PPO), and a lower supervision path uses human preference comparisons to train a reward model $\RewardModel(\ModelInput, \GeneratedResponse)$. The reward signal drives PPO updates, while the frozen SFT checkpoint supplies a reference for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence penalty. The penalty discourages departure from that reference; it does not impose a hard bound on every response or establish policy compliance.

title: Reward Hacking Loop
caption: **Reward Hacking Loop**: Maximizing measurable rewards, like clicks, can incentivize unintended model behaviors that undermine the intended goal of user satisfaction. In the illustrated possible feedback loop, the recommender serves content and the resulting clicks enter later training data. If optimizing clicks rewards behavior that undermines long-term user value, retraining can reinforce the mismatch. Establishing this mechanism requires evidence about the deployed policy and the user-value criterion; targeting a proxy does not by itself prove that it has ceased to provide useful information.
alt: A circular loop of four boxes joined by curved arrows: ML recommender, optimizes the proxy, serves served content, clickbait and outrage, which elicits clicks, which are logged as training data, which retrains the recommender. The center of the loop reads loop closes on the proxy. Outside the loop, a proxy metric box, maximize clicks, sends reward down to the recommender, and a true goal box, long-term user value, points to the proxy labeled measured by. A dashed red arrow labeled undermines runs from served content to the true goal.
context:
Recommendation systems illustrate why a measurable engagement proxy such as click-through rate (CTR) or watch time\index{Optimization!ctr, proxy misalignment} needs evaluation against broader user welfare. A published production architecture optimizes expected watch time [@covington2016], while a separate audit examines recommendation paths through politically extreme content [@ribeiro2020]. Those observations motivate investigating proxy misalignment; together they do not prove that a particular reward objective caused an individual user's beliefs or behavior. Specification gaming and reward hacking[^fn-reward-hacking-specification] describe the risk that optimizing a measured objective defeats its intended purpose [@amodei2016concrete]. Goodhart's law\index{Goodhart's law!proxy optimization} names the general pattern, in which a measure that becomes a target stops measuring what it was chosen for [@goodhart1984]. In one possible feedback mechanism, engagement rewards content that undermines long-term user value, and the resulting interactions become new training data (@fig-reward-hacking-loop). Establishing that mechanism in a deployment requires evidence about both the policy's effects and the welfare criterion it is meant to serve.

[^fn-reward-hacking-specification]: **Reward hacking**\index{Reward hacking!value misalignment}: When an AI system maximizes its reward function through unintended means that violate designer intent. A hypothetical cleaning robot rewarded for collected dirt might create messes it can clean up, illustrating how a proxy can reward behavior contrary to the intended task. Specification gaming\index{Specification gaming!objective design} is an overlapping term; the gap may lie in the stated objective or in its implementation, so neither term is restricted to software bugs. For production ML systems, reward hacking manifests subtly, as in recommendation models that maximize engagement by promoting addictive content, or chatbots that maximize helpfulness ratings by being sycophantic rather than accurate. The failure mode scales with model capability.

title: Measured Driverless Exposure and Crash Rates
caption: **Measured Driverless Exposure and Crash Rates**: (a) Cumulative rider-only miles, driven with no human driver, by Waymo's fleet in its published releases from June 2024 to June 2026. (b) Crash outcomes per million miles through June 2026 for that driving (red) and for Waymo's human-driver benchmark on the same roads (gray), with 95 percent confidence intervals on a logarithmic axis. Lower rates still produce a growing number of incidents as exposure grows. Benchmarks follow the method of @kusano2024waymo; data from @waymo2026safetyimpact.
alt: Two stacked panels. Top: cumulative rider-only miles in millions rising from about 22 in June 2024 to about 271 in June 2026, steepening over time. Bottom: horizontal dot plot on a logarithmic axis of incidents per million miles for five outcomes, each with a red Waymo point and a gray human-benchmark point with confidence intervals. Police-reported crashes are about 1.4 against 5.6, any injury about 0.67 against 3.8, airbag deployment about 0.29 against 1.6, serious injury or worse about 0.011 against 0.21, and fatal about 0.007 against 0.027, where the Waymo interval is wide.
context:
:::

Exposure is the multiplier that turns a small per-mile rate into many incidents. Waymo's driverless fleet logged about `{python} DriverlessExposure.first_miles_str` million rider-only miles by June 2024 and `{python} DriverlessExposure.last_miles_str` million by June 2026, a `{python} DriverlessExposure.growth_mult_str` increase in two years (@fig-autonomous-miles-scaling, panel a) [@waymo2026safetyimpact]. Its published crash rates sit well below a human-driver benchmark on the same roads, for example `{python} DriverlessExposure.injury_rate_str` injury crashes per million miles against `{python} DriverlessExposure.injury_bench_str` (panel b) [@waymo2026safetyimpact]. At that exposure its vehicles were still involved in `{python} DriverlessExposure.injury_count_str` injury crashes and `{python} DriverlessExposure.fatal_count_str` fatal ones, so a fleet's safety case must budget for incidents in absolute numbers as well as in rates. At any constant per-mile rate, a `{python} DriverlessExposure.growth_mult_str` rise in exposure raises the expected cumulative incident count by the same factor, even though no individual vehicle became less safe. The count is an expectation, not a realized outcome, and it is cumulative; an operator sizing weekly incident-response capacity needs weekly mileage instead.

title: Bias Amplification Feedback Loop
caption: **Bias Amplification Feedback Loop**: When ML systems retrain on their own outputs, historical bias in training data propagates through model predictions, downstream outcomes, and reinforced data before feeding back as even more biased retraining data. The edges ('trains on', 'produces', 'creates', 'feeds into') show a possible reinforcing mechanism, not a guarantee that every iteration increases disparity. Green intervention arrows mark where preprocessing (data audit and reweighting), in-processing (fairness constraints), and postprocessing (threshold calibration) can break the cycle.
alt: A circular loop of four boxes joined by curved navy arrows labeled trains on, produces, creates, and feeds into: biased training data, biased model predictions, disparate outcomes (the only red box), and reinforced bias in new data; the center reads possible reinforcing loop. Three green intervention boxes each send an arrow to a green bar that cuts one arc: preprocessing, audit and reweight, cuts the feeds into arc; in-processing, fairness constraints, cuts the trains on arc; postprocessing, threshold calibration, cuts the produces arc.
context:
The sociotechnical feedback invariant (principle \ref{pri-sociotechnical-feedback}) captures this dynamic. Deployed models shape the environment they operate in, so that future data $\ProbabilityFunction_{\FeedbackStepIndex+1}(\ModelInput)$ is a function of the model's past decisions $\ModelPredictor_{\FeedbackStepIndex}(\ModelInput)$. Here, $\ModelInput$ is the model's input, as in $\BinaryClassifier(\ModelInput)$ earlier in the chapter; $\ProbabilityFunction_{\FeedbackStepIndex}(\ModelInput)$ denotes the input distribution observed by the system at time $\FeedbackStepIndex$, while $\ModelPredictor_{\FeedbackStepIndex}(\ModelInput)$ denotes the deployed model or decision policy acting on those inputs. Such systems require closed-loop governance\index{Closed-loop governance!feedback loop dynamics}; reliability requires modeling the closed feedback loop rather than feed-forward inference alone.

Machine learning systems do not merely observe and model the world; they also shape it. Once deployed, their predictions and decisions often influence the environments they are intended to analyze. This feedback alters future data distributions, modifies user behavior, and affects institutional practices, creating a recursive loop between model outputs and system inputs. Over time, such dynamics can amplify biases, entrench disparities, or unintentionally shift the objectives a model was designed to serve. The compounding cycle\index{Bias!amplification feedback loop} passes through four interconnected stages (@fig-bias-amplification), from biased training data through model predictions and disparate real-world outcomes to reinforced bias in newly collected data. The three intervention points of @sec-responsible-ai-bias-detection-mitigation-9174 each cut one arc of the cycle: preprocessing audits and reweighting at data ingestion, in-processing fairness constraints during training, and postprocessing threshold calibration at the serving layer.

title: Layers of Responsibility
caption: **Layers of Responsibility**: Effective human-centered AI implementation requires shared accountability across nested layers. From the core Development Team outward through the Organization, Industry, and Government/Society, each surrounding layer enforces norms the inner layers cannot self-impose. External anchors, including ISO AI management standards, fairness testing, model cards, red-teaming, impact assessments, GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law, bind these layers to practice [@isoiec420012023ai; @gdpr2016; @euaiact2024].
alt: Four nested rectangles around a central AI system box, from outer to inner: government and society, industry, organization, and development team. The tint deepens from the pale outer layer to the inner layer, and the AI system at the center is a dark filled box. Each layer's anchor is written into a gap in its own top boundary, so the norm forms part of the wall: GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law; ISO standards and external audits; impact assessments and ethical review boards; and fairness testing, model cards, and red-teaming.
context:
:::

The responsibility for ethical system behavior is distributed across multiple constituencies, including industry, academia, civil society, and government. The resulting governance hierarchy surrounds the AI system with four concentric tiers (@fig-human-centered-ai). The development team executes technical controls (fairness testing, model cards, red-teaming). The organization governs operational processes (impact assessments, ethical review boards). Industry establishes consensus baselines (ISO standards, external audits). Government and society enforce legal boundaries (GDPR, the EU AI Act, sector-specific statutes) [@shneiderman2022human; @shneiderman2020]. Within organizations, this distribution must be mirrored by mechanisms that connect technical design with strategic oversight and operational control. Without these linkages, responsibility becomes diffuse, and well-intentioned efforts may be undermined by systemic misalignment.

section: Six Principles of Distributed ML Systems {#sec-conclusion-six-principles-distributed-ml-systems-746a}
context:
:::

Placed on the fleet stack, the six principles follow its four bands\index{Fleet Stack!layered architecture}\index{Fleet Stack!working discipline} (@fig-fleet-stack-conclusion). The Infrastructure band determines physical capability. The Distribution band partitions execution and therefore carries both communication and failure recovery, one principle per row. The Serving band bounds runtime delivery by its contract. The uppermost Governance band carries two principles that divide it by obligation rather than strictly by row. Responsibility, placed beside the Assurance row, covers every obligation owed to the people the system affects, including both the security and robustness of the Assurance row and the fairness and accountability work that @sec-responsible-ai develops in the band's top row. Sustainability, placed beside that top row, covers the resource obligation alone. The arrow that runs the length of the stack marks the scale moment. Rather than acting as a seventh principle, it is the premise on which this book opened, and crossing it is what turns each of the six from a local concern into a fleet-wide constraint.

title: Telemetry-First Triage
caption: **Telemetry-First Triage**: An anomaly is traced first to the telemetry source that shows it, then to the specific signal, and only then to the C$^3$ axis that binds. Thermal throttling and PCIe link degradation both lower per-device throughput and so point to compute, credit stalls point to communication, and a single rank that is always last points to coordination. The 85 °C threshold is illustrative.
alt: Four-level tree. A top box, telemetry anomaly, step time or MFU off baseline, splits into node telemetry (MFU, temperature, PCIe errors) and network telemetry (pause frames, credits, step tails). Node telemetry splits into two red signal boxes, thermal throttle (GPU above 85 degrees C) and PCIe AER retries (link width below x16), each leading to a blue box labeled Compute C1, with clock throttling and host link degraded. Network telemetry splits into two red signal boxes, IB credit stalls (PFC pause frames) leading to an amber box labeled Communication C2, fabric congestion, and high tail latency (one rank always last) leading to a violet box labeled Coordination C3, straggler at barrier.
context:
### Diagnostic decision tree {#sec-appdx-c3-diagnostic-tree-details}

Triage starts from whichever telemetry source shows the anomaly and narrows to the specific signal before naming the binding axis (@fig-c3-telemetry-decision-tree). A node-side signal points to the compute axis, while a network-side signal separates fabric congestion, a communication cost, from a single straggler that holds every rank at the barrier, a coordination cost.

title: The Queuing Hockey Stick
caption: **The Queuing Hockey Stick**: For an M/M/1 queue, $\ServingUtilization/(1-\ServingUtilization)$ is the expected number of requests in the system, including the request in service. Its hyperbolic rise near saturation explains why production systems retain utilization headroom; the shaded operating bands are illustrative rather than universal thresholds.
alt: Plot of the expected number of requests in an M/M/1 system versus serving utilization rho_serv from 0 to 1. The curve rises gradually at low utilization, bends upward through illustrative headroom and caution bands, and rises sharply as utilization approaches 1.
context:
2. **Utilization-target threshold (batch size `{python} PrefillServing.b_target_str`)**\index{Batching!utilization headroom}: At `{python} GPT3ServingResults.b8_util_pct_str` utilization, the system meets the `{python} PrefillServing.rho_target_pct_str` target, but queuing delay still contributes substantially to latency (`{python} GPT3ServingResults.b8_wait_ms_str`). The steep occupancy trajectory charted in @fig-queuing-hockey-stick isolates why. Batch sizes between the stability boundary and this threshold push utilization past the $\ServingUtilization \approx 0.80$ hockey-stick knee into the caution band, where queuing delay surges nonlinearly as the curve approaches saturation.
3. **Latency knee (batch sizes `{python} PrefillServing.b_lo_str` to `{python} PrefillServing.b_hi_str`)**\index{Batching!latency knee}: Mean latency is lowest in this range, with the model's minimum near $\BatchSize=$ `{python} PrefillServing.b_best_str`. Batch size `{python} PrefillServing.b_hi_str` trades a few milliseconds of additional total latency for lower utilization and queue wait time (`{python} GPT3ServingResults.b16_wait_ms_str` vs. `{python} GPT3ServingResults.b8_wait_ms_str`), while $\BatchSize=$ `{python} PrefillServing.b_top_str` leaves still more utilization headroom but pays too much batch-accumulation delay.
4. **Diminishing returns (batch sizes beyond `{python} PrefillServing.b_top_str`)**\index{Batching!diminishing returns}: Further batch size increases reduce utilization in this surrogate but increase accumulation delay. The separate KV-cache example below supplies a decode-memory bound; it is not part of this prefill-time calculation.

#### Trade-off curves for visualizing the operating region {#sec-appdx-inference-scale-tradeoff-curves-visualizing-operating-region-9f95}

Batch execution sets two pressures against each other. As batch size $\BatchSize$ grows from 1 to 128, throughput climbs with diminishing returns as fixed overheads are amortized. Batch service time expands steadily, so a latency budget caps how much of the throughput gain a server can take (@fig-batch-tradeoff-curves).
